5006	Going Out to Eat and Drink : Old delis at the centre of the soul system : Delicatessens are the culinary outposts of our European immigrants .
5007	Ellen Galford joins the queues in Scotland to buy heritage over the counter
5008	By ELLEN GALFORD
5009	FOR immigrant communities — Italians , Jews , and others who have the passion for good , simple food bred into their souls — a traditional delicatessen is the centre of the universe .
5010	The name of the old homeland may have been wiped off the map , the native Tuscan village may have mutated into Chiantishire , but in London 's Soho or downtown Manhattan , in Glasgow or in East Coast America 's polyglot suburbs , these are the places where history — private and collective — is still alive .
5011	Originally , the deli was an antidote to culture shock , where all the salt , sweet , hot , sharp , garlicky flavours of home could be conjured up between two pieces of bread .
5012	Meals were eaten on shop premises — noisy , welcoming outposts of the mother country .
5013	To post-war generations , the deli has become a way to stay connected , through the taste buds with their roots .
5014	Scotland 's Italian immigrants have been the most generous and benevolent of culinary missionaries .
5015	Their contributions to the serious arts of fish-frying and ice-cream making are well documented ; they have allayed indigenous suspicion about garlic ; and , in Glasgow and Edinburgh , they have established two of the country 's finest delicatessens .
5016	In Glasgow , Fazzi Brothers ' Caffe-Bar , adjoining the Cambridge Street branch of the family 's 70-year-old delicatessen business , fits in nicely with the Glaswegian notion of la dolce vita : sparky but unhurried conversation , compulsive people-watching , searching critiques of the nearby Sauchiehall Street shoe shops , and comparative study of each other 's purchases , all washed down with copious amounts of coffee and a plate of voluptuous cakes .
5017	In the morning , breakfasts may be classic continental with fresh fruit juice and Italian-style croissants and pastries , or savoury treats such as focaccia — slabs of rich bread dough baked with herbs and olive oil .
5018	The beans for the house coffee are roasted fresh every day in the Fazzis ' other premises in Clyde Street .
5019	By some mysterious alchemy it seems possible to drink two or more cups of the mellow cappuccino or caffe crema without suffering the jangle of caffeine overload .
5020	The espresso , in small cups , is dark and serious and packs a more powerful punch .
5021	Italian-style cold drinks , such as iced coffee granita or a zingy blend of fresh fruit juices and grenadine , are also worth exploring .
5022	For a more serious snack , aficionados make time to study the delicatessen counter before ordering .
5023	Any of the meats , cheeses , marinated vegetables or salads on sale can be made into a custom-designed sandwich .
5024	The charcuterie , with seasonal variations , includes about two dozen different Italian salamis and sausages , Parma ham and the more delicately flavoured San Daniele .
5025	Look out also for such exotica as malegato , an aromatic Italian equivalent of traditional Scots black pudding .
5026	At lunch hours things get busy as customers queue up for the small range of soft pasta dishes and such daily specials as vegetable lasagne or a spicy Italian-sausage casserole — all moderately priced and consistently good .
5027	For those with a sweet tooth ( few Glaswegians are without one ) , the gateaux are suitably elaborate .
5028	As Fazzi Brothers is to Glasgow and the west of Scotland , the magisterial Italian food and wine merchant Valvona and Crolla is to Edinburgh and the east .
5029	Here , unfortunately , no restaurant area is yet available to allow customers to eat what they buy where they buy it , but the time spent waiting for a takeaway sandwich will be an invaluable education in Italian food .
5030	The shop , established in 1934 and now run by the founder 's grandsons , is undoubtedly one of the most important delicatessens in the country , vast in its range of goods and uncompromising in its quality .
5031	Outside , it is easy to miss : the narrow shopfront is identified only by the Italian flags hanging overhead .
5032	Inside , customers thread their way between stacks of every imaginable pasta , pickles and condiments , flasks of vintage olive oils , stacks of imported biscuits , panforte and panettone .
5033	Service is at a counter backed by one of Britain 's most comprehensive collections of serious Italian wines : more than 500 different varieties are on offer .
5034	To the novice first impressions may be chaotic , but the temptation to turn away and come back at some quieter time should be resisted .
5035	There are few , if any , quieter times .
5036	Here again , all the glories of the delicatessen counter — marinated artichokes , sun-dried tomatoes in virgin olive oil , seafood salads and the rich home-made pesto — are available in sandwich form .
5037	Those wanting to voyage further than comparatively familiar delicacies such as coppa , pancetta or fennel-flavoured salami , should look upwards .
5038	At certain times of the year , hanging from the ceiling amid the festoons of dried sausages , cheeses , onions and garlic , will be a haunch of wild boar .
5039	When manager Victor Contini judges that the moment is right , the haunch is brought down to be skinned , boned , cured and thinly sliced like Parma ham .
5040	At £5 per quarter , this rarity is not exactly a budget snack , but with a focaccia still warm from the oven and accompanied by a few herb-steeped olives , it could be the most extraordinary sandwich you ever eat .

5073	Food : Feast of indelicate edibles : Chaim Bermant hankers for herrings
5074	By CHAIM BERMANT
5075	DELICATESSEN , as the name suggests , means delicate edibles , but delicate these edibles are not .
5076	They assault the sense , savage the palate , ravage one 's innards and announce themselves in loud , pungent terms so that one gets wind of them long before one catches sight of them .
5077	But I love them .
5078	Basically they are titbits and are designed to excite the appetite rather than assuage it .
5079	As food they are meant principally for the non-hungry , the non-domesticated , those who can just summon the energies to open a tin of pate de foie gras or unwind a rollmop .
5080	I was born in what is now Russia , and when I came to Scotland shortly before the war the small Jewish grocery shops in the Gorbals district of Glasgow were my main link with home .
5081	I still remember their names : Ixe 's , Fogels , Ettingers , Callendars .
5082	And their wares : huge , steaming loaves of black Russian bread , glossy bagels , crispy pretzels , cinnamon cakes , long , crudely circumcised phallic rolls of salami , pickled gherkins and — their hallmark - open barrels of salt herrings .
5083	I only had to shut my eyes and inhale and I was back in Russia .
5084	To me delicatessen means herring , 1,001 varieties of herring , but I did not always regard them as such if only because I virtually lived on them .
5085	The herring was to the Eastern European Jew what potatoes were to the Irish , which is surprising , for the herring is a salt-water fish and in Russia and Poland one rarely got a glimpse of the sea .
5086	But Jews know a good thing when they taste it and alighted on the herring because it was inexpensive , piquant , nutritious and versatile .
5087	The herring was never quite considered a member of the fish family .
5088	The carp and pike , which were found locally , were kitted out with lavish trimmings and served on the Sabbath and at festivals .
5089	The humble herring was treated as crude workaday fare , and in our household we might have pickled herring on Sunday , soused herring on Monday , herrings in sour cream on Tuesday , schmaltz herring on Wednesday , and herrings fried in matzo meal on Thursday .
5090	When we moved to Scotland I discovered the greatest delicacy of all — the smoked herring , or kipper .
5091	I am sure the warm affinities between Scots and Jews arise out of appreciation of herrings .
5092	I also came upon a mysterious animal I had not seen before : much larger than the herring , redder and infinitely more expensive .
5093	They called it smoked salmon and I immediately concluded it was some sort of rich man 's herring .
5094	The Gorbals is no more and neither are the small Jewish grocery shops .
5095	One is hard pressed even to find them in London .
5096	Instead one has delicatessens which are more brightly lit and infinitely more hygienic than the small corner shops I have known , but with their fridges and freezers and extraction fans they have tamed their wares and robbed them of their pungency .
5097	One 's sense of smell , always deeply involved in the joy of the delicatessen , has been rendered virtually redundant .
5098	But more than that , all the goods , and especially the innumerable varieties of herring , have gone upmarket .
5099	If salmon is still the rich man 's herring , one can no longer think of herrings as the poor man 's salmon for they have become so expensive that one buys them by the troy ounce .
5100	All of which shows that one man 's staple is another man 's delicatessen or , rather , that the necessities of one generation can become the luxuries of the next .

5109	SECATEURS are likely to be the tool most in demand now .

5123	In the Garden : Planning to beat a leafy retreat at home : In the first of a series for novice gardeners , Anna Pavord stresses the value of careful forethought
5124	By ANNA PAVORD
5125	PLANTS should come a long way down the list of priorities for the novice gardener .
5126	There are many things to think about before even the first tentative daffodil bulb is sunk into the ground .
5127	The first and most important question to mull over as you gaze at your patch is : What is this garden for ?
5128	If you start writing down some of the responses to that question , you will find you have along the way acquired a ragbag of elements that will have an important bearing on the design .
5129	If there are small children in the equation , there will need to be a flat , soft area where they can fall off swings and climbing frames .
5130	If you like hanging out washing rather than drying it in the bowels of an expensive machine , you will need to tuck away a line and make a dry path to get to and from it .
5131	Some novice gardeners may not want to do much actual gardening at all , but conversely , do not want to look out every day over a scene of threadbare grass and rotting fence .
5132	Their ideal garden will look good and demand little attention .
5133	If you are a dedicated sun-worshipper , you need to mark out the part of the garden where the sun lingers longest .
5134	It may not be the part nearest the house , though this is where sitting out areas always tend to be made .
5135	You may , even as a novice , care so passionately about plants that all you want is the maximum space to grow them in .
5136	Raised beds built down an unpromising alley could provide extra gardening space .
5137	Privacy is an important consideration .
5138	A first time garden is usually small and certainly the typical one I am imagining for this series is no more than 40ft x 20ft and surrounded on all sides by other houses .
5139	Privacy is a ticklish business where close neighbours are concerned .
5140	To throw up an impenetrable Berlin Wall between you and them could be tactless .
5141	Trellis is a useful compromise and you can always pretend it was forced on you by the speed of growth of your climbing rose .
5142	Aesthetes among the novices will by now be thoroughly irritable and complaining that gardens should have as much to do with the soul as with the necessity or not of a washing line or a barbecue pit .
5143	So they should , and when the list of necessities is securely written down , you can ask the second question : How do I want this garden to feel ?
5144	This question produces as varied a response as the first .
5145	Some urban gardeners , as short of space inside as they are out , want their gardens to be extensions of their homes , with a great deal of hard paving , good furniture and lighting .
5146	The garden for them should feel like an extra sitting room , gnat-ridden perhaps , damp occasionally , but an important overflow of living space .
5147	Closet countrysiders may want to pretend their patch is actually a corner of some Sussex meadow and picture it swagged with honeysuckle and waving with ox-eye daisies and scabious .
5148	This is a difficult trick to bring off with suburban trains hurtling by on one side and lorries grinding through their gears on the other .
5149	A leafy retreat is an excellent goal for a small town garden , but it is best made acknowledging the urban setting , using un-wild plants such as bamboo , acanthus , fig , vine , alchemilla , euphorbia , wisteria .
5150	While you are working through this process , take note of the features in the garden that you would like to keep .
5151	On a new estate , there may be nothing .
5152	In an old garden , there may be a fruit tree , or a good bulwark of evergreen laurel or box that , tidied up , could add a dash of venerability to the new garden that will emerge around it .
5153	If you do not know what a tree or shrub is , exercise clemency and give it a year 's grace to demonstrate its worth before you turn it over to the axeman .
5154	The mood of the garden will dictate its eventual style .
5155	It may be clipped classical , random cottage , modern high-tech , or some intensely personal vision of Byzantium , that no one has ever imagined before , but which exists in your head and wants to get out .
5156	Do not let anybody , particularly gardening writers , tread on your dreams .
5157	All this thinking and doodling will have done nothing physically to change the view outside the window , but it is a vital part of the gardening process .
5158	Before you can make , you have to know what it is you are making .
5159	In the Garden : Drawing the line at great design : Anna Pavord delves into a book that reveals the gardens architects have imagined could accompany their creations
5160	By ANNA PAVORD
5161	THE drawings of the Royal Institute of British Architects form one of the less well-known collections in London .
5162	Architectural historians have already raided it to good effect , notably Mark Girouard for his book on the sixteenth-century architect Robert Smythson and Jill Lever , the curator of the collection , for the book she wrote with Margaret Richardson , The Art of the Architect .
5163	Jane Brown is the latest to emerge triumphant from the RIBA library in Portman Square with The Art and Architecture of English Gardens ( Weidenfeld &amp; Nicolson , £40 ) .
5164	She looks at the collection with a view to its bearing on garden history .
5165	Her book is not a comprehensive history of English garden design , but a much chancier , though equally delightful narrative depending for its emphasis on what happened to find its way into the collection .
5166	These quirks of fate , combined with Jane Brown 's own enthusiasms ( she is the author of a fine book on the Lutyens-Jekyll partnership ) have resulted in a narrative in which the gardens of the Arts and Crafts movement , a relatively short period between 1890-1914 , get twice the space of the gardens of either the eighteenth or the nineteenth century .
5167	This is fine by me .
5168	The talented crew of Voysey , Newton , Baillie Scott , who created the beautifully put together houses of that period , evidently also had the gift of persuasively selling their ideas .
5169	Who could have resisted Charles Voysey 's design for Oakhurst , Ropes Lane , Fernhurst in Sussex ?
5170	A pool of blue scillas lies to the left of an entrance through yew hedges .
5171	The house is softened by sprawls of climbing roses .
5172	Hollyhocks and wallflowers tower over the gaily filled flower border .
5173	His client , Mrs Chester , sensibly did not resist and the house was built in 1901 .
5174	Oliver Hill 's plan ( 1913 ) for the paving of the water garden at Moor Close , Binfield , Berkshire , shows staggering attention to detail .
5175	Red tile set on edge was to be used for the centrepiece , Portland stone for the surround , brown pebble paving for an infill , blue and white pebbles to make a star design , white marble for the path through the pergola .
5176	The plan , beautifully drawn and lettered , as are all the plans of this period , is particularly poignant .
5177	No architect gardeners came this way again .
5178	The story told in Jane Brown 's book does not end with the Arts and Crafts movement , however .
5179	It continues with the relatively little known work of the Modern Movement , curtailed by the war , through the idealistic beginnings of the Span housing estates in the mid-Fifties , to Sir Geoffrey Jellicoe 's plan , now being executed , for the Moody Botanic Gardens at Galveston , Texas .
5180	Sixteen drawings for this massive project form the book 's final chapter ‘ Towards the 21st Century ’ .
5181	After this chronological march through the archives , Jane Brown devotes the second part of her weighty book to the delightfully rich seam of garden buildings and ornament designed over the last 400 years .
5182	Here is Sir Jeffry Wyatville 's design for a Swiss Cottage to be built at the Duke of Bedford 's rural retreat , Endsleigh , Devon .
5183	The ‘ bijou rustic pavilion ’ as he describes it , still survives and has recently been restored by the Landmark Trust .
5184	Here too is Lutyens 's design for a fowl house , a wooden building perched on staddle stones with lantern and a thatched roof , a residence to please the most demanding chicken .
5185	Architectural drawings may seem dry fodder to provide the stuff of an exciting book .
5186	Jane Brown 's gift is to vault the divide that has unfortunately grown up between architects and the rest of us and bring their drawings alive in the most agreeable and informative way .
5187	One does not always agree with her .
5188	She commends Barry for ‘ his ability to build well and to last ’ , but Barry 's work at Kingston Lacey in Dorset and elsewhere was outrageously shoddy .
5189	She credits the Crystal Palace built by Joseph Paxton for the Great Exhibition in 1851 as the inspiration for later conservatories and ‘ the whole future of growing plants indoors ’ .
5190	The revolution in glasshouses had surely started rather earlier than that with the radical design built in 1820 by W&amp;D Bailey of Holborn for Lady Rolle at Bicton in Devon .
5191	But these are quibbles , and in no way detract from Jane Brown 's achievement .
5192	This is a fascinating book .

5201	Property : Forward Planning : Making Proposals : Influencing the decision-makers : Allison Flight fills in the background to a planning application
5202	By ALLISON FLIGHT
5203	THE planning system is designed around the idea that people should have a say in what happens to their immediate surroundings .
5204	But how do you find out about whether a planning application has been made in the first place ?
5205	Whether you are proposing or opposing an application , what is the best way to influence the decision that is eventually made ?
5206	Finding out about an application : Under section 28 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1971 the planning authority — usually the local council — is supposed to advertise certain planning applications in the local newspaper .
5207	The proposals covered are development in a conservation area , works to a listed building or which affect the setting of a conservation area or a listed building , and developments in Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty .
5208	The planning authority also has to advertise locally any proposals involving large buildings ( those more than 20 metres high ) , or any ‘ unneighbourly uses ’ — such as a casino , scrap yard , cemetery or slaughterhouse — and put up a notice on the site itself .
5209	Some local authorities publish a list of all their new planning applications in the local paper .
5210	Often they circulate these lists to local conservation and amenity groups , residents ' associations and subscribers .
5211	Ring the local planning authority to find out .
5212	When the council receives a planning application it often consults people who might be affected such as neighbours , other residents and community groups .
5213	The consultation process usually takes the form of a letter describing the application and inviting you to come and look at a copy of the application and any drawings submitted with it .
5214	There is no legal obligation on the council to carry out any specific consultation process .
5215	However , if the authority concerned has a code of practice dealing with consultation and fails to carry it out , the Local Government Ombudsman may find the authority guilty of ‘ maladministration ’ .
5216	The planning department of a local council keeps all current planning applications on a register which is available to the public .
5217	As a result of recent changes in the copyright laws , if you can not see the application at the council 's offices then you can ask the planning department to send you a copy of the application and the drawings .
5218	But this can be expensive , so find out first .
5219	If there is a particular site for which you want to be kept informed of any future development , you can ask the planning department to tell you if it receives an application affecting it .
5220	How to comment on a proposal : When you make observations on a planning application you should only comment on planning grounds .
5221	This will exclude many issues which are probably important to you personally , such as the fact that a development will reduce the value of your property or spoil your view .
5222	The council will take a number of factors into account when making up its mind whether to give a development the go-ahead .
5223	These will include : Does the scheme comply with the policies contained in its local plan ?
5224	Is the proposed use compatible with the surrounding area ?
5225	Will there be enough parking provision and will the development cause traffic problems once it is complete ?
5226	The design of the building , particularly its bulk and size .
5227	Any loss of daylight or sunlight to adjoining properties .
5228	These matters will be looked at before a firm decision is taken .
5229	The council can negotiate with the applicant in advance to ask for changes to the scheme and these can result in new drawings being submitted .
5230	Be careful : if you were asked by the council to comment on the original application , it may only inform you of these new drawings if you specifically ask .
5231	If you are particularly worried about a proposal , it may be possible to make an appointment with the appropriate planning officer for a meeting , either in the council offices or on site , so you can explain your objections in person .
5232	The planning officer is an employee of the council who handles the application up to the point when it is put to the planning committee , made up of elected councillors , for a decision .
5233	He or she will usually make a recommendation to the committee about what its decision should be , but it does not have to follow this advice .
5234	There is a set time allowed for the council to receive comments on an application .
5235	This varies but it will be stated in the consultation letter .
5236	If you have not had time to object , contact the planning officer and ask for extra time .
5237	He may agree , and he is often the one who decides what issues will be dealt with and when .
5238	The committee may only meet once a month .
5239	All comments should be in writing and these letters are made available to the public when the case is decided .
5240	If the council receives a large number of letters about a development , this will give it an idea of the strength of feeling involved and it is much better than a petition .
5241	Many councillors take the view that it is easy to drum up names for a petition although you may have more impact if , say , the petition is restricted to immediate neighbours of the development .
5242	Nevertheless , just because a lot of objections are received does not automatically mean an application will be refused .
5243	If the development is large or controversial , it may be worth forming an action group to give local opposition a focus .
5244	If you are applying for planning permission yourself , include a letter stating the planning merits of your proposal and also any personal circumstances you think are relevant — for example , that you are building an extension for an elderly relative .
5245	If you think your application will be unpopular ( such as a mini-cab office or a bed and breakfast hostel ) , you can ask the council for a ‘ personal ’ or ‘ limited period ’ planning permission , so the council can review the situation at a later date .
5246	How the planning committee makes up its mind .
5247	When the council has considered all the factors involved , the case will either be decided by the chief planning officer under delegated powers ( if it is a minor or uncontroversial issue ) or it will be decided by the elected councillors at the planning committee meeting .
5248	To influence the decision in your favour , contact the planning department to find out whether an application is to be heard at committee or dealt with under delegated powers .
5249	If the case is going to committee you are able to see the agenda and relevant background papers three working days in advance of the meeting , which will be held in public .
5250	This right is given to members of the public under the Access to Information Act 1985 .
5251	If there is an application you feel strongly about , find out the names of the councillors on the planning committee from the planning department or ‘ members ’ secretariat' of the council .
5252	Write a letter stating your objections or support for the application and send a copy to every member as well as the chief planning officer .
5253	Contact your ward councillor and try to interest him or her — even if they are not on the committee they may be able to influence the councillors who will take the decision .
5254	They may also be able to tell you some of the preferences of those councillors , which can make a big difference to how you lobby them .
5255	The actual meeting will be open to the public .
5256	Sometimes a limited number of people will be allowed to address the councillors for or against a proposal at the meeting .
5257	This is fixed in advance .
5258	Often there is a limit on numbers and it works on a first-come-first-served basis .
5259	Talk to the planning officer beforehand .
5260	Whether an application is dealt with by the council in committee or under delegated powers , you should receive a letter stating the outcome of the case if you submitted comments .

5301	Property : Houses that are going , going , gone : Fed up with trying to sell , more people are auctioning their home instead .
5302	Andrew Bibby reports
5303	By ANDREW BIBBY
5304	IN THE small Devon town of South Molton , Julie Widlake is waiting with anticipation for Friday 20 October .
5305	She and her boyfriend have had their future planned for some time : they want to start farming in a nearby village , where they also intend to build a bungalow .
5306	First , they have to sell their present house , a two-bedroom cottage in the centre of the town .
5307	As is the case almost everywhere else , the market in Devon is depressed and selling has not been easy .
5308	So instead of waiting indefinitely for a buyer , they have decided to try selling their house by auction .
5309	It comes under the hammer at 2.15pm on the 20th , at the Barnstaple Motel .
5310	‘ We accept that we might not get very much for it , but on the other hand we could get more , ’ says Julie Widlake .
5311	‘ We 've been waiting to move for a long time , and we need the money to build the new house . ’
5312	Their South Molton cottage ( guide price £44,000-£46,000 ) is one of more than 20 lots to be put up for sale at the Barnstaple auction by Bristol and West Property Services , and one of more than a hundred which the building society subsidiary will be auctioning in eight West Country venues over a three-day period .
5313	Bristol and West claims these auctions will help to bring some action to an otherwise slow market , and says it was overwhelmed by the response from people wanting to sell in this way .
5314	Auctions certainly speed up the house-buying process .
5315	Once the hammer has fallen , the successful bidder for a house must exchange contracts immediately and pay a deposit .
5316	Completion normally takes place four to eight weeks later and there is no opportunity for second thoughts .
5317	As the Bristol and West explains , if a bidder does not sign the contract , the auctioneer can sign on their behalf .
5318	‘ From the vendor 's point of view , the house is actually sold once a successful bid is made , ’ says Graham Harrison , director of Bristol and West Property Services .
5319	‘ Many people have suffered from sales falling through and from house-buying chains , and some of our vendors feel that now 's as good a time as any to sell . ’
5320	From the purchasers ' point of view , auctions can also be attractive — if slightly nerve-racking as you wait for bidding to start for the house of your dreams .
5321	The problem is that normally potential purchasers have to incur the expense of undertaking surveys and arranging mortgage finance , without any idea whether they will be able to afford the final selling price .
5322	Not surprisingly , several estate agents report difficulties at the moment in attracting enough serious bidders .
5323	‘ With an auction , you 've got to be certain that at least two buyers are there who can commit themselves , and the difficulty is that buyers who can proceed are few and far between , ’ said David Phillip , a director of Yorkshire estate agents Dacre Son and Hartley .
5324	Bristol and West hopes that by arranging collective auctions it will be able to overcome this problem .
5325	It is also guaranteeing mortgages at 1 per cent below the normal interest rate , for endowment or pension-linked policies , on several of the houses up for sale , an interesting and innovative service for would-be bidders ( mortgage surveys will already have been undertaken for these houses ) .
5326	The building society will be staffing a mortgage desk at each auction , and says buyers could arrange finance there and then , subject of course to proof of income and status .
5327	Obviously , however , Bristol and West hopes to hear from interested people in advance — if only so it can gauge the likely demand for each property before the auction starts .
5328	‘ We 're trying to smooth the path for purchasers , and streamline the system , ’ says Graham Harrison , pointing out that live telephone bidding will also be available for those unable to attend .
5329	Holiday homes and commercial property have been included among the lots to be auctioned .
5330	Although collective property auctions take place regularly in London ( often primarily for investors rather than house-hunters ) , in country areas the more typical auction will be just for one house , and as likely as not will take place in a nearby pub or village hall .
5331	In fact , country auctions are often the nearest many villages get to live theatre .
5332	‘ The locals come for the entertainment , and to see who 's buying into their village , ’ observed one auction-goer .
5333	Pub landlords are usually only too happy to provide free accommodation .
5334	‘ It 's very exciting and gets the adrenalin going , ’ says David Phillip , whose firm usually undertakes auctions in the Otley area .
5335	Only certain types of property normally come to auction , however .
5336	Traditionally , country cottages and houses which have unusual or unique features or are in need of a lot of renovation may be auctioned , if only because valuation is likely to be difficult .
5337	Sometimes , too , houses have to be sold by auction to satisfy the legal requirements of trustees or executors ( auctions provide adequate proof that the property has been sold at the going market value , and protect trustees from future claims of negligence ) .
5338	Less happily , but for the same reason , repossessed houses are often auctioned .
5339	Anyone considering selling by auction needs to be aware that the costs involved will be higher .
5340	Advertising costs and any expenses incurred in hiring premises are normally passed on by the estate agents to the vendor , whether or not the auction results in a sale .
5341	In addition , agents may charge slightly more commission than usual for a successful sale .
5342	In Bristol and West 's forthcoming auctions , a set fee of £375 plus VAT will be charged to everyone entering property to sell , with its usual agent 's commission ( about 2 per cent plus VAT ) charged on top when sales are made .
5343	‘ We accept that we could lose the money we 've paid to go to auction , but that 's a risk we 're prepared to take , ’ says Julie Widlake .
5344	The secret of a successful outcome depends partly on setting the right reserve price , a task the auctioneer undertakes in conjunction with the seller .
5345	Normally , the reserve is set only days or hours before the auction , when the agents will already have a good indication of how much interest has been shown .
5346	Too high a reserve price can mean no sale , and disappointment all round .
5347	‘ You need to understand what your clients ’ expectations are beforehand , ’ says Graham Harrison of Bristol and West .
5348	Agents and their clients may also have the dilemma of deciding whether to accept any offers made prior to the auction .
5349	Inevitably they do not always get it right .
5350	Peter Crowther , managing director of a Leeds business centre , recently bought two semi-detached stone cottages in Bramhope , on the outskirts of Leeds , at an auction in the village pub .
5351	His successful bid was for £190,000 although he had made a higher prior offer which had been turned down .
5352	On the other hand , sometimes the drama of the auction and the competition between bidders can have the opposite effect .
5353	Another recent auction in Leeds saw a run-down stone farmhouse without water or other amenities finally fall under the hammer for £330,500 .
5354	‘ Success is by no means guaranteed at auction , ’ says Graham Harrison .
5355	‘ In a tough market you need to get the programme right , the price right and have a little bit of luck . ’
5356	Bristol and West Property Services ( 0272 294271 ) has produced a brochure covering all eight West Country auctions .

5401	Design : Crossed lines over the toytown tram : City transport could soon be back on the right track , says Jonathan Glancey
5402	By JONATHAN GLANCEY
5403	MODERN trams , as most continental Europeans know , neither shake nor rattle , nor do they roll .
5404	Sleek , solidly built , gentle on the environment , they are often an ideal form of city transport .
5405	They also exert a fascination very much of their own as they slither round circuses and brush through old city gates , flashing arcs of lightning as they switch tracks on winter nights .
5406	Single-car , articulated or double-decker , trams are one of the most reliable and enduring forms of public transport invented .
5407	The orange-liveried ‘ 1500 ’ series trams in Milan , for example , date from 1927 .
5408	Eventually they will be replaced , but more than 60 years on they run with the rhythmic reliability of a Swiss watch .
5409	They are as much a part of Milan as La Scala or the Galleria Vittore Emmanuele .
5410	Last month it was announced that Britain will get its first new-wave trams in 1991 .
5411	Destined to run in Manchester , they will relieve traffic congestion and help to reduce the levels of carbon monoxide in the city centre , outlying suburbs and satellite towns of Bury , Altrincham , Salford , Oldham and Rochdale .
5412	In Britain , with the main exception of Blackpool ( not forgetting the single-deckers of the Isle of Man and Llandudno ) , trams had been largely relegated to the history books .
5413	Otherwise , the best place to see working trams has been the tram museum at Crich in Derbyshire or else in old British Transport Commission films and Ealing comedies .
5414	Trams disappeared from most British cities in the 1950s .
5415	London 's venerable red and cream double-deckers rumbled along the Thames embankment for the last time in 1952 .
5416	Somehow the image of the tall , thin , mournful double-deck tram with its wooden body , slatted wooden seats and growling electric motor has stuck in the British mind .
5417	Trams , it was believed until surprisingly recently , are old-fashioned .
5418	They had something to do with fish and chips wrapped in newspaper , men in hats , National Health specs , smog and powdered egg .
5419	They held up the bright new diesel buses and , even worse , blocked the progress of private motorists in bulbous Austins and lumpen Humbers in canyon-like city thoroughfares .
5420	They picked up power from a spider 's web of unsightly overhead wires .
5421	They were inflexible in operation , draughty , and mobile reminders of TB epidemics with the enamelled ‘ Do Not Spit ’ signs screwed to their bulkheads .
5422	But the modern tram could hardly be more different .
5423	It plays a key role in keeping city streets on the move and is even the object of the best modern designers ' desire .
5424	In Milan , for example , the commission to design the new generation of ‘ Jumbo ’ trams , which went into service in 1979 , was one that leading Italian architects and designers fought over .
5425	After all , the Jumbo , a handsome and imposing articulated unit designed by architect , engineer and critic Klaus Giovanni Koenig , will be seen on the streets of Milan for the next half-century .
5426	Spotlessly clean and popular , the Jumbo is a long-term advertisement for Koenig 's design skills .
5427	The modern tram is a green machine .
5428	Assuming the power station at the end of the line burns cleanly , the tram is virtually pollution free .
5429	Standing at traffic lights a Koenig-designed Jumbo is , save for the chatter inside , completely silent .
5430	The overhead wires are so slight that you have to look hard to see them .
5431	Powers of acceleration and braking are remarkable , the latter far greater than any car .
5432	But sadly , there is no indication that the GMA consortium which will design , operate and maintain the first of the new generation British trams in Manchester will share the looks of their Milanese counterparts .
5433	Artists ' impressions show a tram that has more in common with the flat-faced , characterless light trains of the toy-like Docklands Light Railway .
5434	There is still time for GMA ( GEC , Mowlem , Amec and Greater Manchester Buses ) to consider employing an inspired architect or industrial designer .
5435	After all , Mancunians and visitors to the Manchester conurbation are going to have to look at these mechanical millipedes for well into the twenty-first century .
5436	Now that buses are no longer designed to enhance the streets they serve , Manchester has a chance to make a fresh start with its trams .
5437	Manchester is not alone .
5438	Other British towns , Croydon and Southampton among them , are also considering modern tramways .
5439	These are all referred to as ‘ supertram ’ networks , the implication being that the new-generation tram is an altogether more dynamic form of transport than its pre-war predecessors .
5440	What it really means is that the new trams are a hybrid between street car and lightweight suburban train .
5441	Although they will slip through the city centre serving the essential parts — shopping malls , leisure centres , theme parks , amusement arcades and museums — the Manchester supertrams will also head out of town on a mix of reserved track and existing railway lines .
5442	The supertram is , in effect , a low-cost replacement for British Rail 's ageing fleet of suburban diesel multiple-unit trains , those rasping diesels which change gear to the accompaniment of voluminous clouds of acrid black exhaust fumes and the blessing of train spotters .
5443	They will perform some of the same functions , but they will not be an exact replacement for traditional trams .
5444	And although the supertram concept will spread through major cities during the next decade , Blackpool will still be alone in its use of traditional double-deckers .
5445	Keeping the fabric of history : Taking care of old clothes requires more than just mothballs , writes Jo Levin
5446	By JO LEVIN
5447	HOARDING clothes has long been a British vice .
5448	The current exhibition of Indian dress at Liberty ( Regent Street , London W1 , until October 21 ) shows many a garment bought by an Empire wife and stored in a trunk , along with christening dress , lace collars and evening gowns .
5449	These surviving pieces of history need care if they are not to deteriorate .
5450	So will the new wedding dress .
5451	The craft of caring for clothes vanished with the ladies ' maid and the most common modern method of storage — hanging them , shrouded in plastic , on a wire coathanger — is less than ideal .
5452	Items of value , real or sentimental , are worth the trouble of proper storage .
5453	Lynda Hillyer , head of textile conservation at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London , is concerned with the care of fragile and valuable textiles from the time of Tutankhamun .
5454	But the basic rules she recommends apply to all .
5455	Keep textiles out of light , which both fades dyes and supplies the energy to begin the process of breaking the fibres down , as with the shredded silk curtains of many a National Trust mansion .
5456	Pack , swathe and support garments with acid-free tissue paper .
5457	Normal tissue paper , like most paper , contains acid which encourages fading and decay , including the gradual yellowing of white fabrics , a process which may be seen after only a few years .
5458	Acidic conditions are particularly bad for cellulose , so cotton and linen fabrics are especially at risk .
5459	Wood — in a drawer , wardrobe or chest — may also be acidic : line all drawers and storage compartments with acid-free tissue .
5460	Fragile and heavy garments are best stored flat on a dust-free shelf or , ideally , in an acid-free cardboard box .
5461	Insert sausage-shaped rolls of acid-free tissue paper in folds , so that they do not become permanent — caused , as a microscope would show , by fibres cracking .
5462	Use pads of acid-free tissue paper to bulk out shoes .
5463	If using hangers , pad them to about three times the usual extent with acid-free tissue or with polyester wadding covered with white cotton ( which can also be used to pad out the shoulders and shapes of packed costumes ) .
5464	Foam padding , often used on coat hangers , is not ideal .
5465	Make sure the whole shoulder area is supported — the hanger should fit its breadth .
5466	If a dress is heavy , support the skirt separately with tapes .
5467	Use cotton dust-covers — white — and wash them every few months .
5468	Dust is abrasive and may contain metallic particles .
5469	Of course everything to be stored must first be clean .
5470	Do not store clothes in plastic , which will attract dust and , if there is any moisture in the air , encourage the growth of mould .
5471	Check the clothes every few months , or moths and mould may flourish unhindered .
5472	Wrap mothballs in muslin and do not let them touch the textiles .
5473	Specialist private dry cleaning of antique textiles : Bernard Dore works for the National Trust and national museums as well as dealers .
5474	Write or telephone before visiting : 0304 373684 , 271 Sandown Road , Deal , Kent .
5475	Conservation cleaning is an expensive process and prices vary wildly , though it is worthwhile for a valuable or fragile article : Mr Dore will give an estimate in advance .
5476	The conservation unit of the Museums and Galleries Commission has a register of private conservators including specialists in textiles .
5477	The unit checks references on all conservators , and has a leaflet on how to choose the right restorer : write to 7 St James 's Square , London SW1Y 4JU .
5478	Compare and date your own textiles with those at the Victoria and Albert Museum 's Textile Galleries , from room 96 to 101 , which include samples from ancient Egyptian times to the present century , and with the museum 's Dress Collection .

5556	Wild isle of the strange and absolute : Alison Lurie followed Flaubert , Colette and Sarah Bernhardt to find drama and mythology on Belle-Ile , off the coast of Brittany
5557	By ALISON LURIE
5558	At the siege of Belle-Isle I was there all the while ; All the while , all the while , At the siege of Belle-Isle Until last month these lines were only a nursery-rhyme to me , accompanied in my memory by a crude illustration of a tower by the sea and square-rigged warship balancing on humped waves .
5559	I thought of the place as an imaginary island , a sort of French Never Never Land .
5560	But there is a real Belle-Ile in the Atlantic about eight miles off the coast of southern Brittany : a mysterious , beautiful , isolated island shaped like a fish swimming north-west , edged with black cliffs and coves of pale-brown sugar-sand .
5561	Just off its shore stand giant rocks carved into strange jagged patterns by the sea .
5562	The place has always attracted writers and artists and lovers of strange and dramatic scenery .
5563	Colette went there at 21 .
5564	While her unpleasant husband shut himself in his room and wrote letters , she explored the island with Paul Masson and for the first time in her life ‘ tasted and touched the salt , the sand , the seaweed , the odorous soft bed of the receding sea , the dripping fish ’ .
5565	The sea-gravel seemed to her to be composed of ‘ shattered rubies tinted with mauve ’ .
5566	Flaubert describes Belle-Ile at length in Par les Champs et par les Greves ; Courbet , Monet , and Matisse lived and painted there .
5567	Later , Andre Breton , Salvador Dali , and other surrealists stayed and worked in a now-destroyed hotel on its wild western shore , the famed Cote Sauvage .
5568	I reached Belle-Ile by ferry from the peninsula of Quiberon , after a seven-hour drive in 27-degree heat from the Paris airport that nothing on earth would induce me to repeat — though my two companions , one British and one French , conversed enthusiastically on opera , European politics , and structural anthropology .
5569	( A better alternative might be to travel by rail or plane to L'Orient , 30 miles west , and rent a car . )
5570	As a result of the journey , however , I can report that French motorway food is greatly superior to American .
5571	We were offered fresh do-it-yourself salads , good local cheeses , strawberry tart and chocolate mousse .
5572	The souvenirs on sale , though , were of intriguing awfulness ; my favourite was a plastic female head enclosing a dried and shrivelled bouquet — a dead-metaphor version of the French custom of naming women after flowers , perhaps .
5573	Quiberon is just south of the village of Carnac , where mile-long alleys of menhirs , or standing-stones , erected in prehistoric times , wade through fields of tall rose-beige grass .
5574	It is a crowded tourist centre , heavy on souvenir shops and jokey exploitation of local sights ; the cafe opposite the ferry landing was advertising a giant hamburger called Le Menhir .
5575	Belle-Ile , however , seems to belong to a past era of modest and amateur tourism .
5576	Le Palais , where the ferry docks , is an agreeable , unspoilt little town of ancient houses and cobbled squares .
5577	It is dominated by the imposing Citadelle de Vauban , constructed in 1549 to defend the island against invaders .
5578	The citadel 's rough , sheer pale-brown outer walls and ramparts resemble a giant sandcastle built on the edge of the sea .
5579	It is now a museum of military history , but was once full of armed men and artillery .
5580	The siege commemorated in my nursery rhyme took place in 1761 : an English fleet cut off supplies to the citadel , and after 38 days the garrison surrendered .
5581	Until about 20 years ago the citadel still served as barracks and prison , and seems to have been thought suitable for confining revolutionaries .
5582	Placide Touiss ant-L'Ouverture , son of the liberator of Haiti , was imprisoned there , and so was , more recently , Messali Hadj , the Algerian nationalist .
5583	After the political disturbances of 1848 , Karl Marx , with other radicals , spent time in an internment camp on the island .
5584	In the summer the ferry also runs from Quiberon to the little fishing port of Sauzon , which is almost postcard-pretty from a distance but given satisfying reality in close-up by the sounds and smells of its trade and the stacks of water-roughened lobster traps and water-soaked nets and floats .
5585	On the jetty near the little lighthouse is a remarkably good restaurant .
5586	We sat on its terrace overlooking the harbour , watching the sky blush rose-red and devouring plum oysters , crabs , and langoustines caught that same day — and the first snails I have ever had that did not taste like bits of black rubber boot fried in garlic and olive oil .
5587	The Atlantic coast of Belle-Ile is known as the Cote Sauvage , and in most places is sufficiently savage to deter any invader .
5588	In the nineteenth century the actress Sarah Bernhardt , ‘ attracted by the Absolute , ’ as one guidebook puts it , built a chateau high on the cliff near its northernmost end , the Pointe des Poulains ( Foals ' Point ) , where the offshore rocks are said to resemble young horses galloping in the swaying navy-blue sea .
5589	Her house is in ruins now , covered with flowering weeds and inhabited only by seagulls .
5590	While we were on the beach below another tourist tried to climb up to the ruin ; but a flock of dive-bombing gulls , screaming histrionically , drove him off .
5591	hree kilometres south of the Point des Poulains is a spectacular sea-level cave , the Grotte de l'Apothicairerie .
5592	Its name comes from the cormorants ' nests which in the past were ranged in rows along shelves in the wet black rock , like jars in a chemist 's shop .
5593	Now only the sea thunders rhythmically through the grotto , flinging up fans of salty spray .
5594	Further along the coast is the most amazing sight of all , the Aiguilles ( needles ) de Port-Coton : a chain of huge , spiky dark rocks that emerge from the sea like the petrified remains of some prehistoric monster .
5595	The waves around these rocks churn up a salty froth that is said to resemble cotton-wool , though to me it seemed more like the foaming spit of an angry sea-serpent .
5596	After touring the Cote Sauvage we had a perfect lunch in a crep erie : galettes — whole-wheat crepes made from sarazin ( black wheat ) — filled with ham or melted cheese and accompanied by foaming mugs of Breton cider ; then crisp lacy brown crepes with sugar and jam or chocolate sauce , which bore no resemblance to the limp pancakes served under that name in America .
5597	As the afternoon temperature rose our thoughts turned to the beaches .
5598	There are many on the quieter north shore or Cote du Dedans , all beautiful and uncrowded .
5599	The best-known is Les Grands Sables , over a mile long and backed by cliffs where the gorse-bushes were explosions of butter-yellow fireworks .
5600	On the Cote Sauvage is Port-Donant , where the surf is exciting and sometimes dangerous .
5601	It is popular with summer bathers , but at other times the water is cold and the fine sand dotted with jellyfish like complicated hot-weather dishes : semi-transparent yellow-streaked boeuf en daube and deep magenta grape aspic .
5602	The central part of the island seemed at first to belong to another and less dramatic world .
5603	We passed gently rolling pastures where fat sheep and cows grazed , empty dusty roads edged with white convolvulus and daisies , and fields of grain rippling in the soft wind like beige velvet stroked by an invisible hand .
5604	But even here there were signs that we were not far from the sea or from strange phenomena .
5605	The cypress es on the heights had grey wind-contorted branches and trunks , mimicking the twisted layers of rock by the ocean ; and at a distance the whitewashed farmhouses , with their triangular gable ends , looked like fleets of sailboats moored beyond the farthest field .
5606	Standing in the fields in the centre of the island were two tall stone menhirs , known locally as Jean and Jeanne .
5607	According to legend they were young lovers whom the druids forbade to marry .
5608	When they disobeyed they were transformed into pillars of rock and placed where they could see each other but never meet .
5609	Once every 100 years they resume their human shapes and renew their embraces ; anyone who sees them then is turned to stone .
5610	Flaubert , who visited the island in 1847 , got lost in these deserted , deceptively placid fields , of which he wrote : ‘ One would have said that all those who owned them profited from them but did not like them . ’
5611	He preferred the shore , where the long vistas of rocks with their thick coverings of seaweed appeared to him as the heads of ‘ black phantoms emerging from the underworld , ’ and the grottos were full of strange brilliantly coloured rocks and polished white beds of gravel which seemed about ‘ to receive the water-nymph when she emerged from the waves ’ .
5612	Like Flaubert , I left Belle-Ile hoping to return — and hoping , too , that the island 's isolation and the occasional fogs that cover it would discourage too many other tourists .
5613	Alison Lurie is Professor of Children 's Literature at Cornell University , New York .
5614	Her latest book The Truth about Lorin Jones ( Abacus , £3.99 ) has just been published in paperback .
5615	Alison Lurie 's next book Do n't Tell the Grown-ups , on children 's literature , will be published next year by Bloomsbury .

5617	Normal economy return is £262 .

5627	Skiing : A Swiss role on the slide : Chris Gill asks why few British skiers choose the cantons
5628	By CHRIS GILL
5629	THOSE who care about such things are at present locked in combat over the issue of whether the greatest number of British skiers go to Austria ( which traditionally enjoys the distinction ) or to France ( which is the flavour of the decade ) .
5630	Both , according to the latest figures conjured out of a hat by the French , have just over 35 per cent of the market .
5631	Of much more interest to Alp-watchers is the performance of the other great Alpine skiing nations .
5632	The French reckon that Italy now gets 7 per cent of our custom and , more surprisingly , that Switzerland gets only 5 per cent .
5633	Once upon a time , this might have been 95 per cent .
5634	This is partly a consequence of simple arithmetic .
5635	Switzerland has lots of Alps , but they are now less densely equipped with skiers ' dormitories than those of France and Austria .
5636	Many of the big names of Swiss skiing have fewer than 10,000 beds ; the total for Val d'Isere/Tignes approaches 50,000 .
5637	But it is more a consequence of the view we have of Switzerland and of Swiss skiing .
5638	A dominant factor is the idea that Switzerland is expensive .
5639	It is not entirely without foundation : holidaying on the cheap in such places as super-smart St Moritz , Zermatt and Gstaad is next to impossible , whatever the tourist offices there might say .
5640	But it is not expensive when you compare like with like — that is , when you compare French with Swiss .
5641	Of course , if you squeeze yourself and your mates into a ‘ compact ’ studio and live on bread and cheese , you can live more cheaply in France than in a Swiss hotel .
5642	But in the important area of mountain lunches , for example , my experiences ( and the distilled findings of those who report to The Good Skiing Guide on such matters ) point to parity between France and Switzerland , with Austria and Italy providing worthwhile savings .
5643	It remains true that Switzerland is not a place for ‘ convenience ’ skiing in the way that France is .
5644	Ski areas tend to be as fragmented now as they were 20 or 30 years ago .
5645	In some cases this may be attributable to the Swiss tendency to conserve ( money , not nature ) ; in others , the terrain makes links between areas impracticable or unnecessary .
5646	Zermatt , for example , is a resort where many skiers must have wished for better links .
5647	In Davos and St Moritz , the areas are so widely spread and rewarding individually that the idea of linking them scarcely arises .
5648	One resort seizing the bull by the horns is little old Adelboden , which for 1991 is building a big new gondola to link two of its smaller ski areas to its major one .
5649	Whatever its weaknesses , Switzerland always has a couple of aces up the sleeve .
5650	The first is that there are no Alps like the Swiss Alps .
5651	The French , Italian and Austrian Alps have their spectacles , but they are not presented so conveniently for the the idle downhill skier ( or even non-skier ) as the great set-pieces of the Swiss .
5652	The second ace is the country 's near-monopoly of traditional traffic-free villages — or what pass for traffic-free villages in these days of electric taxis and buses .
5653	It is from these villages and their ski areas that the most impressive mountain scenery is to be seen .
5654	The famous trio of Eiger , Monch and Jungfrau loom over the pistes of tiny British-dominated Wengen , and are seen to even better advantage from even tinier Murren ( the one resort which genuinely is traffic-free ) .
5655	Money-dominated Zermatt is synonymous with the unreal pyramid of the Matterhorn ( which is unrecognisably ordinary when seen from Italian Cervinia , next door ) .
5656	The peaks surrounding glacier-dominated Saas Fee may be less distinguished , but the ice-falls of the Feegletscher hanging over the village are in their way just as striking .
5657	Of course , we must not forget that these are ski resorts .
5658	Wengen 's skiing is extensive , but for piste skiers is mostly easy ; Murren is very limited , with one spectacular descent from the famous Schilthorn ; Zermatt has something for everyone and lots for experts , but to reach its full potential needs better snow than it often receives ; Saas Fee has an excellent glacier , but again needs abundant snow to provide much more than that — in particular , to satisfy better skiers .
5659	But the quality and quantity of the skiing to be done in these places is almost a secondary consideration .
5660	Perhaps that explains why most British skiers are n't inclined to go to Switzerland — and why a minority would n't dream of going anywhere else .

5679	The churches built on wool : Angela Lambert enjoys the riches at the heart of East Anglia
5680	By ANGELA LAMBERT
5681	UNTIL six or seven years ago , outsiders associated East Anglia with fens , flatness and the vanished Edwardian nannies of Frinton .
5682	Its old churches , green fields and long beaches were cherished by the inhabitants of Essex , Suffolk , Norfolk and Cambridgeshire , but not yet on the tourist agenda .
5683	Today , I was told , villagers living around the great wool churches of Lavenham and Long Melford have to bar their doors and ignore the knocking of tourists , who take them for antique shops and offer to buy their furniture .
5684	The tourists are right .
5685	East Anglia on a sunny weekend is a place of matchless beauty .
5686	Its villages look too good to be true .
5687	Lavenham and Long Melford , for example , have no telegraph poles , to preserve the timeless air that pervades them .
5688	Yet you only have to read Ronald Blythe 's Akenfield to realise that these picturesque , half-timbered cottages , often painted the characteristic Essex pink ( pale salmon ) , ochre or spring-leaf green , are more prosperous now than ever in the ‘ real ’ past .
5689	Many are still elaborately decorated with pargeting , an ornate , patterned plasterwork practised in this area since the early thirteenth century .
5690	Most of East Anglia 's prosperity today is due to City commuters , the second-homes market and tourism .
5691	The ideal hotel from which to explore is Dedham Hall , set among tall trees in the Vale of Dedham , looking directly across towards Dedham church on one side and Flatford Mill on the other : both painted by Constable .
5692	The hotel lies in five acres of fields and garden , and the Slingos , who own it , make the most of their beautiful surroundings by running painting courses for about £200 a week ( including breakfast and dinner ) , or £90 for a long weekend .
5693	These are so popular that you will need to book at least a couple of months in advance .
5694	The other great joy of Dedham Hall is the food .
5695	The Slingos have their own vegetable garden , chickens , ducks , sheep and cows .
5696	Everything is home-grown , home-made and fresh : it tastes like forgotten food .
5697	If Dedham Hall is fully booked — and it may well be — try the best bed-and-breakfast we have ever found , just a few miles away at the Old Vicarage , Higham , near Colchester .
5698	It is a rambling Tudor house run by John and Margaret Parker , whose breakfast room and drawing room look out over a wonderful walled garden , beyond which fields of grazing cows stretch down to the river .
5699	Another hotel that would make a good starting point for a weekend — or longer — in East Anglia is the Black Lion at Long Melford .
5700	It changed hands recently and is now run by Stephen and Janet Errington .
5701	After dinner there , when the moon was full and low and deep orange , we walked up the road from the hotel to Long Melford church .
5702	Its vast walls of flint and glass and Gothic tracery were brilliantly floodlit and the churchyard cat , sleek and black as tar , greeted us querulously and led us right round the church and through the gravestones at the back , glimmering and pale in the moonlight .
5703	We were quite alone and the great church , the size of a cathedral , was unearthly in its floodlit , moonlit beauty .
5704	Long Melford is one of the wool churches that commemorate the wealth of East Anglia in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries .
5705	Another is at Lavenham , 10 minutes ' drive up the road .
5706	Just inside the front porch , a handwritten book is prefaced with the words ‘ This book has been compiled that something , more than their mere names , may be known of the Lavenham men who gave their lives for their country in the Great War . ’
5707	This is followed by 50 or so names , each with a description .
5708	The much-thumbed book is deeply moving , and sets the tone for a walk round this glorious building , which has seen the christenings , marriages and burials of the folk of the village for more than 600 years .
5709	East Anglia is exceptionally rich in churches and cathedrals .
5710	There are several splendid houses near Long Melford that would make for a gentle afternoon 's potter through the rooms and possessions of the rich of a few centuries ago .
5711	The loveliest , to my mind , is Melford Hall , whose charming , octagonal Jacobean gatehouse is reached along an avenue of clipped yew trees and , with its high windows flooding the octagon with light , is my fantasy of the ideal study .
5712	Lavenham is often called the finest medieval village in England .
5713	It is an image of the world we have lost , its gently sloping streets converging upon the market place .
5714	Here stand the early sixteenth-century timbered Guildhall , now a museum to 700 years of the cloth industry .
5715	Next to it is The Little Hall , dating from the fourteenth century , with its floorboards gleaming with the patina of age , low-beamed ceilings and a tiny , unruly , charming walled garden .
5716	Precisely next door to this is a restaurant called The Great House .
5717	Here , in the cool , pretty setting of the dining room that was once Stephen Spender 's , you will be served an exquisite three-course lunch for £9.50 , £6 for children .
5718	The wine list is small but perfectly chosen .
5719	The service is impeccable .
5720	East Anglia has bookshops filled with titles like 101 Things For A Boy To Do …
5721	Constable landscapes …
5722	Gainsborough 's house … to say nothing of huge grey sweeps of empty beach from which , at Aldeburgh , you can buy goggle-eyed skate direct from the fishing boats as they come out of the water .
5723	It has Colchester oysters .
5724	It has Ely Cathedral , its great green windows casting a translucent light across the Lady Chapel .
5725	With all this , small wonder it also has tourists .
5726	Sore pedal push to the pagodas : A mountain bike is the perfect way to explore the byways of Nepal , says David Reed
5727	By DAVID REED
5728	THE FIRST thing to do in Kathmandu is dump your bags and hire a bike .
5729	A bicycle is to the medieval streets of Nepal what a convertible is to a California freeway : appropriate technology .
5730	Until recently , Nepal knew only one brand , the Hero , a clunky steel one-speeder .
5731	Now , Kathmandu has discovered mountain bikes .
5732	They 're everywhere , not just in the capital but exploring crannies where no other form of transport will go .
5733	A mountain bike is the perfect touring vehicle for Nepal 's roads , which in recent years have deteriorated badly .
5734	After this summer 's monsoon , the Kathmandu-Pokhara highway ( the country 's most popular tourist route ) probably looks like a donkey track .
5735	A serious petrol shortage is only making things worse — bus travel , crowded at the best of times , is now cruel and inhumane .
5736	I joined a group going to Nagarkot , a hilltop resort on the rim of the Kathmandu valley .
5737	Organised by Kathmandu 's only cycle tour operator , the trip was n't too long or demanding , and was designed to introduce Nepalese culture , history and ( in theory , anyway ) Himalayan views at the top .
5738	We were a group of eight Australians and Americans , led by a former Atlanta debutante named Frances Higgins .
5739	She 'd come to Nepal with a back-pack three years earlier and ended up marrying the US embassy dentist .
5740	After a ritual distribution of chocolate and biscuits — they came in handy later — we wheeled out of the Kathmandu Guest House and into the demolition derby of old Kathmandu .
5741	Pedestrians were the main hazard , but rickshaws , curio sellers , money-changers and the odd sacred cow also had to be manoeuvred around .
5742	And the bumps .
5743	I quickly found that mountain bikes do n't particularly spare you the bumps .
5744	We pedalled eastwards , first past the new Royal Palace — a weird , menacing building with bats hanging in the trees like handbags — and on to the great domed stupa , or Buddhist monument , of Bodnath .
5745	It was Buddha 's birthday .
5746	An army of beggars and lepers had turned out , each crouched behind a cloth heaped with rice grains and coins .
5747	For pilgrims , the ritual prostrations and prayer-wheel-spinning were out of the question , because beggars blocked the shrine .
5748	Once out of Kathmandu we started getting long stares from villagers , laying out spring wheat on the road to be threshed by passing cars and carts .
5749	I felt pretty silly wearing a plastic walnut shell on my head .
5750	The flashy gear turned you , however unwillingly , into a sort of pied piper of Western materialism .
5751	We stopped in Thimi , a village obscurely famous for a type of papier mache mask .
5752	An instant crowd formed , mostly children .
5753	Two or three pairs of hands roamed sensuously over the alloy frame , tentatively flexing the brakes and fiddling with the gear shift .
5754	‘ How much you pay for this ? ’ asked a lad in a Michael Jackson T-shirt , hopefully .
5755	I did n't buy any masks , but I was tempted by the matching two-foot-high figurines of King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya .
5756	The King is said to be a reincarnation of the Hindu god Vishnu .
5757	Ten miles from Kathmandu we pulled into Bhaktapur , the best preserved of the three ancient cities of the valley .
5758	The tall brick houses would have looked like Victorian mansions , except for the pagoda roofs and the intricate wood lattices in place of glass window panes .
5759	The alleys between them were dark and damp , rich with the smell of onions hung from the eaves .
5760	To park the bikes we had to strike a deal with the children in the main square .
5761	They wanted a few rupees as protection money — a common arrangement .
5762	We lunched in a cafe overlooking a five-tiered pagoda temple , tall and slender like a square bullet .
5763	After Bhaktapur , the real biking began .
5764	As the land rose , the rectangular paddy fields gave way to thin terraces that carved the valley into steps ; here and there an irrigated paddy glistened in a green crescent .
5765	The road angled towards the rim of the valley , climbing 2,000 feet in eight relentless miles .
5766	The grade was manageable in the lowest of 18 gears , but it was like riding an exercise cycle in a sauna .
5767	The weather was fiendishly sticky , what they call the ‘ pre-monsoon ’ .
5768	Clouds rose in thin columns up the mountain sides , grey upon grey , and started smudging out the valley .
5769	The hilltop we were aiming for looked like an angry volcano .
5770	I asked Ms Higgins what the difference was between the monsoon and the pre-monsoon .
5771	‘ Oh , ‘ bout two weeks , ’ she said from behind her Ray-Ban sunglasses .
5772	We climbed into the clouds and a cooling drizzle began to fall .
5773	I noticed I could see my breath .
5774	We kept spiralling up towards a high point on the ridge , and when we reached it there was a lodge , perched improbably like a ski-lift station .
5775	Next to it was a bamboo out-building with a big sign saying : ‘ The Restaurant at the End of the Universe ’ .
5776	We sat there drinking hot chocolate and watching the clouds scrape raggedly past .
5777	They seemed to be breaking up , and to the west a different valley - the one we would descend into the next day — was filling with a luminous gold haze .
5778	But to the north , where the main Himalayan chain should have loomed , the curtain never parted , and it was the same story in the morning .
5779	‘ Y'all should see this place in the fall , ’ Ms Higgins apologised .
5780	I 'd seen the Himalayas in the autumn , so I was able to imagine them .
5781	On my previous visit , at dawn , the range had floated eerily above a sea of fog .
5782	At sunset the slabbish , orange peaks had appeared like ghosts out of the clouds and then , in less time than it took to wind on a camera , swirled away again .
5783	Sore bottoms on saddles , we pointed our fat tyres down the steep track .
5784	The descent was nerve-racking and it reminded me of the slow , queasy way light planes come in to land in Himalayan valleys .
5785	At the first sign we came to , women were bashing wheat sheaves against rocks and men squatted in the dust playing a game with pebbles .
5786	We were back in the sultry heat of the valley .
5787	FACT FILE Flights : Royal Nepal Airlines has begun direct flights from London to Kathmandu : return fares cost £520 through Babin Travel ( 01-383 4314 ) .
5788	An alternative is Pakistan Airlines via Karachi .
5789	Mountain bike operators : Himalayan Mountain Bikes , located in the courtyard of the Kathmandu Guest House , runs trips all over Nepal from 1 to 13 days , with costs ranging from $20 to $1,940 ; the Nagarkot trip costs $80 .
5790	Price includes everything — equipment , food , hotel or tent and , on longer trips , an escort vehicle .
5791	Overnights can be arranged in Kathmandu , but longer trips should be booked by writing to the company at PO Box 2769 , Kathmandu , Nepal .
5792	Mountain bikes can be hired for $8 a day from America Nepal Mountain Bike Rental , south of the Old Vienna Inn in Kathmandu .
5793	Books : A Guide to Trekking in Nepal by Stephen Bezruchka , The Mountaineers , £8.95 .
5794	David Reed is also writing a guide to Nepal .
5795	Health : Hepatitis ( gamma globulin ) , typhoid and Japanese encephalitis jabs are recommended ; malaria pills may be advisable for lowland areas .
5796	Visas : 14-day visas , extendable to one month , available on entry at the airport ; for longer stays , apply in advance to the Royal Nepalese Embassy , 12a Kensington Palace Gardens W8 , London ( 01-229 1594 ) .
5797	Trekking permits are necessary only for off-road trips in certain areas .
5798	Maps : The Schneider map of the Kathmandu Valley is invaluable ; outside the valley , the Nelles map of Nepal should be taken with a pinch of salt .
5799	Trekking maps sold in Nepal may prove useful .
