5807	Tavel Update : Credit caution
5808	By DAVID REED
5809	IF YOU buy air tickets by telephone , be very careful about giving your credit card number .
5810	David Rundle of Slough rang a London agency , seeking a return seat-only deal to Athens .
5811	The agent was able to offer a ticket and quoted a fare of £153 .
5812	‘ I said I was very interested and gave my credit card number as requested . ’
5813	The agent told Mr Rundle that she had to check his ‘ card rating ’ and put him on hold — to the accompaniment of taped music .
5814	‘ This played for at least 10 minutes and finished and the phone went dead .
5815	I rang again and the agent said she thought I 'd put the phone down . ’
5816	He said that he had n't , and he was put on hold again — and again the phone went dead .
5817	‘ By this time I had waited about 15 minutes hanging on the phone and the clerk had not confirmed any booking . ’
5818	His patience exhausted , he called another agent and booked a dearer ticket .
5819	He was surprised to receive shortly afterwards an invoice from the first agency informing him that his Visa account had been debited for £153 for tickets he did n't know he had bought .
5820	The second agency had warned him he was entering into a contract by giving his credit card number .
5821	He demanded a refund from the first agents but they refused , arguing that because he had given them his credit card number he had entered into a contract .
5822	Mr Rundle took his case to Save &amp; Prosper who issued his Visa card .
5823	On investigation , they discovered that the first agency had failed to get proper authorisation from Visa for the transaction .
5824	According to Ian Lindsey , a director of Save &amp; Prosper , if the agency had obtained authorisation there is ‘ no way ’ Mr Rundle could have received a refund .
5825	‘ Never , ever give out your card number until you have reached agreement , ’ Mr Lindsey said .
5826	Medieval bridge-builders to tourists : Hilly Janes found Bruges full of foreign hordes and historical haunts
5827	By HILLY JANES
5828	The first thing the lady in the hotel pointed out when she showed us our room overlooking the canal was an electric mosquito killer .
5829	‘ Infested with tourists and mosquitoes ’ — the verdict of some friends who had spent a weekend in ‘ the Venice of the North ’ earlier in the summer flashed through my mind .
5830	Fortunately , in the cooler weather of late September , the scarlet geraniums in the window-boxes were still in bloom , but the mosquitoes seemed to have wilted .
5831	Not so the human swarm .
5832	If you perceive yourself as a traveller rather than a tourist , read no further .
5833	If walking down streets teeming with non-residents induces mild panic , or if it strikes you as undignified to whizz around a museum in 10 minutes , because entry is part of the combination ticket you have bought from the tourist office , then forget Bruges .
5834	You would be better spending a weekend in Antwerp , about 15 miles to the east , less well preserved architecturally but with more comprehensive museums and galleries , and much more the feel of a ‘ real ’ town .
5835	Almost entirely surrounded by a circle of water that formed part of the original fortifications , and still linked to its neighbours and the port of Zeebrugge about eight miles away by canals , Bruges ' attraction is that its medieval architecture is remarkably intact .
5836	Cobbled streets with gabled houses are criss-crossed by a network of tree-lined waterways linked by more than 50 arched bridges ( which is how the city got is name ) .
5837	A trip in a motorised open punt , with stripy red and white umbrellas at hand as shelter from the Belgian drizzle , is an enjoyable way to find your bearings , and at £2 for half an hour , offers a quick fix of what exactly hooks all these tourists .
5838	As the boat chugs under the low arched bridges , the driver catalogues in Dutch , French , German and English the exhibits in this living museum .
5839	There is St John 's Hospital , the first in Europe , built in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries , although founded much earlier , and still in use until the 1970s ; the Beguinage , a religious foundation for women that dates back to the twelfth century , now a convent ; the thirteenth-to fifteenth-century Church of our Lady , with a 350ft tower ; the Stadhuis , a magnificent Gothic town hall dating from 1376-1420 .
5840	The Blue Guide lists almost 20 museums , churches and galleries within a circular area about half a mile across .
5841	The contents of these buildings are no less spectacular than their exteriors .
5842	The St John 's Hospital allows a glimpse of early health care , with mock-ups to show how the patients were housed in rows of wooden cots , and cared for by nuns and friars .
5843	Displays of early surgical instruments give a chilling glimpse of the pain the sick must have endured before anaesthetic was invented .
5844	The hospital 's fifteenth-century chapel houses a small collection of works by Hans Memling : exquisite , jewel-like portraits and interpretations of biblical scenes and Christian legends , as vivid as when he painted them 500 years ago .
5845	In the chapel at the Beguinage , you can listen to the nuns chanting their prayers wearing the white headresses and black robes of the original beguines .
5846	The Church of our Lady has a Michelangelo sculpture of the Madonna ; the Gothic hall in the Stadhuis is crowned by a magnificent wooden vaulted ceiling .
5847	Elsewhere there are Breughels ; walls covered with Delft tiles ; a medieval belfry with 366 steps from which you can gaze down on the town 's steep , red tiled roofs ; holy blood brought back from the crusades .
5848	You begin to feel dizzy with history .
5849	Of course , the well-groomed head of modern Bruges pops up all over the place to remind you that this is not really a medieval theme park at all .
5850	On Saturday morning , we watched outside the Stadhuis , where couples still marry in the Gothic hall .
5851	Limousines drew up to disgorge a wedding party ; women in elegant outfits topped with splendid hats were a fanfare for a bride who stepped out of an old white Daimler , tanned beneath her white silk .
5852	Very bourgeois , but that is probably what Bruges has always been .
5853	The patrons of all this art were merchants in the thirteenth century , who profited from cloth manufacture .
5854	From the fourteenth to fifteenth centuries , Bruges was the chief market of the powerful Hanseatic trading league .
5855	At the end of the fifteenth century , one enterprising family realised there was money to be made from all the foreign merchants , and turned their house into sort of prototype stock exchange .
5856	The family name , Beurze , explains the origins of the name for similar operations all over the Continent .
5857	Their house is now a bank .
5858	Nowadays the bourgeoisie is more likely to patronise the city 's luxurious food and clothes shops , all housed in the medieval streets .
5859	The oldest tavern is the Vlissinghe , of which mention was first made in 1552 , but there are hundreds of little bars and cafes , many of them housed in olde-worlde buildings that have the Americans squealing with delight .
5860	Plenty have terraces from which to watch the world go by accompanied by a hot waffle or a glass of beer .
5861	There were once 40 breweries in Bruges , and although now there are only two , the choice of Belgian beers is still enormous .
5862	One cafe lists 300 .
5863	My rich , dark Trappist practically knocked me for six at lunchtime , while a deep red cherry beer , Kriek , tasted like alcoholic cough mixture .
5864	For more substantial meals there are plenty of bigger cafes and restaurants offering set-price menus .
5865	The north side of the market square , the Markt , is lined with them , and for about £6 you can have three basic courses .
5866	For a little more many include fish treats such as half a dozen oysters in season ; waterzooi , fish cooked in a light stock and served with leeks and carrots ; a fillet of turbot or chunks of eel in a green herb sauce .
5867	An enormous bowl of mussels cooked in a delicious liquor with celery , onion , parsley and plenty of black pepper can be had for about £4 .
5868	The open air fish market does brisk business every morning except Sunday and Monday and is well worth a visit for its display of fresh and smoked specialities , as well as a huge range of shellfish .
5869	It is best not to leave eating too late .
5870	Bruges goes to bed early and can hardly be said to be throbbing with night-life .
5871	Last weekend the highlights were marionettes miming to Die Fledermaus at the puppet theatre and a country music festival .
5872	We did try a night cap in a ‘ classical music pub ’ but as it was in the underground of a shopping arcade , and the clientele seemed more interested in chomping through their steak and chips than appreciating Karajan 's version of the Emperor Concerto , we just had the one .
5873	Once fully saturated with culture , food , drink or any combination of the three , it is possible to escape the tourist honeypots , which are mostly in the centre and south of town .
5874	To the north the streets are quieter , and by following the canals — a smelly exercise in high summer , no doubt — or simply the end of your nose , Bruges can be appreciated on a more domestic scale .
5875	The flat-fronted facades are often decorated with intricate brickwork , and even modern restorations seem to be strictly controlled in a style that combines discreet Post-Modern twiddly with forms and colours that are in the spirit of the original .
5876	There are few cars here , though lots of bicycles , very few dogs and almost no dog mess ( even the horse-drawn buggies for tourist joyrides have built-in pooper scoopers ) .
5877	Best of all , there are hardly any other tourists .
5878	Accommodation : The Bruges tourist office produces a comprehensive guide .
5879	Independent travel : Bruges is four hours from Victoria by train via Dover and the 90 minute jetfoil to Ostend .
5880	Alternatively you can fly to Brussels or Antwerp and take the train to Bruges .
5881	Eating Out : Plenty of places in all price ranges — just look at the menu displayed and take your pick .
5882	Serious eaters look at the red Michelin Benelux guide , which lists about 25 restaurants in the centre , a handful of which have one star .
5883	Appetites should be matched by pockets , as here you are entering £30-a-head-plus territory .
5884	Markets : Apart from the fish market , there is a general market every Saturday morning on T'Zand , on the west side of town , and every Wednesday on the Burg , in the centre .
5885	A flea market along the Dijver , one of the main canals , takes place on Saturday and Sunday from March to October but looks like a real tourist trap .
5886	Books : Blue Guide to Belgium and Luxembourg ( Black/Norton , £11.95 ) , good for historical sights ; Brugge Inside Out available locally for about £4 is useful for more down-to-earth matters .
5887	Useful information : From October to March the Tourist Information Office in the Burg ( 44 86 86 ) is open Mon-Sat 9.30am-12.45pm and 2am-5.45pm , closed Sundays .
5888	It sells combination tickets to four museums for about £3 .
5889	Agenda Brugge is a useful free guide to what 's on each month .
5890	Ostend Ferries : P&amp;O European Ferries ( 0304 203388 ) has up to six sailings a day in each direction from Dover to Ostend , crossing time four hours ; a 60-hour return for a 4.5 metre car and two adults costs from £50 to £89 depending on sailing .
5891	Zeebrugge Ferries : North Sea Ferries ( 0482 77177 ) has a daily sailing from Hull to Zeebrugge : crossing time 14 hours .
5892	Short break fares including one night 's hotel accommodation in Bruges , cost from £78 per person — cars extra .
5893	P&amp;O European Ferries ( 0304 203388 ) has five sailings a day in each direction from Dover to Zeebrugge : crossing time four and a half hours .
5894	A 60-hour return for a 4.5 metre car and two adults costs from £50 to £89 , depending on sailing .
5895	P&amp;O has two sailings a day from Felixstowe to Zeebrugge , crossing time five and a half hours .
5896	A 60-hour return for a car and two adults costs from £55 to £94 .
5897	Dunkirk Ferries : Sally ( 0843 595522 ) operates five sailings a day from Ramsgate to Dunkirk : crossing time is two hours , 30 minutes .
5898	A 60-hour return for a 4.5 metre car and two adults costs from £47 to £84 , depending on day and time of travel .
5899	Market : The town market takes place on Wednesday and Saturday in the place Jean Bart .
5900	Hypermarket : The best is Auchan on the RN1 , en route to the Sally ferry terminal .
5901	It accepts Visa cards .
5902	On the horns of the Bull Ring dilemma : The people of Birmingham should be allowed to vote on the future development of their city , Jonathan Glancey believes
5903	By JONATHAN GLANCEY
5904	BIRMINGHAM 'S infamous and exhausted retail hub , the Bull Ring , just 25 years old , has been placed on architecture 's death row .
5905	There will be no stay of execution and few mourners for this spoiled concrete child of the Sixties .
5906	Old before its time , the Bull Ring has been accused of the systematic rape of the second city .
5907	It also stands accused of murdering the much-loved area around the old Bull Ring market that had grown up in piecemeal fashion over the 800 years since Birmingham was granted a market charter in 1150 .
5908	This had survived the worst the Luftwaffe could do , but was no match for ‘ comprehensive redevelopment ’ .
5909	The Bull Ring , completed by Laing Developments in 1964 , rammed together four levels of shopping , a market hall , a multi-storey car park , an office block , a bus station and a banqueting suite all in one vast complex .
5910	Snaking between its constituent parts was the controversial and overwhelming city ring road designed by the successive and all-powerful city engineers , Herbert Manzoni and Neville Borg .
5911	The most militant fan of Sixties architecture would be hard pressed to support a last-minute appeal for the Bull Ring , although crocodile tears will be shed over the probable demolition of the Rotunda , a monumental steel and glass phallus , that , in the absence of a sky-piercing cathedral , acts as the city 's one instantly recognisable focal point .
5912	But what is going to replace the Bull Ring ?
5913	Given the stupendous costs involved , should the city be looking to powerful private developers working with big firms of commercial architects to take the lead and replace like with like , albeit in a more acceptable architectural garb ?
5914	Or should development be given over to a broad church of interest groups and realised by a catholic mix of architects working in a number of complementary styles ?
5915	The debate in Birmingham has reached something like fever pitch , now that the city council is faced with two rival development schemes .
5916	On the one side is the developer , London &amp; Edinburgh Trust ( LET ) and its architects , Chapman Taylor Partners .
5917	On the other is the pressure group , Birmingham for People , championed by local architect Joe Holyoak .
5918	LET is in a strong position .
5919	It has owned the leasehold of the Bull Ring and surrounding sites since 1985 .
5920	As LET's partner in charge of the Bull Ring project , John Newman , says : ‘ We do n't have to develop the Bull Ring .
5921	We could just sit back and collect rents from an ever-decreasing number of tenants .
5922	Instead , we 're willing to take the risk and give Birmingham the retail centre it deserves and needs if it is not to be completely undermined by rival out-of-town attractions . ’
5923	The LET scheme is , in outline at least , straightforward .
5924	It envisages replacing the Bull Ring development with a vast new shopping complex , almost free from the graffiti-sprayed subways that have characterised central Birmingham since the mid-Sixties .
5925	Shoppers approaching what LET have named The Galleries from New Street and High Street will be channeled along a brand new street flanked by granite and stone-clad pseudo-Classical shops and offices , entering the new mall under a vast glazed dome , second in diameter only to that of St Paul 's Cathedral .
5926	From this generous lobby , looked down on by diners perched high in the dome 's galleries , shoppers will be able to pass either directly down to the open-air market in the shadow of old St Martin 's church , explore the curving three-storey shopping halls or snack in a galaxy of glitzy cafes .
5927	The attractions of LET's scheme are easy for city councillors to appreciate .
5928	The Galleries will act as a one million sq ft magnet to six million shoppers , not just from Birmingham , but from the entire West Midlands conurbation and beyond .
5929	Birmingham is well served by public transport , while its frequently denigrated ring road system allows traffic to flow at a remarkably fast pace ( 17.5mph in rush hours compared to central London 's 9 or 10mph ) .
5930	Parking for 3,500 cars , either underground or else in a well disguised Post-Modern palazzo , will encourage shoppers to steer away from rival retail developments in surrounding Solihull , Leamington Spa and Kidderminster , along with the out-of-town Sandwell Mall and Merry Hill Centre .
5931	The Galleries will bridge the snarling ring road , which will be buried in decorous tunnels .
5932	Rodney Karen , the affable architect in charge of the design of The Galleries , guarantees that they will have a truly urban character .
5933	This will not be theme park shopping , Karen insists , nor will The Galleries be closed at night .
5934	They will form a integral part of the city , opening up new pedestrian routes , while upgrading existing ones .
5935	But Joe Holyoak and the Birmingham for People group believe The Galleries will simply repeat the mistakes made in the early Sixties , but on an even bigger scale .
5936	Holyoak 's attack , published in a recent issue of The Architects ' Journal , is based on two premises .
5937	First he takes the city council to task for presenting the LET scheme as a fait accompli , criticising it for ‘ accepting without question LET's objective of redevelopment in the form of 500-metre-long , inward-looking building ’ .
5938	Holyoak gleefully points out that architect Tony Ridell , of Chapman Taylor Partners , has , rather unfortunately , described The Galleries as ‘ a huge aircraft carrier settled on the streetscape of the city ’ .
5939	Second , Holyoak attacks the monumentality of The Galleries which , in his words ‘ is the latest in the big developers ’ move to privatise city centres — to eat up public space and reshape it as internalised , homogenised , security-patrolled private space' .
5940	Instead , Holyoak proposes a People 's Plan for the Bull Ring .
5941	This consists of a return to traditional principles of town planning , of conventional streets , markets and shops .
5942	The People 's Plan includes houses , which the LET scheme expressly discounts .
5943	‘ A healthy city , ’ says Holyoak , ‘ needs a diversity of uses as well as diversity of design . ’
5944	But , more than that , the People 's Plan is an attempt to allow for incremental growth and change .
5945	‘ Its development , ’ says Holyoak , ‘ would not necessitate the great cataclysm of demolition ; the plan is designed so that parts of it can be built independently in phases . ’
5946	Holyoak has another trump card up his sleeve .
5947	‘ The removal of through traffic , pedestrianisation , new public spaces , new mixed uses , living in the city , environmental quality , removal of subways : all these aspects of the Peoples ’ Plan are city council policies contained in the City Centre Strategy published in 1987 . ’
5948	Holyoak believes that the council has been bamboozled into adopting LET's monolithic scheme which has had outline planning permission for the last year .
5949	‘ If , ’ he says , ‘ the city council grants full planning permission for The Galleries in the next few weeks , it will not simply be shooting itself in the foot but blowing off its entire leg . ’
5950	John Newman of LET is unrepentant .
5951	‘ Holyoak talks about building houses in the centre of Birmingham .
5952	But who wants to live there ?
5953	Would you ?
5954	I think he 's lost in a Victorian vision of Britain . ’
5955	But what about using a variety of architects and splitting the scheme into a number of smaller related parts ?
5956	Newman explains that LET works with big practices of commercial architects because time and time again they come up with the goods , on budget , on time and with none of the tantrums of the prima donna .
5957	LET's experience of working with ‘ name ’ architects has not been very fruitful .
5958	‘ Chapman Taylor on the other hand , ’ says Newman , ‘ understand exactly what the retailer wants . ’
5959	Chapman Taylor architect Rodney Karen thinks Holyoak 's scheme is a case of ‘ fiddling while Rome burns ’ .
5960	He warns : ‘ Birmingham has to compete with outlying attractions .
5961	At the moment all the centre offers is anxiety .
5962	I see The Galleries as a focal point , a powerful force aiding the city , a proper part of the centre designed to enhance its life and character . ’
5963	But what sort of character ?
5964	Whether Birmingham city council should push ahead with the LET scheme or stop to consider Holyoak 's counterblast must turn on what sort of centre the city wants .
5965	Does Birmingham want a centre where people live and work , or a shopping complex that draws in people who live and sleep at the end of the bus routes ?
5966	Do they want to plan for organic change or reap the fruit of a retail giant that might , no matter what the quality of the architecture , be redundant in another 25 years ?
5967	It is difficult not to sympathise with the People for Birmingham 's scheme .
5968	It might be quixotic , it might be full of contradictions and loopholes ( how will the traffic flow if the ring road is downgraded as Holyoak plans ? why save the Rotunda , when trying to recreate a traditional city centre ? ) , but it does recognise that a city centre works best when it is the sum of a number of interrelated parts .
5969	The people of Birmingham ought to be allowed to vote on this all-important issue .
5970	Are they , and do they want to be , urbanites or suburbanites ?
5971	Both Joe Holyoak and his rivals really ought to know .
5972	A prayer for the brick cathedral facing St Paul 's : Bankside Power Station is a masterpiece worth preserving , Gavin Stamp argues
5973	By GAVIN STAMP
5974	FROM the top of the dome of St Paul 's Cathedral the view is no longer dominated by City church steeples but by an intrusive cacophony of drab , characterless Sixties boxes .
5975	One building stands out in this dispiriting panorama of post-war mediocrity : a dark powerful mass of brickwork with a tall central tower that stands right across the Thames from Wren 's dome .
5976	This is not an office block , nor a church — although its sublime form might suggest that its architect was adept at designing cathedrals .
5977	It is , in fact , the now redundant oil-fired electric power station that sits on Bankside next to the site of Sam Wanamaker 's new Globe Theatre .
5978	Bankside Power Station should never have been built .
5979	Its architect had spent the war years with fellow Royal Academicians planning the orderly and spacious London of the future , free of smoke and industry .
5980	But , when asked in 1947 to replace an old dirty power station that had been on the site since 1891 , he soon forgot such idealism and , like any architect , was glad to have the job .
5981	The project was controversial and the power station was only permitted providing the smoke was clean and the building did not challenge the visual dominance of St Paul 's .
5982	So the single chimney rose only to 325ft , some 45ft below the height of the cross above the cathedral .
5983	The irony is that had the tower been higher and had the teak ‘ scrubbers ’ been less efficient , the smoke would have gone straight up into the air .
5984	As it was , the ‘ smokeless shimmer of vapour ’ was so cooled by cleaning that it drifted across the river to cause mischief with the leadwork on Wren 's great dome .
5985	Bankside Power Station should not have been built .
5986	But , as it was built , it should not now be demolished .
5987	That is because it is a magnificent structure , the supreme architectural expression of the heroic , monumental phase of power station design and the creation of a great architect .
5988	Bankside was the work of Sir Giles Gilbert Scott , OM , the architect of Liverpool 's Anglican Cathedral , the rebuilt House of Commons and some of the last vital products of the Gothic Revival .
5989	He was a designer of extraordinary versatility , being responsible for the standard ‘ traditional ’ red telephone kiosk , Waterloo Bridge and several power stations .
5990	Bankside represents the fullest realisation of his industrial aesthetic .
5991	Scott 's first venture into this unlikely field of design was at Battersea where , in 1930 , he was wheeled in as a famous knighted architect by the London Power Company to try to make acceptable the coal-fired monster power station to which the residents of Chelsea and Westminster were taking strong exception .
5992	This was a brilliant move .
5993	Scott was so successful in styling the building in fine brickwork with ‘ jazz-modern ’ fluting ( as John Betjeman called it ) that , when the Battersea ‘ A ’ station was opened in 1934 it was widely acclaimed as a supremely successful modern treatment of a building type that seemed quintessentially twentieth century .
5994	When , in 1939 , The Architects ' Journal conducted a survey to find what were considered the best modern buildings in Britain , Battersea was placed second — and was the favourite of such unlikely celebrities as Sir Kenneth Clark , Rebecca West and Charles Laughton .
5995	Scott was so pleased with the style he had evolved at Battersea , a treatment that humanised industrial forms without denying their function , that he also used it on the Guinness Factory at Park Royal , west London .
5996	At Battersea , Scott could not alter the basic design of the building and he much disliked the ‘ upturned table ’ appearance created by the four corner chimneys .
5997	At Bankside , however , he was able to persuade the engineers , Mott , Hay &amp; Anderson , to gather all the flues into a single ‘ slender tower or campanile ’ .
5998	As a result , he was able to create a symmetrical , monumental composition of great power .
5999	As at all his power stations , Scott faced the building in a fine Worcestershire brick that has weathered to a lovely pinky-brown .
6000	But there is nothing homely about the general effect .
6001	Vast overlapping planes of brickwork are modelled with careful set-backs and subtle bands of detail .
6002	The result is an expression of the monumental aesthetic of the early twentieth century , with strong American overtones .
6003	When the campanile is seen from a distance , it seems to belong to some strange Expressionist church one has not noticed before .
6004	Not for nothing were such power stations described as ‘ brick cathedrals ’ ; Bankside is the finest manifestation of this tradition .
6005	Now it is redundant .
6006	Smoke shimmers no longer from the tall tower .
6007	But Bankside is nevertheless a sound structure which , like the best mills of the Industrial Revolution , is well worth preserving and is perfectly capable of adaptation for a new commercial use .
6008	Such re-use is , of course , much encouraged by a building being listed , something which , until recently , was not possible with architecture of so recent a date .
6009	Two years ago , however , the Department of the Environment at last began the listing of post-war buildings in England that were more than 30 years old .
6010	Bracken House , the former home of the Financial Times , became the first candidate and English Heritage then submitted some 70 recommendations to the Department of the Environment ; these included Bankside .
6011	This , however , was too much for the Government and , using the excuse that public opinion was not yet ready to accept the protection of many unpopular modern buildings , Lord Caithness , the Minister of State for the Environment , arbitrarily whittled down English Heritage 's list to 18 buildings - excluding Bankside — although it represented a more traditional approach in the Fifties to the now-unfashionable Modern Movement .
6012	However , Caithness himself stated that this first selection was ‘ in no way a definitive list …
6013	I have no doubt that others will be added .
6014	The important thing is that the Thirty Year Rule is in force and that we can respond to developing perceptions of our times . ’
6015	Earlier this year , in my capacity as chairman of the Thirties Society , I asked Caithness 's successor , Virginia Bottomley , to reconsider English Heritage 's recommendation of Bankside for listing .
6016	My argument was that , as Michael Heseltine had so boldly listed Battersea Power Station in 1980 , it was illogical not to protect a much finer and more complete industrial work by the same architect .
6017	Furthermore , the listing of Battersea had ensured the building 's survival for conversion to a new use — in that case , as an entertainment centre which the Prime Minister herself had praised and inaugurated .
6018	After two months ' silence , I was informed that ministers stood by their decision .
6019	I wrote back asking the reasons for this , pointing out that , if any large modern power station deserved to be listed , it was Bankside .
6020	I have received no satisfactory reply .
6021	Of course , I know perfectly well why the Department of the Environment declines to list it .
6022	Listed building procedures might impede the full commercial realisation of the site when the electricity industry is privatised .
6023	Furthermore , British Rail has its eyes on the Bankside site for bringing up the spoil from the tunnel for Channel traffic which it is , so absurdly , driving under the middle of London at astronomical cost .
6024	Listing , in theory , is an objective assessment of architectural or historical importance which does not necessarily prevent demolition .
6025	In the case of Bankside Power Station , the ultimate ‘ temple of power ’ and a masterpiece of industrial architecture by a major twentieth-century British architect , our historic building system is being perverted for purely political reasons .

6045	MUSIC / Beware the pitfalls of sincerity : Composer Robin Holloway considers the difficulties of assessing a new piece of music .
6046	By ROBIN HOLLOWAY
6047	How to ensure a sympathetic reception for a new piece of music ?
6048	Ideally the subject should combine Ecology ( with special reference to tropical rain-forests ) with Protest ( preferably shrill and futile ) .
6049	It should climax with an ecumenical prayer ( in every known language simultaneously ) for intergalactic peace .
6050	The musical material should include at least three of the following : Jewish cantillation , Catholic plainsong , Tibetan chanting , Aboriginal drumming , whalesong .
6051	The idiom should be middle-of-the-road , artfully diguised with mod cons ( clusters , glissandi , electronics ) : there should be a strong pop-music element , plenty of repetition a la Philip Glass .
6052	When inspiration fails , fill the gaps with ritual gong-strokes , prolonged and amplified to the threshold of pain .
6053	But such cynicism will not do ; this is a serious matter .
6054	A recent first visit to the USSR brought into focus for me the large question of evaluating music whose basis of appeal is grounded in extra-musical circumstances .
6055	The first problem is the dispassionate judgement of compositions that emerge from , and in some cases directly express , political oppression .
6056	The wide current appeal of such music seems to touch a nerve of communal masochism .
6057	Audiences yearn to groan under the yoke of suffering they may never have experienced .
6058	There is even a kind of envy for the depth of vision which this fate is thought to produce .
6059	The conspicuous case is Shostakovich , a composer of enormous gifts and awesome copiousness , the only one to satisfy , if intermittently , both his masters and the West .
6060	Ever since the ‘ just criticism ’ meted out to his early excesses , then the gigantic success of the Leningrad Symphony in the 1940s , he has symbolized the artist caught in the net of public events .
6061	As we now know something of the appalling story of his hounding by cultural officialdom , the raucous irony of the middle works and the bitter blackness of the last become entirely comprehensible .
6062	His is the only post-war body of symphonic and chamber music to achieve genuine popularity .
6063	Yet it is drastically imperfect .
6064	Impressive inspirations mix with the coarsest triteness ; there is an inordinate amount of padding and bombast ; the reliance on formulae is the most shameless since Telemann .
6065	Nor did things improve as he grew beyond subjection to state reproof .
6066	Some late works , notably the Fourteenth Symphony and the songs on Michaelangelo texts are among his greatest .
6067	But in the succession of late string quartets , poverty of substance and spiritual exhaustion are exemplified rather than expressed .
6068	Shostakovich , obviously pre-eminent among Soviet composers , had to bear the cruellest treatment .
6069	Bold spirits in the satellite countries were able to take liberties at home ( Lutoslawski , Penderecki , Kurtag ) when they did n't get away in person ( Panufnik , Ligeti ) .
6070	The recent change of policy has unfrozen a flood of music by younger figures who have not undergone similar cultural repression , though the conditions of their work remain poignant and precarious .
6071	Recently it has been well-aired in this country through broadcasts and festivals ; enough to form an initial overall view .
6072	I believe that music-lovers are deluded when they claim to find artistic pleasure in any but a fraction of this music .
6073	Here , as with most of Shostakovich , the content they locate is a projection of what they know of its circumstances - by which only a heart of stone would not be moved .
6074	Take away this knowledge and the appeal would vanish , for the music is rarely able to stand on its own merits .
6075	The second problem is the evaluation of new music that ‘ deals ’ with religious subject-matter , however vague .
6076	A nostalgia has become apparent , after an era of aggressive atheism , either for the great organized beliefs or for substitutes chiming better with the would-be freer spirit of the times .
6077	In the Sixties Gurus and pop music were the thing ; the present mood is sombre and apocalyptic .
6078	In both , the identification with music that attempts to express any part of this vast area tends to be one of self-deceiving empathy .
6079	A spiritual void needs to be satisfied , so what is offered as serious and sacrosanct must be as good as it pretends .
6080	Instances would include the St Luke Passion by Penderecki and the St John by Arvo Part , Messiaen 's Transfiguration , Britten 's War Requiem .
6081	Tippett 's Mask of Time and Birtwistle 's Mask of Orpheus , Steve Reich 's Desert Music , much of the output of John Tavener and Jonathan Harvey ; above all , Stockhausen 's seven-day wonder , Licht .
6082	Such religious/humanitarian subject-matter — even the Holocaust , Hiroshima and Aids have not escaped — makes a fortress as unassailable by criticism as the art produced under tyranny .
6083	The worth of individual pieces is , obviously , very various ; consistent is the appeal to piety , ensuring that the elevated theme produces a warm-hearted response .
6084	These composers are not coldly exploiting their audiences ' kindness ; they are all equally the victims of the going ideology .
6085	And sincerity is not in question .
6086	But the hard truth , nailed with all-time accuracy by the other great composer from Leningrad ( the one who got out ) is that sincerity does not guarantee quality .
6087	‘ Most art is sincere , ’ Stravinsky added , ‘ and most art is bad ’ .
6088	Ersatz emotion replaces musical content .
6089	The genuine difficulty of understanding intricate artistic designs is evaded by the factitious difficulty of being exalted or troubled by important messages which have nothing to do with musical worth .
6090	Artistic value is not an ‘ extra ’ even in a threnody for Chernobyl .
6091	Without it , message or vision are wishful thinking .
6092	Audiences ' large capacities for ersatz-importance show how eager they are to be deeply stirred ; how easily gulled ; how low the threshold of enjoyment must be set for music of our time .
6093	What little appeal it has seems to depend heavily on these impurities .
6094	No one would deny that music can embody great humane and religious themes .
6095	That it does so , so profoundly , is a vital part of what it is for .
6096	There is spiritual value in the very handling of its primary elements to write a little song or dance , even an exercise ; even , as Bruckner used to show his classes , in a fifth or octave struck at a piano .
6097	The essence of music 's higher flights is transcendental in the highest degree imaginable , in ways that are manifestly intelligible and effectual , and quite insusceptible to verbal accounting .
6098	Debussy 's answer to a journalist who asked if he was familiar with heaven — ‘ yes , but I do n't natter about it with strangers ’ - is not so silly as it sounds .
6099	Evasive certainly , but only to acknowledge what can not be uttered .
6100	The good composer expresses what he feels and makes what he is making , from an essentially musical motivation , by essentially musical means , with all the skill and experience he can command .
6101	The ends are various : here a visionary oratorio , there an opera buffa ; here a craggy piano etude , there a melting morceau de salon .
6102	The degree of craft , the degree of inspiration , are the measure whereby they can be valued ; through these are achieved , consciously or inadvertently , the heights and depths of spiritual expression whereby they are ‘ a joy for ever ’ .
6103	Music can only be judged on the basis of an attentiveness to its musical essence as sensitive and discriminating as possible .
6104	Above all , as specific — an undogmatic reaction to the details in style and technique of the particular composer , piece , or passage .
6105	Naturally this will include transcendental subject-matter if it 's there , and recognize the moments where this sweeps all before it .
6106	All the rest is emotional blackmail .
6107	RECORD REVIEWS / Violent measure : Shostakovich : Piano Concerto No 1 , Chamber Symphony , Seven Preludes Op 34 .
6108	Evgeny Kissin ( piano ) , Moscow Virtuosi .
6109	Vladimir Spivakov .
6110	RCA Victor RD87947 Rachmaninov : Preludes Op 32 .
6111	Shostakovich : Piano Sonata No 1 .
6112	Lilya Zilberstein ( piano ) .
6113	DG427766-2
6114	By SIMON MUNDY
6115	IT IS 14 years since Shostakovich died .
6116	Nonetheless his reputation as at once the most searching and accessible of contemporary composers has not diminished .
6117	If anything , fashion is moving closer to the context of his style with the passage of time .
6118	In the 1970s his language did indeed seem a little old-fashioned .
6119	Now , as composers grope towards a language that satisfies audiences and yet manages to be sufficiently modern , Shostakovich 's music sounds at the front once again .
6120	There has been a welcome pile of new recordings issued recently ; not just of the symphonies , but of the concertos and chamber music as well .
6121	Two of them mark the start of international recording careers for extraordinary young Soviet pianists , Evgeny Kissin and Lilya Zilberstein , who were only children when Shostakovich died .
6122	Kissin , aged 18 , came to prominence a couple of years ago when he appeared to great acclaim at the Berlin Festival .
6123	His recording of the First Piano Concerto is sparklingly assured — crisply articulated but with enough sensitivity to convey the inevitable bitter-sweet character of the slow movement .
6124	This is anyway a stunning disc , thanks to the playing of the Moscow Virtuosi with Spivakov .
6125	Their performances of the orchestral arrangements — the Chamber Symphony ( arranged by Rudolph Barshai from the Eighth Quartet ) and the Opus 34 Preludes ( arranged by Victor Poltoratsky from the piano original ) are superbly polished .
6126	Lilya Zilberstein , at 24 , is also an impressive discovery .
6127	Her first record shows her to be as musical as she is technically accomplished .
6128	The pithy violence of Shostakovich 's First Sonata does not come naturally to her , but she is at home in the limpid impressionism of Rachmaninov 's G major Prelude , which on its own makes this disc worth having .
6129	The lyrical and passionate aspects of Shostakovich , rather than the bitterly satirical , also bring out the best in Julian Lloyd Webber 's playing .
6130	His elegiac tempo for the largo of the Cello Sonata allows him a sustained outpouring of feeling .
6131	John McCabe 's accompanying , too , is wonderfully supportive .
6132	The Sonata is imaginatively coupled with Britten 's , written after his first meeting with Shostakovich in 1961 .
6133	The usual characters of the two composers are reversed here ; there is little of the English scene-painter in Britten 's Sonata , and it stands as one of his most nervous and angry works .
6134	Lloyd Webber and McCabe , both amiable men , sense the unease and respond to it deftly .
6135	Itzhak Perlman 's account of Shostakovich 's First Violin Concerto is a more rough-hewn affair .
6136	Perlman is usually the slickest of violinists , but here he seems to cultivate a rasping sound that emphasises the work 's macabre portrait of Stalin 's Russia in the late 1940s .
6137	This , along with the concerto by Shostakovich 's teacher Glazunov , was recorded live in Tel Aviv in July 1988 so there is a spate of clapping at the end .
6138	But the acoustic captured by the engineers is reasonably spacious .
6139	I have reservations about Perlman and Mehta 's treatment of the Glazunov , though , which seems neither as richly romantic as Oscar Shumsky 's on Chandos , nor as glittering as Anne-Sophie Mutter 's on Erato : the other two versions to appear in the last year .
6140	In this silkiest of works there needs to be an elegant bonhomie , mixed with a hint of gentle sadness , which quite eludes the Israel PO and the soloist , who seem intent on squeezing out each last drip of sentiment — surely a misunderstanding of the composer 's style and aspirations .
6141	MUSIC / Enlightened views : OAE / Mackerras — Queen Elizabeth Hall
6142	By TESS KNIGHTON
6143	HAYDN-LOVERS are in for a good time this autumn : coming up are the Haydn at Esterhaza concerts at the Wigmore Hall ( part of the Magyarok Britain Salutes Hungary Festival ) ; already on display is the Haydn and England exhibition at the British Library ; and just started is the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment 's QEH Haydn series concentrating on his late choral works .

6146	This was music-making of a high order .
6147	Mackerras 's account was compassionate but redblooded , direct but full of charm .
6148	It did not set out to be radically different , though Haydn 's colourful scoring was certainly enhanced by the use of period instruments ( including a fortepiano in the recitatives and a bass line reinforced more consistently by bass trombone and contra bassoon ) , but it succeeded in being unforced and unfettered .
6149	He made the most of his superb wind section , used the extra clarity of the strings to underline the richness of the harmony , and encouraged the brass to cut through the texture and pin down the rhythm as , for example , in the exhilarating chorus ‘ Achieved is the Glorious Work ’ .
6150	The audiences at the first performances of The Creation in Vienna in the late 1790s were entranced by Haydn 's musical depictions of every living creature from the mighty eagle to the lowly worm .
6151	Only a short while later these were accused ( by Schiller amongst others ) of being not worthy of him - ‘ Fit only for the nursery , to use in connection with Noah 's Ark ’ — but the truth is they are irresistible .
6152	Lynne Dawson 's clear voice soared and trilled through ‘ The Birds ’ number , while Wilson-Johnson 's worm was creepily sinuous .
6153	This was an uplifting experience — as Haydn intended it should be .
