7071	However , the very preoccupation with identifying causal influences begs more fundamental questions about whether contemporaries shared intellectual assumptions .
7072	For example , the Scientific Revolution of the seventeenth century was constituted not only by the new theories of Descartes , Galileo and Newton but also by new ways of experiencing the world , interacting with it and thinking about it .
7073	According to this claim , the mores of the eighteenth century were radically different from the sixteenth .
7074	Yet this difference is somewhat obscured in Kemp 's analysis by his concern to explicate the details of numerous perspective schemes and the techniques employed by artists .
7075	He thereby pays less attention than he might to interpreting the science of art as a cultural phenomenon .
7076	Ideological and philosophical issues receive inadequate attention and yet these could have helped define the common context ( or , perhaps , the contrasting contexts ) in which art and science were pursued .
7077	Again , Kemp 's subject raises important questions about the structure and function of institutions which he only engages parenthetically .
7078	More generally , a less causal and more structural approach might have been fruitful in illuminating the historical conditioning of the science of art .
7079	Another example of a terminological difficulty arises in the section in which Kemp briefly examines the relation between perspective and eighteenth-century theories of perception .
7080	Unfortunately he predicates his discussion on the contrast between ‘ empiricists ’ and ‘ nativists ’ , a distinction he soon recognises as inadequate .
7081	In the light of Kemp 's historiography , it is not surprising that he concludes that ideas about perception ( which were often explicitly discussed by ‘ scientists ’ and ‘ philosophers ' ) had little impact on artists ( p. 237 ) .
7082	While he has usefully identified theories of perception as an aspect of the science of art , they deserve a more eclectic and sustained analysis .
7083	Let me therefore mention briefly some further dimensions of the subject .
7084	Many artists , scientists and philosophers engaged the question of whether linear ( or any other ) perspective provides the true account of how we perceive .
7085	For some authors perspective provides both the laws of perception and also the key to the true and rational representation of objects .
7086	Learn perspective and you can imitate nature precisely .
7087	However , many artists seriously questioned this wisdom .
7088	In their art they combined perspective with drawing ‘ by eye ’ ; they instinctively knew when to follow the rules and when to break them .
7089	This , for Kemp , is an important clue to the success of Velázquez and Turner for whom perspective was a useful servant but a poor master .
7090	But artists were not alone in considering and debating the truth and limitations of perspective .
7091	A related point on which most ( but not all ) physical scientists ( or , more appropriately , natural philosophers ) of the seventeenth century would have agreed , was the primacy of mathematics in analysing the physical universe .
7092	Their reasons for adopting this view differed somewhat , but we can take Galileo 's position as not atypical .
7093	Echoing Plato , Galileo claimed that God had created the world according to mathematical proportions .
7094	This implied that only in the sphere of the mathematical sciences can the human intellect attain knowledge that is as objective and as certain as it is known to the divine mind .
7095	Through mathematics truth and reality could be laid bare and appearances transcended .
7096	This metaphysical commitment came under scrutiny not only from those artists who refused to be limited by the laws of perspective but also from ‘ scientists ’ and ‘ philosophers ’ .
7097	One of the most forceful attacks was by George Berkeley in his An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision ( 1709 ) .
7098	Here Berkeley argued strenuously against the view that we judge the distance of objects by means of lines and angles .
7099	Although most commentators have claimed that Berkeley 's principal opponent was Descartes , whom he cited as an example only in the second ( 1710 ) edition , he was more generally denying the widely-received assumption that we see according to the laws of geometry — this assumption being central to the perspectivist tradition .
7100	( Berkeley was familiar with perspective machines , one of which he described in a later work . )
7101	Instead , Berkeley sought to show that we learn to judge the distance , magnitude and situation of objects .
7102	This controversial book was widely discussed but whether it was read by artists I leave to further research .
7103	Berkeley was not alone in questioning whether geometrical methods are adequate to account for visual perception since there was a large literature on the subject by ‘ scientists ’ and , as Kemp shows , artists also frequently commented on it .
7104	One of the leading problems in this area was the horizontal moon illusion : the moon appears larger near the horizon than in its zenith .
7105	Since Ptolemy tried to solve this problem in the second century , it has been on the agenda of theorists of perception and is still , I understand , not fully resolved .
7106	In the eighteenth century it was one of the main test cases for the dominance of geometry .
7107	Attacks on geometrically-based theories of vision ( together with the deployment of such examples as the horizontal moon illusion ) provide a theme of common concern to artists , scientists and philosophers and deserve further analysis than Kemp offers .
7108	If there are aspects of the science of art that Kemp fails to engage adequately , the scope of this book is nevertheless very impressive and a number of the issues he discusses impinge on my concerns as an historian of science .
7109	Let me allude to two of these issues .
7110	In the history of science theoria has usually been accorded far greater importance than praxis .
7111	The general view has been that theoria is the engine driving the historical development of science and that praxis is merely the application of theoria .
7112	Although some historians , often Marxists , have rejected this consensus , only recently have aspects of praxis , such as laboratory skills , been subjected to close and sustained study .
7113	In this respect the historian of science has much to learn from an art historian like Kemp .
7114	Moreover , the analysis of skills provides a common topic of research for both art and science historians .
7115	The second issue concerns the art-science relationship which Kemp analyses through the history of perspective and of colour .
7116	The latter case is the more straightforward since he presents the impact of Newton 's theory of coloured light as radically reorientating this area .
7117	With perspective , the key figures of the Scientific Revolution are presented as the heirs to developments in art .
7118	For example , we encounter Galileo as a bit-player who corresponded with Lodovico Cigoli over his lunar and sunspot observations .
7119	More particularly , Galileo used standard perspective procedures in accounting for the foreshortening of the spots which he claimed in 1613 were on the surface of the sun .
7120	Unfortunately Kepler receives even less attention .
7121	Yet in 1600 Kepler made important contributions to optical science , especially to the theory of image formation .
7122	Kepler 's concern with the formation of images was a response to a practical problem .
7123	He noticed that when viewed with a camera obscura the image of the sun was too large but this enlargement was not explained by existing theory .
7124	Instead , he conceived every illuminated point being the source of rays spreading in all directions ; a bundle of these rays ( rather than a single ray ) pass through the hole in a camera obscura ( or the pupil of the eye ) .
7125	Thus the image is enlarged owing to the finite size of the hole .
7126	In his resolution of the problem Kepler represented his rays by strings .
7127	For example , in ascertaining the image of a book on a distant plane , he adopted a procedure familiar to artists for almost a century .
7128	He used a stretched string to plot ray paths that just grazed the book in their transit from the source of the screen .
7129	This method of repeatedly deploying a stretched string to plot the light rays and thus ascertain selected points on an image was incorporated into the perspective machines described by Leonardo and Dürer .
7130	While the example of Kepler illustrates the influence of artistic practice on a ‘ scientist ’ ( which is not Kemp 's primary concern ) , discussion of this instance would have enhanced considerably the author 's argument that both the theory and practice of perspective were significant resources for the Scientific Revolution of the seventeenth century .
7131	He also argues that , in its turn , the Scientific Revolution had some effect on the visual arts .
7132	Military engineers , who were also often mathematicians , such as Simon Stevin and Girard Desargues , contributed significantly to the subject of perspective .
7133	Newton is portrayed as influencing eighteenth-century perspective in an unspecified manner , although his effect on colour theory is seen as considerable .
7134	However , on Kemp 's account few artists took notice of the philosophical , mathematical and scientific innovations of Descartes and Kepler .
7135	By the eighteenth century there was a considerable parting of the ways since the more erudite mathematical treatises on perspective , such as those by Lambert and Monge , were of no use to the practising artist .
7136	Even optical instruments , such as perspective machines , the camera obscura and the camera lucida , were used sparingly .
7137	It appears that once science gained its independent identity , scientists and artists used perspective for increasingly different purposes .
7138	As with de Santillana 's innovatory essay Kemp 's book not only offers new ways of understanding the history of science and the history of art but it also raises a host of historical and historiographical questions .
7139	These questions in turn suggest further lines of research that deserve serious attention by historians of both science and art .
7140	Kemp has performed a valuable service in opening up this area .
7141	I hope other historians will now follow his lead .
7142	ON THE PASSAGE OF A FEW PEOPLE : SITUATIONIST NOSTALGIA
7143	PETER SMITH
7144	An endless adventure … an endless passion … an endless banquet .
7145	A Situationist Scrapbook , edited by Iwona Blazwick in consultation with Mark Francis , Peter Wollen and Malcolm Imrie , Verso/ ICA Publications , London , 1989. 96 pp .
7146	ISBN 0 — 8691 — 983 — 8. £10.95. ( sandpaperback )
7147	On the Passage of a Few People Through a Brief Moment in Time .
7148	The Situationist International 1957 — 1972 , edited by Elisabeth Sussman , The MIT Press/ICA , Boston , Massachusetts , 1989 , 200 pp .
7149	ISBN 0860919838. £19.95 .
7150	I
7151	These books are both related to the exhibition On The Passage of a Few People Through a Brief Period of Time presented at the Musée national d'art moderne-Centre Georges Pompidou , the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London , and the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston , Massachusetts during 1989 — 90 .
7152	The exhibition was conceived and realised by Mark Francis and Peter Wollen with Paul Hervé Parsy .
7153	Francis and Wollen have also contributed articles ( one each ) both of which appear in both books as introductory statements on the Situationist International .
7154	Both books are anthologies of materials by a large number of contributors .
7155	Their titles invoke the Situationists ' rhetorical use of long and rhapsodic titles .
7156	They also denote deliberate obfuscations deriving from Dada and Surrealism .
7157	On the Passage of a Few People Through a Brief Moment in Time ( henceforth ‘ the Boston text' ) is a film title used by Guy Debord in 1959 .
7158	The Situationist Scrapbook includes only two synoptical essays , the rest being made up of a selection of documents produced in various parts of Europe and Britain from the fifties to the eighties , some of which predate the founding of the Situationist International ( henceforth the ‘ SI' ) .
7159	These are followed by documents relating to the SI in Britain which include Ralph Rumney 's Psychogeographic Map of Venice ( 1957 ) , and brief statements by Michèle Bernstein which appear in the British press in the 1950s and 1960s .
7160	The greater part of the Scrapbook largely consists of what the editor identifies as ‘ the British inheritance ’ which covers the period from 1966 — 1988 .
7161	The book is therefore very much an account of the movement 's influence in Britain .
7162	The Boston text relates more exclusively to the movement itself and includes , along with historical material , a brief statement by Mark Francis which is intended to justify and explain the motives behind the exhibition ( the Situationists did not give the event their blessings and none of the past members participated in its planning ) .
7163	‘ What we have sought to do ’ , claims Francis speaking for the organisers of the exhibition , ‘ is not to reconstruct time past but to expose to the light things that have run the risk of acquiring the patina of nostalgia and the glamour of neglect . ’
7164	If this statement betrays a certain uneasiness it is perhaps not surprising given the subversive status of the Situationist project and their condemnation of the art world .
7165	Francis also implies , somewhat unconvincingly , that the event was conceived in a spirit of Potlatch and accepts the Lettrist belief in the legitimate use of plagiarism .
7166	The Lettrists and the Situationists had used ‘ pre-existing elements ’ for their own ends , and so the editors of the Boston text and the curators of On the Passage have , they feel , a certain entitlement to do the same .
7167	This legitimation in turn is related to the principle of détournement , a term which had been coined initially by the Lettrists for their neo-Dadaist practice of cannibalising pre-existent materials ( in the manner of Duchamp 's LHOOQ ) with subversive intent .
7168	My view of the exhibition and these complementary texts is that they seem for the most part to lack the critical motivation and the dialectical irony of the Situationists .
7169	They are normative representations , reverential in tone , recuperative in effect and the ideological positions which they reflect are conveniently distanced from those of the SI .
7170	Self-evidently these texts are strikingly different from original materials issued by the SI in the sense that they have the status of copyrighted property and have been funded by organisations which in the past may have supported progressive art but which do not sound like the champions of revolutionary causes .
7171	The Boston text , for example , is published with the assistance of the Getty Grant Program , Massachusetts Council of the Arts and the Humanities , and additional funding is provided by the Lila Wallace Reader 's Digest Fund ( the benefactor of the American Wing at the Metropolitan Museum of Art , New York ) .
7172	The Scrapbook is also variously supported by Association Française d'Action Artistique , the Ministry of Culture , Copenhagen , the Instituo Banco San Paulo of Turin , Becks Bier , to name some of the backers , and also by the furtively named Friends of the Situationist International , whoever they are !
7173	More prosaically , the sandpaper cover ( which , like the Jorn/Debord text Mémoires of 1959 , is meant to damage your other books ) was donated by English Abrasives and Chemicals Ltd .
7174	One of the first ‘ political ’ statements in the Boston text is the copyright restriction notice .
7175	It appears a few lines away from the plagiarised title of the book .
7176	The proscription is , of course , a legal convention which we would normally take for granted , but is , in this context , inconsistent with the SI anti-copyright policy and , in the light of the Lautréamont axiom : ‘ Plagiarism is necessary — progress implies it , ’ which Francis cites on page 19 , is an unintended irony .
7177	The Boston text is more obviously an exhibition catalogue , if only because it includes a ‘ checklist ’ of the exhibition , which , ignoring the problematic identity of some of the works , distinguishes between works of art and other items ( books , tracts , pamphlets , etc. ) and also carefully identifies the status of individual exhibits by signifying their producer 's relationship to the formally identified Situationist group .
7178	There is another category for Situationist wannabees , which was an additional and problematical area of both books and the exhibition .
7179	Some of the materials in this area seemed to have the purpose of padding out the exhibition , whilst at the same time fulfilling the traditional function of consolidating the achievements of the founding group whose significance it was the purpose of the exhibition to celebrate .
7180	Francis identifies the stages of the SI narrative as a chronological trajectory corresponding to ( i ) the Experimental Laboratory period ; ( ii ) the detonator period ( which refers to Debord 's boast that he provided the explosive machinery that ignited in May 1968 ) ; ( iii ) the Fallout period after the SI disbanded in 1972 .
7181	These stages provide the logic for the ‘ diachronic structure ’ of the exhibition .
7182	In the Fallout section are included artists , writers and others ‘ who all had ( sic ) some contact with the SI ’ .
7183	Periodisation and classification present some difficulties which Wollen hints at when he comments on ‘ the ‘ simulationist ’ art boom of the eighties and its debt to the dry husks of Situationist thought ’ .
7184	It is to be regretted that neither of these books examine the pluralism of the ‘ simulationist ’ period .
7185	To the extent that the Situationists raised questions about cultural hierarchies and the ‘ supersession ’ of art , how should we judge the Fallout period ?
7186	The notion of progression is clearly important in assessing this work , especially as the temptation to isolate , or even dismiss , it as an epiphenomenon of the SI is strong .
7187	The materials displayed in the exhibition and reproduced in the Fallout section of the Scrapbook no doubt express ideas about which strong convictions are held .
7188	What are these convictions , and why are they not articulated ?
7189	Why were the exhibits left to speak for themselves ?
7190	It seems extraordinary that , given the political fervour of the Paris-based SI fraction in its post-Lettrist phase , the exhibition should have been so solemnly organised with little regard to Debord 's caveat on auteurism and his contempt for the art market .
7191	Whatever objectives the organisers might have had , the exhibition turned out to be a quite normative curatorial project .
7192	The contradiction is perhaps a familiar one .
7193	As Debord has commented : ‘ This society signs a peace treaty with its most outspoken enemies by giving them a spot in the spectacle . '
7194	It is noteworthy that the Situationists have produced nothing in the way of new projects for these texts , nor for the exhibition .
7195	Predictably they kept their distance .
7196	At the centre of the re-grouped SI in 1961 Bernstein and Debord refused any separation between artistic and political activity .
7197	It was at this time that Asgerjorn resigned his membership of the SI , although he continued to finance it through the sale of his paintings which were increasingly in demand in the 1960s .
7198	Thus re-grouped , the SI increased their political activity , eliminating all artistic production except in terms of agitational forms which meant , essentially , the use of détourné illustrations in their publications .
7199	The article by Wollen is an important piece of research and a major contribution to both anthologies .
7200	Despite its usefulness as an introduction to the subject , it does , however , judiciously avoid overt criticism of its subject and devotes little analysis to the SI in its mature phase .
7201	Nevertheless , Wollen presents a lucid account of the movement in its formative period and makes an interesting case for André Breton as a figure of some distinction in French intellectual history .
7202	He also traces the Hegelian , and Lukácsian influences on leftist theories in France in the heightened intellectual atmosphere after the Liberation which provided the aesthetic and political context for the Situationists .
7203	Apart from Wollen 's historical and theoretical essay , the other major contribution in the Boston text is Thomas Y. Levin 's ‘ Dismantling the Spectacle : The Cinema of Guy Debord ’ .
7204	This is again a comprehensive and thoroughly investigated article and is probably the first extended account of Situationist cinema in English .
7205	Levin makes a special case for Debord as a film-maker whose aim was to contribute to the ultimate destruction of cinema as a spectacularist medium .
7206	Debord 's cinema for Levin is a paradigmatic vehicle for the movement 's ‘ destructive creativity ’ .
7207	The main purpose of Levin 's article , however , is to reclaim Debord for the aesthetic discourse of avant-garde cinema .
7208	For example , he identifies Debord as the source of Godard 's innovations : ‘ Indeed , well over a decade before Godard 's Vent d'Est , Debord was producing a revolutionary , materialist ‘ counter-cinema ’ . ’
7209	Not having seen Debord 's films ( he refused screenings at the ICA in London ) , Levin 's arguments are in one sense untestable ; nevertheless the article is not without difficulties .
7210	Defensively , he observes what he considers to be Debord 's virtues and comments on the latter 's avoidance of , as he puts it : ‘ the various pitfalls — formalist essentialism , aestheticist myopia , politically naive fetishism of reflexivity , and so on , typical of certain avant-garde practices linked to radical political agendas . ’
7211	Nevertheless , Debord 's place within a reified history of ‘ political modernism ’ is assured , more by virtue of what is claimed for the work than by its testing in public — Levin admits that screenings have been rare , especially outside France .
7212	Both the personality and the work remain famously obscure in a way which seems almost contrived .
7213	Further to this , Levin claims that Debord ‘ does not disparage pleasure ’ and yet argues elsewhere in the essay that his films deliberately refuse to make concessions to the viewer .
7214	An example of this is the early Lettrist film Hurlement en faveur de Sade , with its long periods of blank screen and extended silences .
7215	As far as one can assess the merit of Levin 's text in relation to its subject , it seems somewhat implausible that Debord can be all the things for which he is proclaimed .
7216	Whatever defence is mounted , it is clear that these films , for Levin , exist as auratic objects , and Debord their auraticised progenitor .
7217	Hence the mythologisation of Debord by Levin , and others , has a significant bearing upon the reception of his work .
7218	His remoteness and the scandal and intrigue associated with the SI have significantly contributed to the enhancement of the movement 's reputation .
7219	Levin 's essay , interesting though it is , achieves little more than assimilating Debord into the spectacularised history of the avant-garde cinema .
7220	His hero-worship results in him reiterating the same claims that the cinéaste makes for himself .
7221	In the opening sequence of Hurlement , as Levin notes , Debord provides the audience with a reference to a cinematic tradition in which his own work is putatively situated .
7222	The tradition includes ‘ great landmarks ’ in film history from early ‘ genre classics , ( Levin 's term ) , Expressionist , Dada , Soviet cinema of the 1920s , Surrealist , Chaplin , Lettrist and last , but not least , Debord .
7223	Situationist cinema is therefore important , indeed , self-important , not least because it provides ‘ an alternative sort of cinematic activity , incompatible with the economy of the spectacle ’ .
7224	Levin earnestly considers Situationist film to be an effective oppositional practice .
7225	One of the attractions for Levin is the persistency with which Debord , like the Dadaists before him , continued to explore the medium , whilst contributing to its eventual destruction .
7226	Moreover , Levin claims that the Situationists never lost sight of their own contradictions , ‘ by consenting to act in culture ’ as a precondition of their co-existence in the present order .
7227	Nevertheless , cinema ultimately retains a relative autonomy in Levin 's tribute .
7228	It is like Hegel 's notion of the beautiful soul which denounces the world from which it has withdrawn to avoid having to recognise the extent of its participation in its disorder .
7229	Debord , as a film-maker , and Levin , as his apologist , take refuge in the transcendental space of autonomy where meanings have the illusion of self-regulation and independence of the totality they represent .
7230	Debord takes up his place ( certainly in Levin 's account ) within the lineage of modern masters with its attendant construction of patriarchy , distinction and causal succession .
7231	In Levin 's essay , avant-garde cinema is assimilated into the wider discourse of Modernist art despite their material and institutional differences .
7232	One of the pitfalls of this is that different audiences and different modes of consumption are contingencies largely ignored .
7233	Debord 's apparent contempt for audiences has its counterpart in Levin 's emphasis upon origination and prestige as paradigms of his cultural history .
7234	The blurring of art and film histories leads Levin into the murky waters of Situationist discourse on art .
7235	Suffice it to say that this discourse is generalising and intemperate , and lacks depth and clarity .
7236	Debord , for example , proclaims : ‘ The critical position later elaborated by the Situationists has shown that the suppression and realization of art are inseparable aspects of a single supersession of art . '
7237	There is some sense in this comment which may well explain the position of the Situationists at a particular conjunction , but it is a sense which would also explain earlier avant-garde trends in art ( if not cinema ) since , say , Futurism .
7238	Moreover , the notion of art 's ‘ single supersession ’ , an histrionic claim , would benefit from some kind of historical and theoretical contextualisation .
7239	It sounds important but in fact is an impenetrable statement .
7240	Further clarification might also be required as to how the Situationist negation of art ( and cinema ) related to the wider sphere of cultural-political struggle .
7241	The critique of art as an institution is continuous with earlier formations ( including early Surrealism and Russian Constructivism ) , but Levin remains unclear in his definition of Debord 's avant-gardism .
7242	For Lukács and Adorno the concept of the avant-garde was a touchstone : for the one it was negative and decadent , for the other positive and progressive .
7243	In Levin 's account of Debord , his subject appears to hold both positions at once .
7244	More specifically , on the issue of cultural hierarchies and class relations the Situationists tried to distance themselves from bourgeois notions of progress and their equivalence in the neo-avant-garde of the post-war period .
7245	The SI thus rejected ‘ mechanical becoming , with its notions of progress , merit and causal succession ’ .
7246	This statement reflects the resistance of the SI to piecemeal historicism out of which lineages are made , but in Levin 's history the independent achievements of Debord as a film-maker eventually collapses into it .
7247	In fairness it has to be said that Levin tries to isolate Debord from a purely formal Modernism , and from naive realism ( the politics of the signified ) .
7248	He does this by proclaiming , a ‘ third avant-garde ’ , which avoids the major pitfalls ( of the ‘ two avant-gardes ' ) and secures some theoretical authority for Debord .
7249	However , because this is not adequately related to the political ideals of the SI there is no analysis of the projected means ( theoretical or practical ) by which the sublation of art in the praxis of life might be achieved .
7250	The reverential tone of Levin 's text poses a problem which the movement 's survivors , I imagine , would be quick to condemn .
7251	It is , in short , uncritical in the sense of failing to site Debord 's films within an adequate theoretical discourse .
7252	Levin objectifies his subject through the use of an argument which leaves the SI unexplained as a revolutionary organisation with the potentiality of reflecting , by its own methods , a radical social transformation .
7253	What he provides is the missing chapter in the secret history of the cinema , the missing link between Berlin Dada and postmodernism .
7254	As with other contributors , exaggerated claims are made for détournement ( the communication which contains its own critique ) , firstly because it was an inheritance from Cubism and Dada , and secondly , because , as the exhibition shows , its deployment by ‘ pro-situs ’ has made of it a commonplace , popularised in punk fanzines , and ‘ Biff ’ postcards etc .
7255	The Situationists ' activities within the cultural sphere constituted an attempt to create a unified range of activities which functioned as a radical critique of the conventional boundaries between specialisations embedded in the institutions , practices and agencies of modern life .
7256	The fragmented appearance of their work , especially its Lettrist phase , their repudiation of conventional skills and scholarly manners ( evidenced in their use of personal insults ) have been absorbed by subcultural milieux and in due course adapted by the culture industries .
7257	The influence of the Situationists is clearly demonstrated ( if overstated ) in these books .
7258	If the historical trajectory of the Scrapbook is followed ( SI through Fluxus , Heatwave , King Mob , Jamie Reid , Vivienne Westwood , and the Sex Pistols ) the Situationist role for the intellectual as an informed but passionate critic gives way to philistine incitements to violence ( typified by King Mob in Britain , the Motherfuckers in the USA , and also indirectly the punk phenomenon ) but more commonly a laidback and philosophically weak critique of everyday life .
7259	The political and philosophical origins of Situationist thought to a large degree derives from Marx 's critique of alienation and commodity fetishism , Lukács 's development of this critique , and the Marxist-existentialism of Sartre and Henri Lefebvre .
7260	The rejection of liberal democracy and bureaucratic Marxism led the Situationists away from dominant political organisations and towards libertarian and syndicalist influences .
7261	The ideas of Anton Pannekoek which emerged with the publication of his Workers ' Council after World War One provided a ready-made model of a non-hierarchical political system .
7262	The simple faith conveyed in Pannekoek 's treatise recalls earlier utopian writing , and contrasts with the strident and acerbic tone of Situationist writing .
7263	With the exception of Wollen , the contributors to the Scrapbook and the Boston text convey little concern for the forms of political organisation espoused by the Situationists , and it is perhaps symptomatic of their interest in the SI as a purely aesthetic phenomenon .
7264	The SI clearly endeavoured to produce a revolutionary critique of modern life , and towards this end devised a convulsive rhetoric and an inventive vocabulary .
7265	The revival of interest in its ideas might be explained by this , rather than by its standing as a political organisation .
7266	The remoteness of the movement from working-class experience guaranteed the survival of its bohemian image .
7267	Its re-emergence as spectacle relates more visibly to its cult status and the nostalgic allure of fifties Paris ; a marginalised and dissolute existence in the company of exotic friends and of romantic places with beautiful names .
7268	The Boston text reproduces old photographs of founding members .
7269	The gamine looks of Bernstein and the neatness of Debord have an aesthetic relevance which signifies a rather vague , but nevertheless compelling , reason for their inclusion in the text .
7270	They are not merely documentation .
7271	They are in fact significant elements in the story of ‘ Situationism ’ which is the subtext of the book .
7272	The political reticence evident in these volumes is indicated by a degree of randomness in the choice of materials and by implication a commitment to the more ‘ expressive ’ or irrationalist side of their work .
7273	It is , for example , revealing that there is no indication in either book of the Situationist commitment to political struggles in the Third World and their critique of imperialism .
7274	The introductions in both books are anodyne and brief .
7275	The historical significance of the SI is not questioned , and the importance of the movement is asserted largely on the basis of aesthetic innovations which derive from the Lettrist period prior to the founding of the SI .
7276	Détournement and dérive ( drifting ) are thus reclaimed in terms of their contemporary relevance , or rather for the extent to which they influenced punk and the camp and erudite artistic radicalism which exploited it .
7277	With the exception of Levin 's extended analysis of film , neither the products nor any specific agitations of the Situationists and their epigones are subject to critical reassessment .
7278	The short commentaries and comic imagery in the British section of the Scrapbook are largely printed ephemera with unserious political pretensions .
7279	Some of it is amusing , some of it pretentious drivel .
7280	Clearly much of the material is unsupportable and there is a sense in which this is self-evident in that the Scrapbook is styled as an ‘ anti-document ’ which , like the films of Debord , is co-extensive with the equally unsupportable and qualitatively diminished world to which it relates .
7281	The temptation is to view these publications and the exhibition as a proliferation of surfaces which are in a sense pretty vacant reminders that despite the essentially teleological nature of the Situationist project , it is now immobilised and its documents merely a contribution to culture as the spectacular remains of an abandoned revolutionary ideal .
7282	The tendency is to ignore value distinctions and to undermine qualitative difference so that popular and high art genres are presented side by side in a unified space or text .
7283	There is of course an inside knowledge which makes this ‘ coherent ’ for those in possession of it .
7284	This presupposes the same audience separations , the same hierarchies , the same educational and class difference as before .
7285	Frank Mort has commented on this kind of separation between the new intellectuals who are happy and confident to mix genre and ignore qualitative and semantic difference ‘ because they already know the map of Western culture ’ and are distinct from those ‘ who do not carry with them those levels of cultural capital . ’
7286	He adds to this : ‘ In that sense postmodern discourse with its relativism , its denial of grand narratives and its refusal of questions of value , is a world tailor-made for the new metropolitan intellectual cadres . '
7287	It therefore seems that ‘ in a purely negative way ’ the silence over the question of meaning in the Boston text and in the Scrapbook is perhaps not surprising — — it is an historically appropriate response to the disappearance of the SI .
7288	‘ There is a sorrow in the Zeitgeist ’ bemoans Lyotard , an inappropriateness in the metaphor of the ‘ avant-garde ’ , and consequently a kind of absurdity attaching to the belief in art as a prefiguration of a global collectivist future .
7289	That sorrow hangs over the discontinued struggles of the SI .
7290	The belligerence of their message and the violence of their appeal to negation and revolt is now passed over in silence and their works appear as if they were blank sheets to the privileged audiences of the present day .
7291	II
7292	What I have argued so far is that the Situationists are ill-served by these publications , and that this is partly due to the influence of a certain pessimism which haunts contemporary cultural politics .
7293	What I want to argue now is that there is a sense in which the symptom of this pessimism exist in the movement itself .
7294	The Situationists were idealists in the sense that they perceived themselves apart from the spectacle , always managing to be ‘ other-than-spectacular ’ , as Levin puts it , so that this became a pre-condition of Situationist practice .
7295	Their self-image was that of the chosen few for whom the spectacle provided an inexhaustible supply of objects ( and people ) to hate , and whilst the apparent ease with which they targeted and disposed of their opposition often made good copy ( the endless adventure , the scandal , etc. ) , there is a sense in which the hectoring tone of their documents became repetitive and wearisome .
7296	The effusions of Vaneigem have an air of mystical revelation which is even more intense in recent publications .
7297	Debord 's political fatigue is less evident but his filmwork has finished and he refuses to permit distribution and screening of his work in this medium .
7298	Bernstein is now a journalist and works for a French newspaper .
7299	There are , I think , just three statements which count as unequivocally critical comments on SI in the Scrapbook .
7300	They appear in the documents section and therefore do not , we may take it , represent the views of the editors .
7301	Firstly , Art &amp; Language 's piece ‘ Ralph the Situationist ’ expresses considerable misgivings about the Situationist project : ‘ The texts are effectively incorrigible and self insulating … ’ ; ‘ … bland incoherence — a self-contradictory absurdity — a moral ground to give up reading and remembering … ’ , and so on .
7302	Whatever gave Francis , or whoever it was , the idea that Art $ Language had anything to do with the Situationists ?
7303	On what basis is this reference made ?
7304	There is no evidence of SI influence in their work , which has quite different intellectual roots , and the article itself leaves no doubt as to the extent of their disapprobation .
7305	Furthermore , the inclusion of three early works by the group in the exhibition ( dating from the late sixties ) reveals a kind of make believe idea about an A $ L/SI connection .
7306	There was no such connection .
7307	As late as 1970 members of A $ L , to my knowledge , had never heard of Debord , and if they had were not the least bit interested .
7308	The arbitrary inclusion of artworks in the exhibition is further evidence of a curatorial effort to construct a narrative of ‘ situationism ’ .
7309	The case for Merz , Pistoletto and Buren may be different , but it is not unreasonable to expect a rationale for the proclaimed indebtedness of Arte Povera and Conceptual Art to the Situationists .
7310	Nowhere in these publications are these connections argued for : they are merely dogmatically asserted .
7311	Given the withering contempt expressed by the Situationists for ‘ prositus ’ , one shudders to think what Debord et al .
7312	are going to make of the ‘ quasi-situationists ’ discovered in America by Elisabeth Sussmann .
7313	On the basis of her understanding , it appears that any artist in the USA who uses the conventions of the mass media in such a way as to produce a critique of the media ( and I can think of a good many ) is veritably a ‘ quasi-situationist ’ .
7314	The desire to create a pseudo-history of the movement 's afterlife may be good for business , and may have provided extra material for the book ( I refer to the Boston text , see pp. 10–13 ) but it is not in keeping with the purer aims of the Situationists outlined elsewhere in these and other texts .
7315	The second critical comment I came across in the Scrapbook was George Steiner 's statement from the Sunday Times in 1967 .
7316	Steiner accepted that the Situationists had identified and accurately described the emptiness of everyday life and even accepts their pleas for subversion , but was very sour about what he described as the ‘ depressingly banal ’ prescriptions of Debord and the ‘ turgid creed ’ of Vaneigem .
7317	Christopher Gray , one of the small number of English members of the SI , is the third commentator I found to be not entirely sympathetic .
7318	His comments come from an anthology of Situationist writings he edited in 1974 .
7319	Gray 's comments evoke a kind of mystical disenchantment with the movement which he found to be too focused on an intellectual critique of society .
7320	‘ There was ’ , he complains , ‘ no concern whatever with either emotions or the body .
7321	The SI thought you just had to show how the nightmare worked and everyone would wake up .
7322	Their quest was for the perfect formula . '
7323	The history of the SI is in some ways a struggle for recognition ( despite Debord 's evasions ) sustained by a radically negative critique which ultimately failed to find a middle way between Hegelian metaphysics and the dynamics of political organisation in the pursuit of its utopian objectives .
7324	The declamatory style of writing ( which now seems dated ) too often obscured the probity of the Situationist 's critique of the alienating and manipulative effects of late capitalism and its creation of pseudo-needs .
7325	The movement 's critique proclaimed a uniqueness and originality for its discoveries to which it was never entitled and which served only to reinforce the self-deluding image of its own power and influence in the world .
7326	Anti-authoritarian leftism and the critique of bureaucratic socialism had of course been well established before the foundation of the SI in 1957 .
7327	The rejection of trade unionism was a common demand amongst anarchists and libertarian socialists .
7328	At the end of her life Rosa Luxembourg called for the abolishment of trade unions and promoted the view that workers ' councils were essential organisations in the establishment of socialism .
7329	More generally the idea of the inseparability of cultural and political revolution has a long history within the libertarian tradition with its roots in revolutionary Romanticism .
7330	The more direct inspiration for the Situationists was the Dada-Lettrist connection which provided the aesthetic and political basis for their adoption of non-cognitive methods of expression ( such as automatism , chance and other depersonalising techniques of production ) and also led to the definition of some key terms in their vocabulary .
7331	The critique of scientific socialism and economism has a major place in Marxist debate in the twentieth century .
7332	The Situationists , contribution to this was negligible .
7333	The Frankfurt School 's Marxian approach to cultural criticism , and production and the social effects of technology and the culture industries pre-dates the writings of Debord , and yet , despite its relative lack of revolutionary fervour remains a far more wide-ranging and thoroughgoing critique of the field .
7334	The conjunction of passion and knowledge , of libertarianism and planning , of feeling and thought are conventional oppositions in post-Enlightenment thought which have also bedevilled Marxism .
7335	The more orthodox theorists in this tradition have preserved this separation along the lines of a Romanticist/Utilitarian split .
7336	Others have sought a reconciliation of the positions that these terms represent , and there is an abundance of literature which examines this relationship in advance of the Situationists .
7337	If the Situationist project is flawed , as I believe it is , it is not because antecedent theories of libertarians , Marxists and Council Communists are ignored by them , but rather because they lacked the will to build on this tradition a systematic utopianism consisting of critique and plausible projections into the future .
7338	Like the Surrealists before them , their transcendence of alienation remains abstractly utopian .
7339	Despite revolutionary zeal , or perhaps because of it , they sought immediate compensations for the miseries of daily life , and spontaneous methods of attack which they mistook for political strategy .
7340	The Situationists ' strategy consisted of an exploratory utopianism — a kind of heuristic projection of a future society .
7341	Raymond Williams has remarked that the danger of the heuristic utopia is that it ‘ can settle into isolated and sentimental desire , a means of living with alienation ’ .
7342	Another Surrealist inheritance which distances Situationists from the more radical utopians is their blanket condemnation of work .
7343	‘ Never work ! ’ announced the Surrealists .
7344	It is an amusing quip ( especially for those with private means ) and makes joyful and nonsensical graffiti .
7345	But what does it mean ?
7346	Obviously it is an incitement to refusal , and an indictment of alienated labour .
7347	The refusal is as understandable as it is naive , but seems to constitute at the same time what amounts to an abnegation of intellectual curiosity about human needs .
7348	Its political inflexion contests the middle-class work ethic which is the main purpose of its message .
7349	The aristocracy , for its part , has never needed to be convinced of the importance of not working .
7350	For other theorists such as William Morris , the concept of work is not considered negatively .
7351	Indeed ; for Morris and other Marxists the nature of work necessarily changes in the process of social transformation .
7352	Marx defined labour as ‘ human sensuous activity ’ .
7353	Lukács claimed that labour became the model for any social practice .
7354	The plea for an understanding of ‘ totality ’ in Situationist writing derives from Lukács and Marx whose critique of ‘ separation ’ is directed exactly at the work/leisure distinction .
7355	Asger Jorn 's interest in folk cultures and tribal societies which lacked a notion of ‘ art ’ as a distinct intellectual practice separated from the common culture , was based on an understanding of the extent to which the spheres of art and work have become conflicting practices within bourgeois relations of production .
7356	Despite this the common tendency in SI writing on most forms of directed or purposeful activity ( other than agitation or ‘ destructive creativity' ) is negative .
7357	The aristocratic disdain for manual labour has its counterpart in the Situationist ’ attitude to the working class considered as the moronised victims of the spectacle .
7358	In contrast the Situationists ' notion of pleasure is a negation of work in almost every sense of the word — a kind of involuntary idleness in the land of Cockaigne .
7359	Their notion of pleasure is indistinguishable from a sixties Zeitgeist .
7360	Its meaning is inadequately theorised and remains largely at the level of common sense , a crude alternative to the repressive order of work .
7361	Now that Situationist texts are widely available ( and with these publications adding to the list ) it is ironic that they seem less crucial than they once did .
7362	Their appeal in the past was partly attributable to the popular texture of some aspects of the writing , its accessibility and its festive and irreverent politics .
7363	These writings appealed essentially to a generation of students bored with academic life and attracted by the street credibility of the Situationists , and often provided students with the dubious pleasure of being flattered and insulted at the same time .
7364	The Situationist lifestyle ( in so far as it could be imagined ) had some influence on the hippy sub-culture in the late sixties and punk ideology in the seventies in Britain .
7365	Situationist influence was more menacingly felt in France especially in the universities , although it has to be said that their influence upon the events of May 1968 has been exaggerated .
7366	For the most part , however , the legacy of the movement remained less obviously political , and restricted in its appeal to fairly specific audiences in the cultural milieu and especially the visual arts .
7367	Indeed , the extent to which the Situationist influence has flourished in the spheres of art and popular culture is noteworthy and contrasts with the absence of the movement 's influence in other domains .
7368	The uneven profile of the Situationist group and its existential fragmentation together with the eclectic and impromptu formal character of the artefacts they produced , as I have suggested above , make it an ideal type for the postmodernist critic .
7369	The Situationists ' rejection of the classical model of left-wing monumentalism , and their apparent lack of commitment to the historical overview or the grand narrative is consistent with postmodernism .
7370	Moreover , the freedom with which they juxtapose theory and humour , and plagiarise for artistic effect suggests strong affinity with the postmodern .
7371	The decline of the meta-narrative in favour of aphoristic models of philosophical expression ( following Feuerbach and Nietzche ) has been the favoured form of the Situationists .
7372	The fact that Baudrillard 's name has been linked with the Situationists should not be held against them .
7373	Nevertheless , the de-Marxisation of their project by him and the ‘ death of the social ’ which he has announced should alert us to the doubts raised by Raymond Williams on the issue of certain types of Utopianism .
7374	The concept of the spectacle is an effective term which now has a wide currency , but perhaps only in a sense which approximates its use by the Situationists .
7375	The historical period which has seen its political devaluation is one in which political optimism has become unfashionable , which perhaps is one way of explaining the retrospective or merely historicist character of the Situationist exhibition , and the books I have reviewed .
7376	We have seen a shift from the utopianism of the 1960s to a culture of nostalgia and , as with the more dystopian elements in postmodernism , the exhibition and the books which accompany it look backward in a search for appearances as if they were compensatory fantasies substituting for a forgotten dream .

7416	By Hugh Hebert
7417	THERE was one point when the hair on the back of my head began to lift .
7418	Not at Paul Hill 's remembrance of beatings past , when he could hear the sound of steel-tipped boots running to take part in the fun , and once heard a principal medical officer , no less , telling colleagues : ‘ Do n't walk his face , do n't walk his face . ’
7419	Not even the time he was dunked head first in a tub of dubious liquid , and brought up gasping for breath : ‘ Make him sing God Save the Queen ! ’ they shouted .
7420	Brutality , as Hill describes and felt it , was a bitter part of his prison life ; you just learnt to get down on the floor as fast as you could and cover up as best you could .
7421	But it was Gerry Conlon 's account of being interrogated after the Guildford bombings that made the scalp crawl .
7422	We know your mother works at the Royal Victoria Hospital , they told him , we know where your sister works , and there are sectarian killings down there .
7423	‘ They told me they could arrange an ‘ accident ’ .
7424	And I believed they were capable of murdering my mother , I honestly believe they would have murdered my mother — that 's why I signed the statement . ’
7425	The account he gave just after his release was that the threat had been that a British soldier might ‘ accidentally ’ shoot one of the women .
7426	A few months ago even , this would have seemed improbable .
7427	You might have assumed this was the police bluffing and bullying .
7428	Yet given what we have learned about links between the security services and the Loyalist paramilitaries in Northern Ireland , and the deep suspicion about surrogate murders , you ca n't shrug off the shiver Conlon 's words bring .
7429	There were daunting moments in last night 's First Tuesday ( Yorkshire ) , but few of them matched that hint of a jackboot under the blue serge .
7430	It 's right that the Guildford Four have told their stories now to Grant McKee and Ros Franey and First Tuesday , the programme and the producers who dug away , and did much to keep the case alive .
7431	And they told it without on-screen questioning , though the programme is skilfully structured to give it a coherence it might have lacked .
7432	Carole Richardson 's is the most haunting face .
7433	You have to hope that its blankness will slowly dissolve and let life in .
7434	Just once a couple of tears rolled down .
7435	It was when she described seeing film of the results of the bombing on television , and thinking : ‘ They think I did that ! ’
7436	Armstrong seems the least permanently damaged on the surface .
7437	He pays tribute to his treatment at Gartree prison , he apologises to the bomb victims ' families that they have had to keep reminding them of their loss : ‘ But we had to fight for our freedom . ’
7438	Hill expresses the way time has cheated them : his daughter was born while he was remanded in custody , and is now 14 : ‘ She would change dramatically and I did n't feel a change in myself mentally .
7439	I 'm still 20 in my head .
7440	Nothing 's happened to me .
7441	I have n't lived . ’
7442	But again it was Conlon , the slightly wild-eyed Irish poet of the quartet , articulate , flamboyant — remember that extraordinary exit through the front door of the Old Bailey — who cut deep into the collective conscience .
7443	He described being taken over the years to see his sick , and finally dying and almost certainly innocent father in another prison .
7444	He was convicted with the Maguires in the parallel case of a ‘ bomb factory ’ .
7445	And he tells how none of the assembled guards and officials could look his father in the eye as he protested his innocence .
7446	Only the nurses could do that .
7447	And at the end , Conlon drew the one hopeful conclusion : ‘ If this stops capital punishment ever coming back , the time I 've spent in prison will be well worth it .
7448	If this stops another innocent person going to prison , it 'll be well worth it …
7449	‘ I 've had numerous prison governors say to me , Yes , Conlon , we know you 're innocent , but there 's nothing we can do about it .
7450	We get a custody order , and that 's it .
7451	What sort of system of justice is that ? ’

7457	OPERA : Edward Greenfield finds the Medea at Covent Garden relentlessly loud Cool , but not Callas enough .
7458	IT was Maria Callas who , a generation ago , singlehandedly dragged Cherubini 's Medea back into the 20th century repertory .
7459	This operatic adaptation of classical tragedy , Euripides and Seneca distantly viewed via Corneille , proved then to be a formidable vehicle for a great singing actress .
7460	With her unique vehemence Callas built the crazed obsessions of the heroine into a memorable final scene , when in agony Medea murders her own children to spite Jason , the husband who has rejected her .
7461	With Callas the piece had one 's hair on end .
7462	She recorded it at La Scala , and in 1959 gave five performances at Covent Garden in that same production borrowed from Milan .
7463	Now with a soprano who has already successfully taken the role in a revival at the Buxton Festival , Rosalind Plowright , Covent Garden is staging its own new production directed by Mike Ashman with sets by Bernard Culshaw .
7464	Sadly the whole evening tends to confirm just how single-handed Callas ' achievement was back in the Fifties .
7465	One distinct side of Plowright 's voice has a Callas-like bite , a hard edge combined with vibrancy .
7466	In her portrait of Medea — or Medee as she becomes in this staging of the original French version — this is what she uses consistently .
7467	She is unrelentingly loud , making one long to hear the gentler , sweeter Plowright voice , if only to enhance ( by contrast ) the impact of the outbursts .
7468	Her performance even brings a touch or two of Callas ' distinctive ‘ bottled ’ tone , and under pressure on top the voice tends to spread in a rather similar way .
7469	Yet there is no question of one 's hair rising .
7470	Plowright as an actress is no fire-eater , however hard she tries .
7471	One basic trouble with Medea is the mediocre quality of invention in so much of Cherubini 's score .
7472	It is true that structurally his numbers , with solos and ensembles intermingled , have a freedom and originality that point forward directly to Berlioz and Wagner .
7473	Yet when so much of the writing seems to have been done on automatic pilot , with dozens of sequential passages of unashamed banality — even at the opening of the overture — this is a score that demands some injection whether of fire or persuasiveness in the performers , to make one forget the musical flaws .
7474	It does not help that Cherubini allows too little variety of pace , and that his lyrical gift is limited too .
7475	Even when as in the Act 2 aria for Medea 's servant , Neris , he attempts a flowing canzonetta and decks it with a distinctive bassoon obligato , he lets the number go on far too long , or so it seems when as here the bassoon roars out in determined competition with the mezzo , Claire Powell .
7476	Medea 's aria with the children before the murder in Act 3 also promises a higher musical flight , only to fall into squareness .
7477	Mike Ashman has opted to set the piece firmly at the period of composition .
7478	This 19th of Cherubini 's 34 operas was conceived and written at the height of the Revolutionary Reign of Terror .
7479	Tricolors abound and Jason is made up to look like Napoleon .
7480	But the symbolic period point is overstressed to the verge of comedy , when in the final scene of destruction the figures of Marianne with her red cap of Liberty , the skeleton Death with his scythe and the Angel of Justice are hastily let down in tableau from the flies .
7481	Otherwise the sets are based on a bare raked platform overlooked by a gallery , and with an enormous window let into the back wall for the offstage wedding scene of Act 2 .
7482	Perversely set designer Bernard Culshaw scatters the stage in Act 2 with great polystyrene rocks , and then removes them for Act 3 , when the stage directions do specify just such rocks .
7483	Did he get his acts mixed up , I wonder ?
7484	The Russian heroic tenor , Alexei Steblianko , from the Kirov in Leningrad is the least comfortable with a French accent , but then on the first night he was battling with a throat infection .
7485	Robert Lloyd as King Creon is handsome of voice and person — the most assured principal — and the bright-toned American soprano , Renee Fleming , makes a promising Covent Garden debut in the disappointingly brief role of Glauce ( Dirce in the French ) , Jason 's new bride .
7486	Mark Ermler draws generally crisp and lively playing from the Covent Garden Orchestra , but it is uphill work with such a score , hardly helped by what is happening on stage .

7488	IT WAS Maria Callas who , a generation ago , singlehandedly dragged Cherubini 's Medea back into the 20th century repertory .
7489	This operatic adaptation of classical tragedy , Euripides and Seneca distantly viewed via Corneille , proved then to be a formidable vehicle for a great singing actress .
7490	With her unique vehemence Callas built the crazed obsessions of the heroine into a memorable final scene , when in agony Medea murders her own children to spite Jason , the husband who has rejected her .
7491	With Callas the piece had one 's hair on end .
7492	She recorded it at La Scala , and in 1959 gave five performances at Covent Garden in that same production borrowed from Milan .
7493	Now with a soprano who has already successfully taken the role in a revival at the Buxton Festival , Rosalind Plowright , Covent Garden is staging its own new production directed by Mike Ashman with sets by Bernard Culshaw .
7494	Sadly the whole evening tends to confirm just how single-handed Callas ' achievement was back in the Fifties .
7495	One distinct side of Plowright 's voice has a Callas-like bite , a hard edge combined with vibrancy .
7496	In her portrait of Medea — or Medee as she becomes in this staging of the original French version — this is what she uses consistently .
7497	She is unrelentingly loud , making one long to hear the gentler , sweeter Plowright voice , if only to enhance ( by contrast ) the impact of the outbursts .
7498	Her performance even brings a touch or two of Callas ' distinctive ‘ bottled ’ tone , and under pressure on top the voice tends to spread in a rather similar way .
7499	Yet there is no question of one 's hair rising .
7500	Plowright as an actress is no fire-eater , however hard she tries .
7501	One basic trouble with Medea is the mediocre quality of invention in so much of Cherubini 's score .
7502	It is true that structurally his numbers , with solos and ensembles intermingled , have a freedom and originality that point forward directly to Berlioz and Wagner .
7503	Yet when so much of the writing seems to have been done on automatic pilot , with dozens of sequential passages of unashamed banality — even at the opening of the overture — this is a score that demands some injection whether of fire or persuasiveness in the performers , to make one forget the musi cal flaws .
7504	It does not help that Cherubini allows too little variety of pace , and that his lyrical gift is limited too .
7505	Even when as in the Act 2 aria for Medea 's servant , Neris , he attempts a flowing canzonetta and decks it with a distinctive bassoon obligato , he lets the number go on far too long , or so it seems when as here the bassoon roars out in determined competition with the mezzo , Claire Powell .
7506	Medea 's aria with the children before the murder in Act 3 also promises a higher musical flight , only to fall into squareness .
7507	Mike Ashman has opted to set the piece firmly at the period of composition .
7508	This 19th of Cherubini 's 34 operas was conceived and written at the height of the Revolutionary Reign of Terror .
7509	Tricolors abound and Jason is made up to look like Napoleon .
7510	But the symbolic period point is overstressed to the verge of comedy , when in the final scene of destruction the figures of Marianne with her red cap of Liberty , the skeleton Death with his scythe and the Angel of Justice are hastily let down in tableau from the flies .
7511	Otherwise the sets are based on a bare raked platform overlooked by a gallery , and with an enormous window let into the back wall for the offstage wedding scene of Act 2 .
7512	Perversely set designer Bernard Culshaw scatters the stage in Act 2 with great polystyrene rocks , and then removes them for Act 3 , when the stage directions do specify just such rocks .
7513	Did he get his acts mixed up , I wonder ?
7514	The Russian heroic tenor , Alexei Steblianko , from the Kirov in Leningrad is the least comfortable with a French accent , but then on the first night he was battling with a throat infection .
7515	Robert Lloyd as King Creon is handsome of voice and person — the most assured principal — and the bright-toned American soprano , Renee Fleming , makes a promising Covent Garden debut in the disappointingly brief role of Glauce ( Dirce in the French ) , Jason 's new bride .
7516	Mark Ermler draws generally crisp and lively playing from the Covent Garden Orchestra , but it is uphill work with such a score , hardly helped by what is happening on stage .

7519	By Meirion Bowen Ligeti Festival .
7520	WHETHER writing new pieces or extending old ones , Ligeti comes across — almost like Birtwistle — as a convergent musical thinker .
7521	If all his mature compositions were laid end to end and glued together , they might well form one big work .
7522	This unitary vision was particularly well-exemplified in the final , four-hour concert in the Ligeti Festival at the QEH , which featured the premieres of two further piano etudes and of the five-movement version of his Piano Concerto .
7523	The first six etudes , completed in 1985 , were stimulated by Ligeti 's studies of rhythm in sub-Saharan music and the multi-layered polyrhythms in the pianola works of Conlon Nancarrow : and the two new ones drew partly on ideas from gamelan music .
7524	But all this , along with his fascination with rhythmic displacements in Chopin and others , disappeared within a distinctively Ligetian interplay of line and colour .
7525	It required from the pianist an unbelievable independence of hands and fingers , so that unevenly spread accents and criss-crossing figurations appeared to drop into place without obvious effort .
7526	Volker Banfield here achieved all that was demanded of him technically .
7527	But his playing was studiously uncommunicative and prosaic , unresponsive to the poetry behind the notes — e.g. in the cool Bartokian chords that closed the eighth study .
7528	In the Piano Concerto it was , of course , an asset to have a soloist who could keep his head amid all the intricate polymetrical pulsations of the first and third movements .
7529	Banfield extracted little drama , however , from the exchanges between the piano and different orchestral groups in the fourth and fifth movements .
7530	In his hands , the work became a latterday baroque concerto grosso , with the pianist as one soloist among many , whereas the range of invention and harmonic emphasis in the work implied a far more provocative interaction of roles .
7531	While the concerto had sounded complete and satisfying in its original three-movement format , the additional movements opened up new horizons and changed its structural proportions without distorting any of its existing perspectives .
7532	If anything , its additional colours brought extra glitter to the music , and this quality was certainly seized upon by the London Sinfonietta under Elgar Howarth , who eagerly compensated for the pianist 's lack of a trenchant or subtle delivery .
7533	Reserve and reticence of expression , on the part of solo cellist Christopher van Kampen and the Sinfonietta , were more aptly applied in the context of Ligeti 's Cello Concerto ( 1965 ) , a sparsely-written , lapidaric work that discloses the absolute minimum within its unbroken span of 26 kaleidoscopic episodes .
7534	This work made an effective bridge to the equally spare and fastidious Four Capriccios Opus 9 by Gyorgy Kurtag ( whose music Ligeti has generously welcomed into his Festival , just as he insisted on having the composer share the stage at the end ) .
7535	Kurtag is Ligeti 's opposite — a divergent musical thinker whose every new work might be by another composer , were it not for the extreme compression that is constant to his style .
7536	In the settings of four aphoristic poems by Istvan Balint for soprano and 14 players — which Kurtag began in 1972 and recently revised — the outside influences declared themselves quite readily , whether they were from East European folk music or Webern : and in this performance , the soprano Adrienne Csengery and Sinfonietta excelled themselves with sudden flashes of colour and bursts of intense virtuosity .
7537	Man in the Moon .
7538	By Paul Fisher Ironmistress .
7539	IRONMISTRESS uses heavy metallic imagery to tell of Martha Darby , a character based on a real 19th century widow who inherited an iron works .
7540	‘ His hand was welded to my back ’ , she tells her daughter of the courtship with the paterfamilias now buried in an iron coffin .
7541	During a comical lesson on how to catch her man , Little Cog is told she must weep not buckets but spoons .
7542	The language also taps a Laurentian vein where mud , blood , heat and simmering violence are mashed together .
7543	Read into it what you will : industrial fable , feminist tract , family psychodrama or a sly portrait of the modern Iron Lady .
7544	Martha clangs about her business , her hair dragged into a tight bun , a bustle behind her and keys at her waist .
7545	‘ The first time I held those keys , I put them in my mouth and felt my bones had turned to gold , ’ she announces .
7546	Her assimilation of a male world develops into a psychotic taste for swallowing pens and spoons .
7547	It gives her tummy ache and she administers something similar when she flattens her daughter 's body , locking it in the tightest of corsets .
7548	After that scene there is little else that needs to be said about the strictures on Victorian women .
7549	The daughter opens and closes the play on a swing , her hair free but a soundtrack of synthesised chords and foundry clatter emphasising this is no Fragonard .
7550	Until a routinely hopeless marriage , Louise Waddington delivers Little Cog 's speeches straight at the audience , up into the Gods .
7551	Her pale eyes are everywhere .
7552	Everything pours inwards as Gillian Brown 's dead-eyed Martha discovers obsessive control can lead to personal dissolution .
7553	While she celebrates market forces and a ‘ world where you and me and God are a giant machine with separate bits ’ she is forging fears of her own futility and death .
7554	The director , Thomas de Mallet Burgess , delicately underlines the personal in April de Angelis 's allusive script though he ca n't assert himself when the play slithers into magical realism .
7555	At the end highway robberies , riots and an unspecified sense of comeuppance is what we are left with .
7556	A heavy metal vision of post-Thatcherism , maybe .

7623	The US sets its compass on two trading oceans Notebook .
7624	By Edited by Alex Brummer
7625	CANBERRA may seem an awful long way from exchanges on the floor of the House of Commons over the European Monetary System .
7626	But were it not for the perceived economic might of a more unified Economic Community , the dozen or so nations of the Pacific Rim , who have been meeting in Australia , might not have bothered .
7627	The first , albeit tenative , steps towards forming a new Pacific-based economic union display an astute awareness of the way events are moving within Europe : movements with which Number 10 has yet to come to grips .
7628	Not so long ago it seemed as if the world was to divide into three main trading blocks : the EC based around the West German economy ; a Northern American block based around the US-Canadian free trade area , and a Pacific unit incorporating the Asian tigers with Japan and the yen at the centre .
7629	But the Metternich-like skills of the US Secretary of State , Mr James Baker , are ensuring that America maintains a strong stake in each forum .
7630	It firstly boldly asked for a seat at the top table at the European Community : a suggestion rudely rebuffed .
7631	The US has talked of a genuine North American free trade zone incorporating the US , Canada and Mexico which would have the best of all worlds with high-technology skills and a cheap labour force south of the Rio Grande .
7632	Now it is making a third bid for influence .
7633	It has turned up in Canberra with Japan to develop Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation ( APEC ) and a new 12-nation organisation which will mimic the role of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in Europe .
7634	Preliminary steps taken to conduct studies on trade , technology and investment flows in the region may seem insignificant .
7635	But Mr Baker plainly views it as otherwise .
7636	He noted that the Canberra meeting ‘ is the start of something which could grow into a very significant development not only for the region but for the global economy . ’
7637	If the more economically puny ASEAN countries ( Indonesia , Malaysia , Singapore , Brunei , Thailand and the Philippines ) were to bury their reservations , then the high growth from other partners , including such tigers as Thailand and South Korea alongside the more mature economies of Japan and Australia , could mean a dynamic coalition .
7638	It would then be up to the US and Canada to decide whether they want to face towards the Atlantic or Pacific — or be caught between two great trading oceans .
