7828	French trust group suspends dealings over pricing fears .
7829	By Teresa Hunter
7830	THE French-owned unit-trust company Dumenil has suspended dealings in its funds , worth £33 million , after the disclosure that there may have been pricing errors in recent valuations .
7831	This is the first time a unit trust company has had to suspend funds under the Financial Services Act 's pricing regulations , which oblige it to cease trading once an error is suspected .
7832	It means Dumenil 's 12,000 investors are locked into their investments until the investigation is complete .
7833	As the suspension of a unit trust over a pricing error is unprecedented , it is not known when units can be traded again .
7834	One month has been suggested as a possible suspension period .
7835	Dumenil , which specialises in single country European funds , claims it became concerned ‘ very recently ’ that its valuations on two funds in particular were out-of-line with general movements in the market .
7836	The marketing director , Nigel Herrick , said : ‘ The market would fall , but our prices would not show a corresponding movement . ’
7837	Unit trust industry sources claim that rumours began circulating as long as three months ago that Dumenil had a problem with valuations .
7838	The company stresses the problem has been very short-lived .
7839	But as a precaution it has suspended all its funds , until an investigation pinpoints the root of the problem .
7840	Unit trust prices are calculated on computers using market information supplied by the WM Company .
7841	There is no suggestion that the WM data has been faulty .
7842	Mr Herrick said : ‘ This is an in-house problem .
7843	Right now we do not know the extent of that problem .
7844	We do not know which , if any , funds are affected and we do not know whether there has been an over valuation or an under valuation . ’
7845	Dumenil has called in Touche Ross as independent accountants to assess the scale of the problem .
7846	The regulatory bodies , including the Securities and Investments Board , the Investment Managers Regulatory Organisation and the Life Assurance and Unit Trust Regulatory Organisation are keeping a close eye on the investigation procedure .
7847	If it is proved that unit holders who have traded units recently have suffered as a result of pricing errors , some form of compensation will be made available .
7848	Midland Bank , one of the trustees of the Dumenil funds , stepped in to calm investors ' fears .
7849	A Midland spokesman said : ‘ The assets of the trust have been and continue to be under the control of the trustee whose objective remains that of insuring that the interests of the investors are protected . ’
7850	The aftershocks of the European row tell us that the big tremors are still to come Economics .
7851	By Christopher Huhne
7852	WHATEVER the hopes of the Conservative party 's managers , the divisions over European policy are not going to go away .
7853	There is bound , sooner or later , to be a battle royal over membership of the European Monetary System , the result of which will be either an almost unprecedented humiliation for Mrs Thatcher or the reshaping yet again of a Cabinet in her own image .
7854	On present betting , there is a fair chance the pound will finally join the system by the end of next year .
7855	Mrs Thatcher interprets the Madrid formula more as a pretext for not joining the EMS than as a set of three conditions for joining it .
7856	Moreover , she has been advised by Sir Alan Walters that , once exchange controls have finally been removed by France and Italy in July 1990 , the new freedom of capital flows will break the fixed exchange rate system apart .
7857	On that fond hope , she is likely to be disappointed .
7858	The remaining controls , mainly affecting restrictions on bank deposits , are small .
7859	At some point in the second half of next year , and perhaps even earlier if President Mitterrand decides to bring forward the abolition of French controls , the Government is going to be faced with an inescapable decision .
7860	Controls will have gone .
7861	British inflation will be down ( an odd condition , since one reason for the system is to help reduce inflation ) .
7862	There will have been progress on the creation of a single European market , especially in financial services .
7863	Reasonable people will decide that each of the Madrid conditions has been met .
7864	At that stage , the pressures for full membership are bound to mount at home and overseas .
7865	The pound may now stay at its new post-Lawson level or even decline further .
7866	But at an exchange rate of , say , DM2.70 ( instead of the present DM2.90 ) the trade-offs for the new Chancellor will begin to look different .
7867	He will want to avoid a further decline for fear that import price rises will push up inflation .
7868	For good electoral reasons , EMS membership will look an increasingly attractive alternative to a tighter monetary policy .
7869	The going will be tough enough as it is .
7870	The former Chancellor , Mr Lawson , gave a foretaste of the Treasury 's Autumn Statement forecast when , in his resignation speech , he pointed out that ‘ we are once again on the downswing and I see no need for any further policy tightening .
7871	While this downswing will not be as sharp as the previous downturn ( in 1979-81 ) , not least given the very much lower level of inflation that we now have , a dull 1989 is bound to be followed by a difficult 1990 . ’
7872	The downturn will not , though , undermine the case for EMS membership .
7873	A mild recession will correct but not eliminate the deficit , which is bound to remain high , and may even rise again as another pre-election consumer spree gathers pace .
7874	Outside the EMS , the markets would become worried once again about the Government 's real commitment to exchange rate stability .
7875	They would insist on inflationary falls in the pound , or a deflationary tightening of monetary policy .
7876	What better than EMS membership to reassure them ?
7877	The external pressures for EMS membership will also mount .
7878	It will become increasingly clear that Britain is paying a high political price for its refusal to participate in the EMS , not least in the almost immediate reflex reaction against any British proposals to affect the design of a future monetary union .
7879	No one watching the French reaction to the unfolding events in central Europe should doubt the political importance which the Elysee attaches to monetary union as a way of anchoring west Germany to this end of the Continent .
7880	A single currency is also on the agenda because the balance of the economic argument has also swung sharply in its favour over the last decade , as Professor Michael Artis has pointed out ( 1 ) .
7881	He guesstimates that the existence of different European currencies cost about 1.5 per cent of Europe 's total income each year , merely in terms of the losses incurred by traders and investors when they change currencies .
7882	Even more important , the prospect of a single currency would eliminate an ormous source of uncertainty for businesses .
7883	It would probably unleash another burst of investment as firms took advantage of opportunities which had hitherto been regarded as too risky .
7884	After all , businesses can insure against the exchange rate risk on particular deals — for example , their exports to France — by accepting less sterling today in exchange for the known future quantity of francs .
7885	But they can not hedge investments in the same way ( even if the markets looked far beyond a year or so , which they do not ) .
7886	Assume , for example , that Jaguar had insured itself against a fall of the dollar by covering several years of earnings .
7887	The fall of the dollar would still mean that every Jaguar car sold in the US was less profitable , although the company might have made lots of money on its foreign exchange transactions .
7888	The rational company would cash in its profits on the speculation — and still cut production and investment as it was priced out of the US market .
7889	Exchange rate uncertainty is thus bound to reduce investment .
7890	Some idea of the potential gains from a single currency can be had by looking at previous historical periods when people really believed that exchange rates were fixed .
7891	Mr Tam Bayoumi has calculated the average size of capital flows each year in the major economies under the Gold Standard from 1880 to 1913 , and has shown that they were much larger than during the post-war period from 1965 to 1986 .
7892	Indeed , the average flow , as a percentage of GDP , for eight countries in the sample before 1914 was 3.25 per cent a year ; the average flow for ten countries post-1965 was only 1 per cent ( 2 ) .
7893	The advocates of the Government 's ‘ competing currencies ’ approach suggest that many of these gains would occur by merely moving to a ‘ hard ’ EMS in which currencies became progressively more fixed ( 3 ) .
7894	However , the evidence so far suggests that it is not enough to persuade businesspeople that rates will really be fixed forever .
7895	Moreover , the process of establishing credibility is long drawn out .
7896	The French , despite an exceptionally tough policy , still have interest rates above the German level because they are unable to persuade the markets they mean what they say when they rule out a devaluation .
7897	Nor is it sensible to argue , as the Treasury has , that a European system of central banks in charge of a single currency might prove more inflationary than a fixed exchange rate system where each monetary authority competed to provide a stable benchmark of value .
7898	It is impossible to make any such comparison without knowing what the institutional arrangements of the system would be .
7899	If the system 's charter allowed for a bank governor to be shot at dawn for every month the inflation rate exceeded 1 per cent , it might prove even more counter-inflationary than the Bundesbank .
7900	The potential political and economic gains ensure that the impetus towards a currency union in Europe is likely to prove much stronger today than it did in the turbulent Seventies .
7901	And that , in turn , is likely to feed back on the Government in the form of pressures from the most irresistible of all Tory constituencies , the City .
7902	After all , what would be more likely to gain from a brave new world of free capital flows than the greatest financial centre in Europe ?
7903	This week has not seen the end of the row about Europe in the Conservative party , but merely a regrouping of forces for the battle still to come .
7904	( 1 ) ‘ Europe without currency barriers ’ Samuel Brittan , Michael Artis , The Social Market Foundation , London , £5.00.
7905	( 2 ) ‘ Savings-investment correlations : immobile capital , government policy or endogenous behaviour ? ’
7906	Tamim Bayoumi , International Monetary Fund working paper 89/66. ( 3 ) An evolutionary approach to EMU , HM Treasury , November 1989 .

8014	22COMMENT THE GUARDIANWednesday November 8 1989 More than just another disaster .
8015	THIRTY FIVE people died and others were maimed for life in the Clapham rail disaster in December last year because work was done in a slovenly , haphazard way and was then left unchecked .
8016	The disaster was all the more stunning because people had come to assume that such things did n't happen .
8017	In most years , rail deaths are few : in some there are none at all .
8018	Clapham , indeed , accounts for nearly half the 77 fatalities of the last ten years : compare that with the 5,000 deaths and 300,000 injuries every year on the roads .
8019	Yet yesterday 's report on the Clapham crash , confirming the picture which emerged throughout the Hidden inquiry , makes an event which seemed at the time totally unexpected look almost inevitable .
8020	This was a system hopelessly under strain .
8021	Under strain for a start because it was technically ill-equipped to avert disaster or to cope with the consequences when disaster struck ; under strain from commercial pressures which , as the inquiry puts it , ‘ compromised ’ safety ; under strain above all because the people on the spot could n't or would n't cope , were weary from gruesome working hours ( the senior signal technician who heads the list of the culpable had had only one day off in the past 13 weeks ) , lacked adequate training , or simply could n't be bothered .
8022	The bulk of the blame for all that is placed on British Rail , which knowingly permitted these things to continue .
8023	Though individuals are nailed , the greatest villain of all is the system .
8024	In a desperately competitive climate , where anyone bright and competent could go down the road and pick up a better paid job with kinder hours and more congenial working conditions from someone like British Telecom , the railways ran a service dependent on people who belonged to a narrow and inbred working culture , with outdated procedures of training and promotion , and an institutional reliance on overtime working , whose wholly disgraceful dimensions are symbolised by the fact that maximum weekly hours were only recently cut to 72 hours a week .
8025	The Transport Secretary , Mr Cecil Parkinson , assured the Commons yesterday that financial considerations would not stand in the way of implementing Sir Anthony Hidden 's 93 recommendations .
8026	On the technical side , remedial work is in many cases already on the way .
8027	But the job of lifting the standards of people employed , giving them proper training , and paying a wage which breaks dependence on overtime and lifts morale : this together must far exceed the costs of the technology , and it is n't by any means clear what the bill will be or where the money will come from .
8028	All of which is not just a problem for a properly penitent British Rail : it 's a problem for government too .
8029	Government fixes the format in which BR has to work ; and if , as the Hidden report attests , many of its problems today reflect lack of past planning , lack of farsighted investment , living from hand to mouth , then that is not just BR 's doing .
8030	Government compounds all these problems when it sets down working parameters which fail to reflect the value the country gets from a system that is run efficiently , can shift people to destinations with exemplary speed and safety — as Europe consistently demonstrates .
8031	It is sad , and somewhat ominous , that so little of that should have been reflected in the sombre statement which Mr Parkinson made in the House yesterday ..
8032	A service in chaos .
8033	THE nation 's ambulance service was in manifest chaos yesterday .
8034	There was no service in London , with all 71 stations and 455 vehicles off the road .
8035	The only accident and emergency relief was provided by the police , part-time St John ambulance volunteers running 20 vehicles , and the Red Cross .
8036	Outside the capital , accident and emergency services were being provided in most areas , but the ban on emergency work was tightened .
8037	The service was facing its biggest crisis since the ambulances came to a stop in the Winter of Discontent ten years ago .
8038	Like Labour in 1979 , the Conservatives have put military ambulances on standby .
8039	They move in today .
8040	What has gone wrong ?
8041	There are three key causes of the shambles : Mr Kenneth Clarke ; the failure to separate emergency from non-emergency work ; and the Whitley Council negotiating machinery .
8042	The Health Secretary accused the unions of ‘ posturing and pretending ’ to run a 999 service yesterday .
8043	He was right .
8044	By refusing to keep open two-way radio links , the crews had effectively ended a proper emergency service .
8045	The move was signalled last week and , true to their promised response , management suspended the workers involved in the disruption .
8046	But ‘ posturing and pretending ’ went far beyond the unions .
8047	Mr Clarke has been indulging in just that himself , putting up the luckless Duncan Nichol , chief executive of the health service , to take the initial flak under the pretence that the dispute is not his direct responsibility .
8048	Yet it was Mr Clarke , not Mr Nichol , who was involved in the critical decisions — the cash limit for the NHS , the 6.5 per cent offer to ambulance workers ( compared to seven per cent for nurses , eight per cent for doctors and nine per cent for ancillary workers ) ; and today 's introduction of military ambulances .
8049	Ambulance workers on emergency work do deserve a much higher increase .
8050	They have progressed far beyond routine first aid .
8051	Their paramedical skills cover highly technical procedures : intubation , infusion and defebrillation .
8052	The crews are able to resuscitate heart attack patients , replace fluid intraveneously after severe blood loss , and insert tubes to maintain air supplies in unconconscious casualties .
8053	Yet the ambulance worker is only being offered £10,000 , when a fire officer is being given £13,000 and a Metropolitan police constable can earn £25,000 .
8054	But only two million out of the 20 million journeys which ambulance crews carry out each year are emergency calls .
8055	Nine out of 10 are routine calls , many of which could be carried out by mini cabs .
8056	Mr Duncan Nichol wants to separate the emergency from the non-emergency work .
8057	He is right to pursue this line .
8058	Wiltshire and Northumbria have already shown how much can be achieved .
8059	The ramshackle Whitley Council negotiating machinery is the other reason why the ambulance workers have lost out .
8060	Until this year , the three independent review bodies which make recommendations for nurses , doctors and the professions allied to medicine have given much higher awards than the Whitley Councils .
8061	As Lord McCarthy noted some 13 years ago , the management side of the councils comprise ‘ employers who do not pay and paymasters who do not employ . ’
8062	A much more flexible system which would allow local managers to negotiate local rates — on a national pay spine — is needed .
8063	A crisis ; an agenda for reform and honesty .
8064	One Mr Clarke can not duck away from if he wants to avoid a second Winter of Discontent ..

8314	Army to take emergency calls .
8315	By Keith Harper , David Brindle and Patrick Wintour
8316	TROOPS will be used to provide emergency ambulance cover in London from this afternoon in what the unions yesterday described as a political attempt by the Government to escalate the dispute .
8317	The decision to use the army was taken by the Health Secretary , Mr Kenneth Clarke , despite the fact that ambulance staff are not on strike .
8318	They are still offering to provide an emergency service .
8319	Mr Duncan Nichol , the NHS chief executive , told the Guardian that the Government 's negotiating position is that it wants to split the service so crews with medical skills can earn extra money and non-emergency services can be contracted out .
8320	Mr Clarke 's decision followed the suspension of 2,500 staff at 71 London stations for refusing to work normally .
8321	The crews want an increase on a 6.5 per cent pay offer .
8322	A late night attempt to resume talks today by the London ambulance employers ended in failure just before midnight when the unions rejected the call .
8323	The unions ' chief negotiator , Mr Roger Poole , said earlier on television that emergency services would be guaranteed without conditions .
8324	Mr Nichol said the Government wants to settle the dispute with a deal that would allow local managers to top up the pay of crews with paramedical skills in a move towards the separation of the 999 service from routine work .
8325	It would give designated emergency crews the chance to achieve pay parity with firemen .
8326	According to Mr Nichol , such a deal could increase pay rates in London by 30 per cent and elsewhere by 20 per cent .
8327	The idea was immediately rejected by the main health service union , Nupe , which said last night the Government was trying to split the ambulance staff .
8328	‘ We want a pay deal now to solve all our problems and a formula which would prevent us from taking action in future , ’ a spokesman said .
8329	The Government 's formal negotiating stance on pay was set out by Mr Clarke , who said there was no question of increasing the general 6.5 per cent offer .
8330	The troops will join the police , who were reluctantly involved yesterday after the London ambulance service said it could not cope .
8331	The employers admitted troops would provide an inferior service .
8332	Mr Clarke said : ‘ I see no reason why the NHS management should give a higher offer in response to industrial action and then have to close down beds and reduce patient services to pay for it . ’
8333	Mr Nichol , however , said there was ‘ plenty to talk about ’ , including the idea of a local flexibility deal , put at the conciliation service , Acas , two weeks ago .
8334	The proposed deal would be modelled on a settlement this year for 130,000 NHS administrative and clerical staff .
8335	Mr Nichol said ambulance staff could receive pay premiums worth more than £3,000 , in recognition of extra training , local recruitment problems and other factors such as merit or long service .
8336	Only 10 per cent of the 20 million annual ambulance journeys are emergencies .
8337	At present , crews typically rotate between 999 and routine work , making it difficult to designate crews for higher pay .
8338	It is the first time troops have been brought in during a dispute since 1978 .
8339	Mr Clarke told the Commons he was doing it with great reluctance .
8340	Mr Robin Cook , Labour 's health spokesman , said Mr Clarke had given no good explanation for his precipitate action .
8341	He advised arbitration .
8342	The House was called to order at one stage by the Speaker , Mr Bernard Weatherill , after Mr Clarke accused crews of waiting at stations ‘ pretending ’ to be ready for work .
8343	Mr Chris Spry , for the London ambulance service , said the army 's help was sought because crews were not using their radios to answer emergency calls .
8344	The police could only cover accidents , not doctors referrals .
8345	He challenged the unions to lift restrictions on radios , the movement of staff between stations and the carrying of seriously ill patients .
8346	If this was done , the army would not be employed .
8347	The action in London had an immediate effect elsewhere as crews began to protest at the Government 's intervention .
8348	Greater Manchester shop stewards agreed to halt all routine work in protest against suspensions and Welsh crews promised to stage work-ins if suspensions went ahead .

8350	Army needed ‘ to aid police ’ .
8351	By Keith Harper and David Fairhall
8352	THE South West Thames regional health authority requested the army be drafted in for ambulance work when it became clear the police could not cope , according to ambulance mangement .
8353	Mr Chris Spry , for the London ambulance service , said the police were unable to meet the demand for accident services , particularly those phoned through to hospitals from family doctors .
8354	About 50 military vehicles will supplement 53 from the police and voluntary organisations , such as the St John Ambulance .
8355	The sickest patients will be carried by voluntary groups , the next by the army , with the least ill by the police .
8356	The army will be based at police stations and will be allocated calls via the police .
8357	Of the 103 vehicles in use , 60 will serve London north of the Thames , and 43 the south .
8358	Normally the London ambulance service maintains 175 emergency ambulances on duty during the day and 75 at night .
8359	All military and voluntary vehicles will be given some of London 's equipment , including special orthopaedic stretchers and chairs .

8368	Management yesterday began suspending ambulance staff in retaliation to the work to rule tactics of the unions .
8369	The troops ' intervention in the ambulance strike is being authorised under a Whitehall arrangement which enables one department to request ‘ military aid to the civil ministries ’ from the Ministry of Defence and pay the bill afterwards .
8370	This arrangement means there is no need for Mrs Thatcher to consider declaring a State of Emergency , as Mr Heath 's government did during the 1973 miners ' strike .
8371	That would only be necessary if the troops had been requisitioning other people 's equipment .
8372	Mrs Thatcher has never declared a state of emergency .
8373	Troops have been used more than 30 times since the second world war to replace striking workers .
8374	During the 1970s they were called out to clear hundreds of tons rubbish from the streets of Glasgow during the 1975 dustmen 's strike .
8375	Two years later dozens of Green Goddess military fire engines were brought out of storage to cover the firemen 's strike .
8376	During Mrs Thatcher 's administration , troops have found themselves involved in five industrial disputes — to operate prisons in 1980/81 , to drive ambulances in 1981 and 1982 , to cover for civil servants during a dispute at the Coulport submarine base in 1981 , and to help with car parking during the rail strike of 1982 .
8377	Richard Norton-Taylor adds : Contingency plans for the use of troops in ambulance disputes were drawn up shortly after the Government came to power in 1979 , Whitehall documents show .
8378	They were drafted by the Ministry of Defence and Department of Health .
8379	Department of Health officials wrote to regional administrators in 1980 with details of a new plan — code-named Bittern — providing for ‘ the use of service ambulances and drivers in the event of an industrial dispute ’ — the decision now taken yesterday by ministers .
8380	Two other plans , not activated now , were also drawn up .
8381	One , code-named Concord , dealt with how the armed forces would drive NHS ambulances , and the other , code-named Lionel , with a limited service in a strike involving certain ancillary workers .

8414	More than 20 animals , mostly calves , have died from lead poisoning .

8417	But routine screening of milk for contaminants should have disclosed higher lead levels by mid-October .

8419	Rather than being thrown away , the contaminated milk was poured into tanks of clean milk to dilute the lead down to permissible levels .

8758	Technicians ' wiring mistake caused disaster Dangerous practices and communication failures contributed to 35 deaths BR 's slipshod style ‘ led to crash errors ’ .
8759	By David Sharrock .
8760	AFAILURE of the signalling system — which occurred when a signal box wire that should have been removed was not , thus preventing the signal from turning to red — caused the Clapham rail disaster in which 35 people died last December 12 , according to the report of the inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hidden , QC .
8761	The 56-day public inquiry heard 122 witnesses .
8762	The report lists ‘ many faults ’ inherent in the way the railway had been run for several years .
8763	Noted as relevant to the Clapham accident were the factors that : Working practices were permitted to slip to dangerous standards and quality of supervision was permitted to slip to an equivalent degree ; quality of testing did not meet BR standards ; no proper system of training of installation and testing staff was in use , and there was no vetting of weekend staff to prevent excessive overtime ; and there was failure to communicate both up and down lines of management .
8764	The fault which caused the Clapham crash is traced to the final installation of a new signal , number WF138 , on November 27 , 1988 , by Mr Brian Hemingway , a senior technician .
8765	There was nothing new in signal WF138 's concept or installation , the report says .
8766	Mr Hemingway 's task on the weekend of November 26-27 was to connect the circuit 's new wires and disconnect the old wire at both its relay end and its fuse end .
8767	‘ In fact , no disconnection was made at the fuse end , and although at the other relay end the old wire was disconnected , it was not cut back as it should have been , nor was it secured out of the way of its previous contact . ’
8768	If the wrong circumstances arose , it was physically possible for the old wire to return to its old position .
8769	‘ Those circumstances did arise . ’
8770	Two weeks later , the day before the accident , Mr Hemingway was working on the signal again .
8771	His efforts disturbed the positions of the wires .
8772	‘ The consequences were not only unintended , they were disastrous .
8773	‘ As long as there was a large enough interval between trains running into London , no train would be close enough to the one in front to be affected by the faulty signal . ’
8774	Shortly before 8.10am on December 12 , Mr Alex McClymont , driving the Basingstoke to Waterloo train , noted that the signal was at red .
8775	He had ‘ unwillingly become involved in an incident known in railway jargon as a SPAD ( Signal Passed At Danger ) . ’
8776	BR rules stipulated he must stop immediately and notify the signalman .
8777	‘ When he did so , he would have been holding to an instinctive belief that the signal behind him would inevitably have gone to red .

8810	Army to take emergency calls .
8811	By Keith Harper , David Brindle and Patrick Wintour
8812	TROOPS will be used in London from 2pm today to take ambulance emergency calls in what the unions regarded last night as a ‘ political ’ attempt to escalate the dispute .
8813	With the call-up of the troops by Mr Kenneth Clarke , the Health Secretary , came fresh revelations yesterday that the Government wants to settle the dispute with a deal that would allow local managers to top up the pay of crews with special paramedical skills .
8814	The move would be a decisive step towards the separation of the 999 service from routine ambulance work .
8815	It would give designated emergency crews the chance to achieve their goal of pay parity with firefighters .
8816	Mr Duncan Nichol , the National Health Service chief executive , told the Guardian that division of the service and the putting out to contract of non-emergency work was ‘ likely ’ .
8817	According to Mr Nichol , such a deal could increase pay rates in London by 30 per cent and elsewhere by 20 per cent .
8818	It is already operating in Wiltshire and other parts of the country .
8819	The idea was rejected by the main health service union , Nupe , which said last night that the Government was trying to split the ambulance staff .
8820	‘ We want a pay deal now to solve all our problems and a formula which would prevent us from taking action in future . ’
8821	The Government 's formal negotiating stance on pay was set out by Mr Clarke , who told a press conference there was no question of increasing the general 6.5 per cent offer to the ambulance crews in the face of disruptive action .
8822	The troops will join the police , who were reluctantly involved yesterday in the capital after the London Ambulance Service said that it could not cope .
8823	The employers admitted that there would be an inferior service .
8824	It is the first time that troops have been brought in during an industrial dispute since the firemen 's strike in 1978 .
8825	Mr Clarke told the House of Commons that he was doing it with great reluctance .
8826	The difference between 1978 and now is that ambulance staff are not on strike but are working to rule , and answering all emergency calls .
8827	Mr Robin Cook , the shadow Health Secretary , who advised the Government to call in arbitrators rather than the army , said that Mr Clarke had given no satisfactory explanation for his precipitate action .
8828	Mr Roger Poole , the ambulance unions ' chief negotiator , said that the Government was putting the lives of Londoners at risk .
8829	All ambulance crews would continue to stand by at their stations for 999 calls .
8830	‘ This is a crass decision by Mr Clarke and the Government is playing dangerous game , ’ he said .
8831	Mr Chris Spry , for the London Ambulance Service , said that the South West Thames regional health authority had asked for the army 's help .
8832	About 50 military vehicles will supplement 53 from the police and voluntary organisations , such as the St John Ambulance .
8833	The sickest patients will be carried by voluntary groups , the next by the army , with the least ill by the police .
8834	The army will be based at police stations and will be allocated calls via the police .
8835	The need to call in troops , according to Mr Spry , became apparent by mid-afternoon yesterday when the police could not meet the demand for accident services .
8836	Mr Tom Crosby , chief ambulance officer for London , said the level of care would drop but insisted that the army crews had some medical training and were not basic infantry men .
8837	Mr Chris Humphreys , London secretary of Nupe , said : ‘ It is obvious that Kenneth Clarke intends to try and starve our members back to work .
8838	The Government can not pretend to be concerned with security at army barracks and then , without regard for the soldiers , put them on the streets of London as easy targets for the terrorists . ’
8839	Management yesterday began suspending ambulance staff in retaliation to the unions ' work-to-rule tactics .
8840	Mr Clarke said the armed forces would be withdrawn as soon as the unions agreed to provide a normal emergency service .
8841	The action taken in London had an immediate affect elsewhere as ambulance crews began to protest at the Government 's intervention .
8842	Greater Manchester union officials agreed to halt all routine work in protest against suspensions , and Welsh crews promised to stage work-ins if suspensions went ahead .
8843	Soldiers in front line , page 3 ; Leader comment , page 22 ; Duncan Nichol interview , page 23
8844	Soldiers in the front line of industrial strife David Fairhall on the discreet arrangement that has brought in the troops .
8845	THE troops ' intervention in the ambulance strike is not being authorised under the Emergency Powers Act , but under a Whitehall arrangement which enables one department to request ‘ military aid to the civil ministries ’ from the Ministry of Defence and pay the bill afterwards .
8846	This discreet arrangement means , among other things , that there was no need for Mrs Thatcher to consider declaring a state of emergency , as Mr Heath 's government did during the 1973 miners ' strike .
8847	That would only have been necessary had the troops been requisitioning other people 's equipment , rather than turning out with their own ambulances .
8848	Troops have been used more than 30 times since the second world war to replace striking workers .
8849	During the 1970s they were called out to clear hundreds of tons rubbish from the streets of Glasgow during the 1975 dustmen 's strike .
8850	Two years later dozens of Green Goddess military fire engines were brought out of storage to cover the firemen 's strike .
8851	In 1974 military engineers stood by to operate power stations in Northern Ireland during the protest strike by the Protestant Ulster Workers ' Council , though they could have done nothing without the help of at least the power station managers .
8852	During Mrs Thatcher 's administration , troops have found themselves involved in five industrial disputes — to operate prisons in 1980/81 , to drive ambulances in 1981 and 1982 , to cover for civil servants during a dispute at the Coulport submarine base in 1981 , and to help with car parking during the rail strike of 1982 .
8853	Soldiers never like being asked to do somebody else 's dirty work , especially if they have been called off leave to do it , and are likely to be accused of strike breaking in the process .
8854	On the other hand they will readily respond to civil emergencies such as floods .
8855	In this case the request for help falls somewhere between the extremes of the Glasgow dustmen 's strike and straight humanitarian operations such as rescuing people from snowdrifts .
8856	In the latest situation troops are being drafted in to do jobs they normally do and for which they are trained .
8857	The crews are mostly ‘ medical assistants , ’ which means possessing more than just a knowledge of first aid .
8858	Richard Norton-Taylor adds : Contingency plans for the use of troops in ambulance disputes were drawn up shortly after the Government came to power in 1979 , Whitehall documents show .
8859	They were drafted by the Ministry of Defence and Department of Health .
8860	Department of Health officials wrote to regional administrators in 1980 with details of a new plan — code-named Bittern — providing for ‘ the use of service ambulances and drivers in the event of an industrial dispute ’ — the decision now taken yesterday by ministers .
8861	Two other plans , not activated in the present dispute , were also drawn up .
8862	One , code-named Concord , dealt with how the armed forces would drive NHS ambulances .
8863	The other plan , code-named Lionel , related to limited service assistance in the event of a strike involving certain skilled and semi-skilled ancillary workers .
8864	The circular makes clear that a decision to implement the contingency plans would be ‘ subject to collective ministerial authority ’ .
8865	The Department of Health warned that the number of troops allocated may not be all forthcoming because of commitments elsewhere .
8866	Any disclosure of information contained in the plans , it said , would be ‘ extremely damaging to the Government 's industrial relations policy ’ .

9098	Meanwhile , in the Moldavian republic several people were hurt when nationalists battled with police as growing unrest in the country wrecked some regional celebrations of the Revolution .

9333	It 's for the people .
9334	I 'll go for it .
9335	I 've been through it all .
9336	I was made redundant less than a year after I became a Sheffield city councillor , and I 've never believed in those sorts of coincidences .
9337	You have to fight and fight again . ’
9338	Now , it was n't just the man from the Midland Bank who was clearing his throat .
9339	Everyone in the board room was either clearing his throat , or shifting position in his seat , or doing both at the same time , which is actually rather difficult .
9340	Except Jimmy Boyce , that is .
9341	Jimmy 's audacious move was making everyone feel uncomfortable , except himself .
9342	He had finally settled to his fate : socialist entrepreneur of the grand scale .
9343	‘ It 's early days yet , ’ said Colin Appleby from the Midland , ‘ early days ’ .
9344	He seemed to be saying it as much to convince himself as to convince all the rest .
9345	They were still busy with their ticklish coughs .
9346	But it was now Colin Appleby 's move .
9347	Fate had got him as far as a leading Sheffield estate agents , Blundells .
9348	Colin gave that smile of familiarity , that smile of superiority , that certain smile that says it all .
9349	‘ Ah , Mike 's place .
9350	Yes , I am interested in that .
9351	I think I will purchase it . ’
9352	It was like a red rag to a big , black bull .
9353	Or , given that we were in a quasi-political domain , a black flag to a red bull .
9354	‘ I want to buy up all of the city , ’ said Jimmy .
9355	The statement startled no one .
9356	‘ I 'll be happy with Mike 's place for the moment , ’ said Colin , again rubbing in that he knew a thing or two about some of Sheffield 's leading businesses , and that there is no substitute for that kind of detailed and expert and intimate knowledge .
9357	But now it was time for some wheeling and dealing .
9358	Shares in the Sheffield Development Corporation were up for sale .
9359	Richard Holmes , the sales and marketing officer of the YMCA in Sheffield , had managed to get his hands on some .
9360	He needed to raise capital fast .
9361	The man from the Midland Bank said he had n't the kind of money required .
9362	He would have liked to help him out , but …
9363	All eyes were now on Jimmy Boyce .
9364	He had the capital , but did he have the inclination to buy into yet another business in order to help one of the managers out ?
9365	The minimum bid was established .
9366	Richard assumed that it would be doubled .
9367	‘ It would be a bargain at twice that price . ’
9368	Nobody doubted him , or failed to recognise his temporary financial embarrassment .
9369	It 's just that they were not inclined to help him out .
9370	‘ If you ca n't stand the heat , Richard , old boy , ’ an anonymous voice said .
9371	Jimmy , however , did show some interest .
9372	‘ I 'm always in search of a bargain , sonny — for the people , you understand , ’ he added after yet another of those pauses that suggested it might have been an after-thought .
9373	He eventually offered Richard £10 more than the asking price .
9374	‘ Typical Socialist , ’ someone muttered .
9375	Jimmy heard the jibe .
9376	‘ I 'm a Scot , after all .
9377	Never forget that , sonny .
9378	And I 'm not the one with all the money — just look at the pile that Colin Appleby 's got .
9379	A typical bloody banker , if you ask me .
9380	Not a bit of wonder the country 's in the state that it 's in . ’
9381	For readers already familiar with the transmogrification of Sheffield from the Socialist Republic of South Yorkshire to something altogether more ‘ pragmatic ’ , you could be forgiven for believing that the drama unfolding around the boardroom table was just one more step along this route , with committed socialists playing the stock market with the best of them .
9382	But this was just a game , and before some one points out that the stock market is itself just a game ( for somewhat privileged people ) , I should add that this was just a family game being marketed in Sheffield for Christmas .
9383	It 's called Sheffield Shares , a form of Monopoly for the late eighties .
9384	Local companies are bought and sold , and the involvement and interest that the game generates , as I discovered , is quite intense .
9385	Richard Holmes of the Sheffield YMCA told me about the background to the game .
9386	The idea is that Sheffield companies pay real money for the privilege of being squares on the game — for the obvious advertising benefits .
9387	The Midland Bank , as the major sponsor , is paying £20,000 for the privilege of being two corners in the game , and having its name and logo on all the notes used in the game .
9388	The sponsorship money for the 30 squares amounted to £150,000 and paid all the production and advertising costs for the game .
9389	All subsequent profits from sales of the game , which retails at £13.99 , go directly to the YMCA for its work in the community in Sheffield .
9390	Several other British towns and cities are already committed to developing their own version of this game , with all profits going to the local YMCA .
9391	Keith Wells , general secretary of the Sheffield YMCA , and the fourth player that night , explained that the idea originated in Norway , where 95 towns had produced the game to finance their local YMCA .
9392	In the United Kingdom , Derry/Londonderry was the first and their game was called The Maiden City , presumably in order not to alienate that half of the community which did not approve of either the name Derry or Londonderry .
9393	Keith Wells pointed out that the title Sheffield Shares is deliberately ambiguous — it can be taken to mean Sheffield 's shares , as in ‘ shares ’ which are up for grabs by keen or greedy speculators ( my interpretation ) , but it can also mean Sheffield shares as in ‘ shares its wealth ’ — ‘ and that 's basically what we are trying to initiate here .
9394	We 're trying to get big , local companies to plough some of their profits back into the community through the work of the YMCA . ’
9395	So what kind of advertising do the companies get for their money ?
9396	On the share cards used in the game , not only the name of the company is printed , but also some succinct message about the firm .
9397	Such messages could ( at a push ) be used by players to help them promote the value of the shares in that company in the interminable rounds of wheeling and dealing .
9398	As in ‘ How would you like to buy some shares in Stocksbridge Engineering Works — ‘ Manufacturers of high integrity alloy , stainless and re-melted steels for the aerospace , energy , bearing and automotive industries .
9399	The Strength Behind Engineering Progress ’ . ’
9400	Or the more punchy ‘ How would you like to buy some shares in Gibbs Building Contractors — ‘ Do n't pick your contractor/ By throwing a dice/ Bring GIBBS into the game/ Ask us for a price ’ . ’
9401	Even if it is not read out in the endless rounds of buying and selling shares , then the message , passive though it might be , should still find its way into the living rooms of a high proportion of homes in the Sheffield region .
9402	The plan is to sell 20,000 games in Sheffield over the Christmas period that is , 1 in 20 homes .
9403	There are 4,000 advance orders .
9404	A lot of families , it is hoped , are going to be hearing or reading about Stocksbridge Engineering Works , Gibbs Building Contractors , and a few other Sheffield firms this Christmas .
9405	Colin Appleby , of the Midland Bank , is extremely pleased with the way the game has turned out .
9406	He says that as well as being the major sponsor of the game , the Midland is the largest private sector employer in Sheffield , and the game provided another opportunity for the bank to demonstrate that it is prepared to invest in the city .
9407	But what sort of person will make a good player at Sheffield Shares ?
9408	I 'd already noted the very different methods of the four who had assembled .
9409	It would have taken a blind man , or a very naive one , not to spot some connection between their style of play and the kinds of responsibilities and decisions they have to make in the outside world .
9410	I asked Colin Appleby first .
9411	‘ I liked Jimmy Boyce 's play for his quick decisions .
9412	Richard Holmes was something of an expert at the game , but he ended up as a down-and-out by the end .
9413	I think the main ingredient for success is that you have to have a good sense of timing .
9414	There is nothing wrong with being a bit conservative and building up financial resources , and not just jumping straight in .
9415	Jimmy had a lot of flair but it did n't help him win . ’
9416	Indeed it did not .
9417	Colin 's conservativism and steady timing had won him second place .
9418	Richard Holmes thought that ‘ the best man usually wins , ’ despite the fact that he was last .
9419	Jimmy Boyce put it down nearly all to luck — ‘ with negotiation skills being very important . ’
9420	Jimmy said he really enjoyed playing , but his slight worry about it was that at £13.99 it might prove expensive for the unemployed .
9421	But what did the winner of the game actually think — Keith Wells , the man who had brought the game to England but had never actually played it before ?
9422	There was a long pause , the kind of pause that winners always display as they create a little time to savour their victory .
9423	‘ It 's basically a fine balance between being a good steward of what you have already acquired , and being something of a visionary .
9424	Rather like running the YMCA in fact , although I 'd never thought of it like that before .
9425	It was all jolly good fun as well , of course . ’

9427	Law Report .
9428	Parliament urged to think again on housing issue : .
9429	Queen 's Bench Divisional Court Sandwell Metropolitan Borough Council v Bujok Before Lord Justice Watkins and Mr Justice Hutchison November 2 1989
9430	IF a dwelling house is in such a state of disrepair as to be prejudicial to health or a nuisance , the tenant may lay an information against his landlord alleging the existence of a statutory nuisance under the Public Health Act 1936 .
9431	The tenant is not obliged to ensure that the landlord is aware of the defects in the premises or to give the landlord an opportunity to remedy the defects before commencing legal proceedings .
9432	Although that is the position in law , the court emphasised that as a matter of commonsense a tenant should first complain to the landlord before exercising the right to prosecute .
9433	The facts .
9434	Mrs Bujok and her family occupied a house as council tenants .
9435	In September 1988 Mrs Bujok laid an information against the council alleging the existence and continuance of a statutory nuisance under section 92(1) of the Public Health Act 1936 .
9436	It was alleged that the council , being the owners of the premises , were the persons by whose act , default or sufferance the nuisance arose .
9437	Prior to laying the information Mrs Bujok had not served an abatement notice upon the council or informed them of the alleged defects in the premises .
9438	The justices held Mrs Bujok was not required to ensure that the council were aware of the defective state of the property prior to laying the information .
9439	The council appealed by case stated .
9440	The legislation .
9441	Section 92(1) of the 1936 Act defines ‘ statutory nuisances ’ as ‘ any premises in such a state as to be prejudicial to health or a nuisance ’ .
9442	The decision .
9443	Mr Justice Hutchison said the 1936 Act primarily envisages a system where the local authority has a power and a duty to try to secure that premises are not in a state which constitutes a statutory nuisance .
9444	Action is initiated by the service of an abatement notice requiring remedial work .
9445	If the person in default fails to comply with an abatement notice the local authority is obliged to make a complaint to the magistrates .
9446	If the complaint is proved , a nuisance order is made requiring the defendant to get the necessary work done .
9447	Effectively the sequence is that the person in default is told what is wrong and is required to put it right .
9448	He is given an opportunity to do so , and if he does not , he is subject to sanctions by the court to compel him to do so .
9449	The problem arises in connection with section 99 which adapts or applies the provisions to cases where an individual rather than the local authority wishes to make the complaint .
9450	Need he serve an abatement notice ?
9451	The authorities plainly establish that he need not and can not do so .
9452	Does that mean he may lay an information and bring the matter before the magistrates without first putting the person alleged to be in default on notice of what is alleged ?
9453	The council argued that a landlord , particularly one such as a local authority , can not realistically be expected to have a system of inspection of all its premises and in practice is entitled to depend upon notification by its tenants .
9454	For Mrs Bujok it was argued that the 1936 Act was designed to secure in the interests of the community at large that statutory nuisances did not exist .
9455	It was submitted that an owner can not turn his back on his property because when he purchases and takes on the responsibility of letting , he knows the property will in the course of time deteriorate .
9456	He must therefore satisfy himself on a regular basis that it does not constitute a statutory nuisance .
9457	In Warner v Lambeth London Borough Council ( 1985 ) 15 HLR 45 , 50 , Lord Justice Glidewell said a private person could lay an information alleging the failure to abate a statutory nuisance without first giving notice requiring abatement .
9458	Therefore in the present case the justices came to the correct conclusion .
9459	His Lordship reached that decision without enthusiasm because it seemed that as a matter of common sense , notice should be given in such circumstances before criminal proceedings were launched .
9460	Lord Justice Watkins said he agreed with reluctance .
9461	It was surely repugnant to commonsense that in this area of legal activity a local authority should be prosecuted by one of its tenants without first being given the opportunity by that tenant to remedy the consequences of a neglect to repair the dwelling that the tenant occupied .
9462	In law there was no doubt that Mrs Bujok was entitled to commence proceedings without giving notice of the state of the dwelling to the council .
9463	But in every other conceivable way that action was entirely wrong .
9464	Endless trouble to many people in courts and council offices and much money could be saved by the giving of notice of disrepair .
9465	If the council did not react to that notice , then would be the time for the tenant to exercise the right to prosecute .
9466	Parliament should give fresh thought to enacting a provision placing an obligation upon a council tenant to give notice to the council before being permitted to commence proceedings .
9467	Appearances : John Cherryman QC instructed by Sherwood &amp; Co for the council ; Elizabeth Norman instructed by Michael Arnold &amp; Co , Oldbury , for Mrs Bujok .

9469	Input/Tim Radford We come to hit hypocrites with a brick , not to praise them .
9470	PERHAPS there should be more hypocrisy in the world .
9471	There 's plenty in Britain .
9472	The British go to night classes in it , and particularly savour high-class hypocrites .
9473	They tend to admire people for how they hold themselves and what they say and then blame them more for being found out than for what they do .
9474	After a while you get tainted with hypocrisy even if you try not to .
9475	You begin to see that it 's just another language .
9476	You begin to enjoy the way people can say ‘ The National Health Service is safe in our hands ’ or ‘ Nobody deplores apartheid more than we do ’ or even ‘ We do not have a shoot-to-kill policy ’ and you know that another hospital is going to close and that there will be another stitch-up with Pretoria and that another shooting is going to be quietly forgotten .
9477	It is , admittedly , refreshing to meet the occasional non-slippery politician .
9478	‘ Frankly , Tim , we cocked that one up , ’ an Antipodean politico said to me once .
9479	‘ We made a real dog 's breakfast of it . ’
9480	It was quite a clever move on his part .
9481	Suddenly I did n't have anything else to ask him .
9482	Actually , politicians are never that frank , and never honest : the game is n't played that way .
9483	And anyway , if somebody is too forthright and says what he really thinks you might feel impelled to hit him with a brick .
9484	But then hypocrisy has grades , like judo .
9485	In Britain they are all black belts .
9486	The British murmur ‘ You must come and stay with us some time , ’ and when they part they say ‘ Let's keep in touch ’ and they certainly do n't mean it , but it greases the wheels of intercourse .
9487	And it stops you having to hit them with a brick .
9488	There have been grade-A hypocrites all through history .
9489	The Roman Emperors were much more slippery than anyone gives them credit for .
9490	One of them once issued an edict against promiscuous kissing on New Year 's Day .
9491	He complained about the absurd cost of mullet and in a wild bid to introduce good housekeeping to Imperial Rome he served for dinner what was leftover from the banquet before .
9492	He showed ‘ excessive ’ courtesy to the House of the Senate , saying once ‘ You will , I hope , forgive me if I trespass on my rights as a senator by speaking rather more plainly than I should . ’
9493	It was the Emperor Tiberius , one of history 's unspeakable bounders .
9494	Since this is a family newspaper , one shrinks from recounting the things he bounded round doing on Capri .
9495	But they had nothing to do with cheap mullet .
9496	Tiberius was one of those men you are warned to flee from and report to the police when they arrive offering sweets .
9497	He was one of those men of whom the historian Edward Gibbon , who wrote the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire , reported their disgusting activities ‘ in the decent obscurity of a learned language . ’
9498	That meant he could say it in Latin , which , when you think about it , was another fundamental hypocrisy .
9499	But fundamentalists are not usually hypocrites .
9500	They are a different problem .
9501	They believe in the truth and they are n't frightened of telling you about it .
9502	Their truth of course , but they recognise no other .
9503	Furthermore they do n't know about ‘ good form ’ and ‘ bad form ’ and saying one thing and doing another .
9504	But fundamentalists are also really dangerous , at least for a while , because hypocrites think that everybody is talking double talk , like them , and awful misunderstandings occur .
9505	They do n't have to be religious fundamentalists .
9506	They can just be people who believe they ought to reshape society from top to bottom .
9507	But they are just as difficult to read if you are used to political hypocrisy .
9508	But then the British — or perhaps more properly the English — deal best with their own .
9509	To them , hypocrisy is aggravated assault by other means .
9510	They can execrate someone whom they decide is a useless clown and they do this by making him a Lord , giving him the chairmanship of a quango and telling the chaps at the Athenaeum to hand him non-executive directorships in 15 companies and a merchant bank .
9511	It 's the same as knee-capping , and everybody knows it , but much kinder .
9512	Fundamentalists execrate someone for writing a book that they have n't read , and a famous novelist has to go into hiding for fear of his life .
9513	Well , at least he knew , right there and then , that he had to go into hiding .
9514	There is one thing in favour of total non-hypocrisy : at least you know where you stand , for as long as you are allowed to stand , and , of course , as long as you can be sure they are n't being a tiny bit hypocritical too .
9515	Can the call of the wild stop a highway ? .
9516	Tom Shakeshaft , who is 15 , reveals his dismay at plans to drive a dual carriageway right through the beautiful piece of countryside where he lives .
9517	OUR family lives in a cottage in Scarisbrick ( pronounced Scazebrick ) that is more than 100 years old .
9518	All the windows look out on fields .
9519	It is a magic place , and safe .
9520	There are skylarks and foxes and an owl sits in the apple tree staring at us by the fire in winter .
9521	Scarisbrick is the largest parish in Lancashire with more than 8,000 acres of Grade 1 agricultural land and flat , with copses and woods .
9522	The soil is rich , fertile and dark brown .
9523	We were very upset when we found out that a dual carriageway might be built in the fields past the wild duck pond behind our home .
9524	My sister Lucy is 18 .
9525	We 've lived here since she was a baby .
9526	There is also Laura , 17 , me , 15 , and William is 12 .
9527	William and I decided to write to Prince Charles because we know he loves the countryside .
9528	Mrs Thatcher cares about the environment so we sent her a letter too .
9529	A reply came thanking us for our letter and saying it is receiving attention .
9530	We think a bypass would rip the heart out of Scarisbrick , the village where we live and some farmers would be ruined .
9531	People all over the country eat vegetables grown in Scarisbrick .
9532	The air smells lovely , of leeks and straw and the breeze from the sea five miles away .
9533	Our MP Mr Ken Hind ( Conservative , West Lancs ) wrote to people in Scarisbrick saying that he has pushed the Department of Transport into accepting the need for a bypass between Ormskirk and Southport .
9534	Now it is in the government 's white paper .
9535	Hundreds of residents had a public meeting in the village hall to hear Ken Hind explain about the bypass .
9536	It will cost £10 million and could be 13 years before it 's built .
9537	But it 's in the white paper for road building throughout the country .
9538	We know the main A570 is a busy road and accidents happen and people who live there think a bypass is a good idea .
9539	It must be horrible for them when cars crash outside their homes .
9540	But not everyone here thinks the answer is to dig up the fields and destroy the character of the community .
9541	But the farmer down the lane is worried because he wanted his little lad , who is six , to be the fifth generation of the family to farm the moss land .
9542	He says it is some of the best land in the country , if not the world .
9543	William helps the farmer next to us and he is disappointed because he grows really good wheat and spuds and cabbages .
9544	He was saving the farm for his grandchildren .
9545	Our dad loves walking over the fields when he comes home tired from working in the city .
9546	It helps him relax .
9547	We go with him , and our sisters too , and sometimes a hare jumps out in front of us or a pheasant flies up from the ditch .
9548	We love it here because it is unspoiled and old fashioned .
9549	An old man called Mr Leatherbarrow used to grow prize-winning onions on the moss .
9550	He had a patch of land he ploughed with a hand plough and he told us stories about coming home across the fields in snowdrifts with carthorses .
9551	He had to carry a clothes prop to feel where the ditches where .
9552	Once a horse drowned on the moss .
9553	We bought our cottage from him .
9554	There 's a well in the garden .
9555	If a dual carriageway is built the fields will be just concrete and we 'll lie awake listening to cars zooming past and seeing flashing lights .
9556	We 'd like the people who want to build the bypass to visit the moss .
9557	If they were lucky enough to find a skylark 's nest they might not want to spoil the countryside for all of us .
9558	What future for Britain 's handicapped youth ?
9559	Michele Hanson examines the problems imposed by budget cuts and staff shortages , and looks at the need for long-term strategies .
9560	And in the light of the recent Beverley Lewis tragedy , Adrienne Baker puts the case for self-help groups to relieve the isolation and enormous pressure felt by the mothers of handicapped children A special kind of need
9561	THE 1970 Education Act opened a new world of opportunity for children with mental and physical handicaps .
9562	It declared them educable , took them out of their own homes and hospitals and brought them into full-time schooling .
9563	Bright new facilities and therapies were provided , plus enlightened teaching and special care .
9564	In 1970 in one London borough alone , Islington , nine severely or profoundly handicapped children were born .
9565	They have had the benefit of such an education and now it is over or about to end , together with almost all paramedical help .
9566	At 19 these young people — and hundreds like them all over the country — are likely to be going home and staying there .
9567	It means , as one parent said , ‘ 19 years of hard work down the drain ’ .
9568	Education is statutory , but once it is over such youngsters are legally entitled to nothing .
9569	The Disabled Persons Act 1986 recommends , but does not legislate , that local authorities should define need and provide for it .
9570	Adequate provision will probably not be made for Jonathan Rixon , one of the Islington children .
9571	He has Seckels Syndrome , a rare disease that stunts growth .
9572	He is microcephalic , blind , has severe curvature of the spine , scoliosis , no speech , can not walk and weighs 3 ½ stone .
9573	His knees frequently dislocate and he has a painful hiatus hernia which makes him scream .
9574	His mother Stephanie holds him , rubs him , talks to him , kisses him , stretches his body out over her knee — anything to relieve his discomfort .
9575	She must also change , bathe , feed , exercise , occupy , entertain and shave him .
9576	‘ It 's not hard work , ’ she says , ‘ just constant . ’
9577	When Jonathan leaves school next year , this will be the pattern of their life .
9578	Stephanie can not duplicate the essential therapies and stimulation the school provides .
9579	‘ What will happen to his small world when it all stops ? ’ she asks .
9580	‘ He 'll just have me . ’
9581	Doctors say Jonathan will have a normal life-span and she is worried for the future and what will happen to him after her death .
9582	There are community therapists , but not enough to go around .
9583	They are poorly paid , mainly young and female , have little chance of career progression and no incentive to remain in the profession .
9584	Those available will be busy rehabilitating stroke patients , who take priority .
9585	Fears that handicapped youngsters will deteriorate are well founded .
9586	Ian Squires , severely autistic , returned to Islington in 1986 from a residential school where he 'd been happy .
9587	He waited months for a day centre place ; when he got one it was unsuitable and he refused to go .
9588	He became very fearful of cars , buses and stairs , eventually shutting himself in his room , with the curtains drawn , for 14 months .
9589	He began banging his head against the wall , vomiting up his food , lost a great deal of weight and was eventually taken to hospital .
9590	Islington 's provision is better than most , yet the Director of Social Services , John Rea Price , feels Islington has been penalised for attempting to carry out the Government 's own directives on community care .
9591	Rate capping has meant that for every ‘ profligate ’ pound spent on such provision , £6 has been taken away .
9592	Islington can not even benefit from the ‘ dowry ’ system ( money paid by a health authority to a local authority for each patient returning to the community from hospital ) because their people never went to hospital .
9593	Many local authorities have had their budgets cut by reductions in central government They 've been given better education and higher expectations , but no future .
9594	grants and now have a far greater shortfall of places than Islington .
9595	A white paper is expected at the end of this month in response to the Griffiths Report , which recommended that authorities be given greater responsibility for the mentally handicapped .
9596	‘ Unless Griffiths funding comes quickly to the rescue , ’ says Rea Price , ‘ there is no hope of extra resources . ’
9597	A recent ( and the first ) report by the Social Services Inspectorate on day services for the mentally handicapped finds much to criticise .
9598	It admits that funds are needed for training and basic equipment , and finds that the principles of community care have often not been fully understood .
9599	Few middle management have direct experience of the service , need has not been quantified nor fed through to planners , very few local authorities have involved parents , let alone clients .
9600	Staff feel undervalued and lack any sense of direction , joint philosophies between health and local authorities are rare , there are no long-term strategies to solve the problems and many centres are overcrowded , offering only shared , part-time places .
9601	Centres for the physically handicapped have traditionally taken the elderly , and youngsters finding themselves there after leaving school may feel their adult lives have ended rather than just begun .
9602	Mencap 's Day Services campaign indicates that the most desperate need is for the severely handicapped and those with behavioural difficulties .
9603	For those with more moderate disabilities there are YTS schemes , but these are generalised , not geared to individual needs .
9604	The handicapped may be a minority group but it 's a vast one — the last count , 10 years ago , totalled six million people with identified disabilities .
9605	A hidden and forgotten problem rather than a small one .
9606	‘ We 're fighting a losing battle , ’ says Richard Tomlinson , headmaster of the Thomas Delarue School for young people with cerebral palsy .
9607	‘ It 's not a cohesive group and has no political edge .
9608	To get money you 've got to present an image of disability that reinforces rather than changes the stereotype — flaxen-haired moppets in callipers .
9609	If you actually show people in much greater need , young adults , they 're not so attractive .
9610	They might dribble .
9611	We 're articulate enough to fool ourselves that we 're nice people , but there 's a strong undercurrent to our thinking that encourages us to view people with a disability as lesser , and until we come to terms with that , we will never have a proper support system .
9612	At present the whole thing is on guilt money : ‘ I 'm glad it 's not my kids .
9613	Here 's a fiver . ’ '
9614	The present situation reinforces his ideas .
9615	‘ No social services or Government department will deny that everyone is of equal value , ’ says Mencap , ‘ but the services do n't support that .
9616	Even if people are unattractive , aggressive , distorted , vomit and bite , they still have rights . ’
9617	Things are , of course , better than they were .
9618	In a few areas great progress is being made .
9619	In Herefordshire , education , health , social services and voluntary groups are working together on a Lifestyles Project which enables students leaving college to have a life of their own within the community .
9620	The Spastics Society has begun Alternative Lifestyles courses for disabled school leavers , ‘ providing positive alternatives to paid employment and giving them the confidence to take charge of their own lives ’ .
9621	The Open University has begun a new course for people with learning difficulties .
9622	Hopefully such ideas will spread to the rest of the community , but for the majority of this year 's school leavers it will be too late .
9623	They 've been given a better education , a longer and healthier life and higher expectations , but no future .
9624	LACK of communication is one of the saddest aspects of having a mentally handicapped child .
9625	As a social worker , I met family after family and the isolation that having a ‘ special ’ child brings was a common theme .
9626	The burden inevitably fell mainly on the mothers and it seemed that their loneliness could at least be lessened if they had a regular opportunity to share their experiences .
9627	The group began with mothers responding to my invitation and deciding tentatively whether there was ‘ anything in it ’ for them .
9628	Several women felt too vulnerable or exposed to remain ; another left dramatically , announcing that her anger would destroy the group .
9629	The beginning was also a time when I was asked if I , too , would soon let them down ‘ like all the others ’ and when being there was expressed for all by Janet : ‘ I 'm only here because my daughter is the way she is .
9630	I 'd rather not be here . ’
9631	Or by Shirley , who cried soundlessly and then protested : ‘ I 'm not crying for myself ; I 'm crying for the others . ’
9632	Gradually trust developed and themes emerged : sadness , ‘ A grief with no end ’ ; anger , ‘ Why did it happen to me ? ’ ; and frustration with the professionals who could not fully understand their plight .
9633	The subjective experiences of these mothers became the maintheme ; for example , how rejected they felt by friends or neighbours who crossed the street , not knowing what to say .
9634	They talked of their husbands ' preoccupation with work , of their normal children 's too-early maturing , of integrated and special schools , and of eating — the hoped-for miracle diet for their child or , often , the consolation they found in food .
9635	These mothers had built a cocoon around themselves and their handicapped child which , while keeping away the hurtful comments , wrapped them in with their pain .
9636	Then , one week , the quietest woman in the group said : ‘ This is the only place where I can afford to be honest , ’ and somehow it seemed the healing process had begun .
9637	Leora personified the courage : I remember her trying to calm her screaming autistic son , taking him in her arms , rocking him , comforting him , until at last he became tranquil and quiet and she was left with his violence in her .
9638	THEY were brave women and often poetic .
9639	Zena , a sculptress , took on the responsibility of caring for her Down 's Syndrome grand-daughter when the mother ‘ upped and offed ’ .
9640	She described how she walked around for months ‘ with a pain , almost a physical pain , in my heart ’ ; of how she avoided friends and pulled her hat over her face if she met them in the street ; of how , at last , she knew she must express her thousand emotions about her little grandchild in the way she knew best , in clay .
9641	And when she took this most precious creation to art school , the teacher said : ‘ Zena , why did n't you tell us ? ’
9642	Then she could cry and let people comfort her .
9643	Jean described a trip to the park .
9644	While she queued for coffee , her friend held the handicapped child and Jean ‘ made believe she was n't mine . ’
9645	The sadness came out week by week and we confronted it .
9646	Incredibly , there was laughter , too , and companionship .
9647	We gained energy from each other and I determined that this strength must be used creatively .
9648	Their frustration that they would always remain only a mummy could be challenged .
9649	We considered how much we , ourselves , hold on to an eternally-caring-for-others role .
9650	Stirrings of feminist vitality .
9651	I wanted to help these women to ‘ find a voice ’ and no longer to place their needs at the bottom of the list of priorities .
9652	Gradually we re-evaluated ourselves as women and looked at the way we had always put ourselves down .
9653	One member had described the work she does as ‘ just a little job ’ .
9654	The rabbi 's wife had insisted it was her role to attend to their epileptic daughter several times each night ; her husband must sleep to be strong for the community .
9655	But there was change in the air : one woman began to study and others took their cue from her .
9656	I encouraged them to write .
9657	Together we compiled an article for publication .
9658	It was raw , frank and eventually it appeared in print .
9659	By now the time had come for me to hand back to these women responsibility to go it alone .
9660	I knew that telling them would be hard but nothing prepared me for their anger and grief during our final month together .
9661	‘ Was our sadness too much for you to bear ? ’ asked an Iranian woman .
9662	‘ I too , would like the luxury of resigning , ’ asserted another .
9663	My leaving them was similar to their having to let go of their children .
9664	My task had been to help these women to realise their own strengths and to speak out for themselves with courage and dignity .

9666	Lunchtime sessions that pay dividends London 's local authorities are enjoying a thaw in relations with the Commissioner .
9667	EVERY six months , the Labour council leaders represented in the Association of London Authorities get together for beer and sandwiches with Sir Peter Imbert .
9668	Alternately , the Commissioner and his most senior colleagues invite them to Scotland Yard , or visit them at the ALA building nearby .
9669	According to Walter Easey , the ALA police policy advisor , ‘ under Sir Kenneth Newman , this would have been quite impossible .
9670	We do n't make a big public fuss but he answers our questions , and we answer his .
9671	We try to keep it low temperature .
9672	It 's a very good regular basis for discussing things . ’
9673	The meetings are only the most visible signs of a thaw in the relationship — previously something close to undeclared war — between the Yard and the Labour authorities since Sir Peter 's accession in 1987 .
9674	It affects relations at all levels .
9675	Sir Kenneth , for example , set up multi-agency panels to deal with the cautioning of juveniles , designed to keep as many as possible out of the courts .
9676	But in many boroughs , Mr Easey said , ‘ we began to find that whatever we said , they 'd go ahead and charge them anyway ’ .
9677	Several boroughs withdrew as a result .
9678	The police attitude now , many councils have found , is more receptive , and the panels have been reconstituted .
9679	Authorities have begun to find that multi-agency cooperation in other fields — notably racial violence — need not be a mask for police interference .
9680	The recent attempt by Clive Pearman , the chief superintendent in charge of Notting Hill , to persuade the two local councils to cut off funds to voluntary orgnanisations which he considered inimical was an example of an approach whose shortcomings have come to be appreciated at the Yard .
9681	The ALA has had a major influence in redesigning the police recruitment forms , which have gone through three drafts since the Met tried to interest Labour councils in their campaign to attract more ethnic minority officers .
9682	The concept of indirect discrimination was , according to the councils , at first unfamiliar to police , who also saw no reason why black candidates might be put off by the former question three — which asked the country of origin of spouse or lover 's parents .
9683	These difficulties having been resolved , several former so-called ‘ loony-left ’ councils have mounted police recruitment exhibitions and meetings .
9684	In part , the emerging entente must be attributed to the authorities ' move to the right , towards the Kinnockite orthodoxy favoured by Margaret Hodge , the Islington and ALA leader .
9685	But the Met has shown itself increasingly willing to respond to overtures , for example instituting procedures to check criminal records of applicant child-care workers and foster parents for sex offences .
9686	Camden and Islington councils , meanwhile , have given the Met a free copy of LAFIS — a computer programme which they developed at a cost of £15 million , and sold to other authorities for about £2 million a throw .
9687	It is now being adapted to give the Met its first method for running cost accounting in 150 years .
9688	Five of the 13 Labour authorities still refuse to participate in local consultative groups , although Brent is about to reverse its policy and in Ealing the matter is under discussion .
9689	But as the Labour parliamentary front bench scents the thaw , and surveys the possibility of government for the first time in a decade , the party pressures running in favour of detente are increasing .
